telling-materials-apart.title: Telling Materials Apart
telling-materials-apart.context_blurb:
Picture a table of mystery things: a grey rock, a white powder, a shiny metal ball, a scrap of wool. How can you tell what each one is made of? You test its properties, the things about a material that you can see, measure or try. Each test tells you one thing, and together the tests tell even look-alikes apart.

Start with mass. A thing's mass is the amount of matter in it, and matter is the stuff that everything is made of. A balance finds mass by comparing the thing with masses already known. Volume, the space a thing takes up, is a different property, so a bigger thing does not always have more mass than a smaller one. Mass cannot name a rock either: a big chunk and a small chip of one rock have very different masses.

A ruler is no help for the volume of a bumpy rock, since it measures only a length. Use water instead, in a graduated cylinder, a tall tube marked in millilitres. Sink the rock and see how far the water rises, because a sunk rock pushes aside its own volume of water. A rise from 50 to 65 millilitres means the rock's volume is 15 millilitres.

Many people think heavy things sink and light things float, but weight alone does not decide it. A thing floats or sinks because of how heavy it is for its size, compared with water. A huge pine log floats, because pine is lighter for its size than water. Even a tiny pebble sinks, because stone is more than twice as heavy for its size as water.

A magnet is a quick test for metal. A magnet pulls hard on iron, and also on most steel, which is mostly iron. Most other metals, aluminium among them, are not pulled, even when they shine just like iron. Recycling centres use big magnets to lift steel cans out of the rubbish.

Salt and fine white sand are both little white grains. To tell salt from sand, stir a pinch of each into water: the salt dissolves and seems to vanish, while the sand does not dissolve and only settles to the bottom. A magnet would not help here, because it pulls on neither one.

Heat always flows from a warmer thing to a cooler one, and cold never flows at all. Metal is a good conductor of heat: heat passes through it easily. Wood, wool and still air are insulators, which slow heat down. After a frosty night, a bench's metal arms and wooden seat are at the same temperature, yet the metal seems much colder. The metal feels colder because it draws heat from a hand much faster than wood does, and the hand feels that quick loss of heat as cold.

A wool hat uses the same rule. Wool traps still air among its fibres. So on a cold evening, a wool hat slows the heat leaving a warm head for the cool air around it. The warmth is the wearer's own, for a hat is no heater: a thermometer tucked inside a hat lying on a table reads no warmer than the room.

To test for electricity, join a battery and a bulb with wires, leaving a gap between two bare ends. Touch the ends to a thing, and the bulb glows only if electricity can flow through it. Metals such as steel and aluminium are conductors that let electricity flow, so a steel paper clip lights the bulb. Rubber, plastic and glass are insulators that stop electricity, which is why wires wear a plastic coat.

Hardness is tested by scratching, for a harder material scratches a softer one, never the other way round. So if a fingernail leaves a mineral unmarked but a steel knife scratches it, the mineral is harder than a fingernail and softer than steel. Geologists rank minerals this way, from soft talc up to diamond, which scratches every other mineral. The test even unmasks fool's gold: pyrite has the colour and shine of gold, but it is far harder than soft real gold.

solids-liquids-and-gases.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
solids-liquids-and-gases.context_blurb:
Everything around you is a solid, a liquid or a gas: the three common states of matter. A rock is a solid, the sea is a liquid, and the air is a gas. Water can be all three: ice, liquid water, and a gas called water vapour. Adding heat or taking it away moves a material from one state to another.

A thing's volume is the amount of space it takes up. A solid has its own shape and its own volume, so a quartz crystal looks just the same in a box or a jar. A liquid keeps its volume, but it takes the shape of whatever holds it: a litre of seawater is still a litre in a jug or a bucket. A gas spreads out to fill any container, and it can be squeezed into a small space, the way air is packed into a diver's tank. Seawater and air both take the shape of what holds them, but only the seawater keeps its own volume.

Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, and ice melts at that same temperature. In a mix of ice and water, the heat that flows in goes into melting the ice, so the mix stays at 0 degrees Celsius until all the ice is gone. On the Fahrenheit scale, that temperature is 32 degrees. At sea level, pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, which is 212 degrees on the Fahrenheit scale. Once it boils, more heat turns more water into vapour but makes it no hotter. High on a mountain, where the air pressure is lower, water boils below 100 degrees.

Every material melts at its own temperature. Iron melts only at about 1,538 degrees Celsius, but the soft, silvery metal gallium melts at about 30, cooler than your skin. In a warm palm, a lump of gallium slowly becomes a shiny puddle. Heat flows from the warm hand into the cooler metal, and a solid that takes in enough heat melts. No cold flows out of the metal, for cold never flows at all.

Freezing means a liquid turning into a solid as it loses heat, and it does not have to be cold. Lava is melted rock that bursts from a volcano hotter than a thousand degrees. As lava loses heat, it hardens into solid rock such as basalt while still hundreds of degrees hot, and that change is freezing too. Melting is the opposite change, from solid to liquid.

Water vapour is invisible, and the air around us holds some of it. When vapour cools, some of it condenses, turning back into tiny drops of liquid water. Watch for it on a chilly morning. When warm, damp breath meets cold air, some of its vapour condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, and those drops make the white puff you see. The puff is not ice, for a fog of ice crystals needs air far colder, about 35 degrees below zero.

The same thing happens on a cold jar of ice. Even with the lid screwed on tight, drops of water soon bead on the outside of the glass. The drops come from the water vapour in the air around the jar: when that air touches the cold glass it cools, and some of its vapour condenses into drops. None of the water comes from inside, for glass lets no water through.

When water boils hard, bubbles of vapour form all through it, not just at the top. The big bubbles that rise and burst are water vapour, which is water in the form of a gas. Boiling makes no new substance: cool the vapour, and it turns back into liquid water. The tiny bubbles that show up as water first warms are something else. They are air that had dissolved in the water.

matter-made-of-tiny-particles.title: Matter Made of Tiny Particles
matter-made-of-tiny-particles.context_blurb:
A rock, a puddle, the air and your own hand look nothing alike. Yet every one of them is built from particles far too small to see. Nobody can see these particles, but you can test for them with a ball, a syringe or a dish of seawater. The tests show that even things you cannot see, like air, are real stuff.

Scientists call that stuff matter. Matter is anything that has mass and fills up space. Air, steam and smoke all have mass and take up room, so all three are matter, even though they are hard to see or hold. Sunlight has no mass, so a beam of sunlight is not matter: light, like heat and sound, is a form of energy.

All ordinary matter, from the air to rocks, seawater and your body, is made of tiny particles called atoms. Your body is also built of living cells, but cells are not the smallest bits: every cell is itself made of atoms, and so are the crystals in a rock.

Atoms are tiny beyond belief: a single human hair is about a million atoms wide. Even a hard steel nail is made of particles far too small to see, packed so close that the nail looks like one smooth piece. Not even the strongest school microscope can show them, and there is no air in the tiny gaps between them.

How do we know air is matter? Weigh it. Weigh a basketball while it is flat, then pump it up and weigh it again. The full ball weighs a little more, because air has weight, and the pump has squeezed extra air inside. Many people think air weighs nothing, but the scale says otherwise.

Air takes up space, too. Press a thumb hard over the tip of a syringe that seems empty, then push the plunger. It goes in a little way, then will go no farther. The syringe was full of air all along, and the air trapped inside it, squeezed into less space, pushes back on the plunger. Lift the thumb, and the plunger slides all the way in as the air rushes out. Nothing was stuck: the trapped air did the pushing.

Particles can travel, too. You can smell a rose from across a room before your eyes even find it. The scent of roses is made of tiny particles that come off the roses and drift through the air into your nose. The air itself does not turn smelly: the scent's particles just mix in among the air's, too small to see but still matter.

Stir some salt into water, and soon it is gone from sight, while the water stays clear. The salt has broken up into particles far too small to see, and they have spread all through the water. It has not melted, since salt melts only when heated to about 800 degrees Celsius. The salt is still there: the water tastes of it, and the salt comes back when the water dries up.

Seawater shows the same thing in reverse. It looks clear, yet it holds salt in bits too small to see. Leave some in a shallow dish in the sun, and the water slowly rises into the air as water vapour. The salt cannot rise with the water, so it is left in the dish as white crystals. Salt-makers dry seawater in shallow ponds in just this way.

mixtures-and-solutions.title: Mixtures and Solutions
mixtures-and-solutions.context_blurb:
Pour a bag of trail mix into a bowl. The nuts, raisins and chocolate drops get jumbled together, yet each piece is still itself, and you could pick them apart by hand. That is a mixture. Beach sand, muddy water and the salty sea are mixtures too, and each one can be taken apart again.

In a mixture nothing new is made, so each substance keeps its own properties. Iron filings stirred into pale sand are still iron. Pass a magnet over the dish, and the iron filings jump up and cling to it, while the sand stays put. Pale sand is mostly quartz, a mineral that magnets do not pull.

A sieve is a screen full of holes: grains smaller than the holes fall through, and bigger ones stay behind. So a sieve sorts grains by their size alone. A small grain drops through, heavy or light. Geologists, who study rocks, shake sand through a stack of sieves with the biggest holes on top, so each sieve lower down holds finer sand.

Some bits are too small for any sieve. Stir sand and a pinch of salt into water, and the salt dissolves, breaking into bits far too small to see. Pour it through filter paper in a funnel, and the salt bits slip through the paper's tiny holes with the water. The sand grains are too big, so only the sand is caught on the paper. To get the salt back, let the water dry away.

Salt water is a solution: a mixture that is the same all the way through. Its dissolved bits spread evenly and are too small ever to settle. Copper sulfate, a poisonous lab chemical, has bright blue crystals that dissolve and turn water blue. Seal some in a flask for a month, and the colour never sinks. A drop from the top and a drop from the bottom are the same shade of blue, because a solution is the same in every part. Sand stirred into water is different: its grains sink to the bottom.

Salt water also freezes differently. Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, but salt water must get colder first, and the saltier it is, the colder it must get. Water that is 8 percent salt freezes only at about minus 5 degrees. So road crews scatter rock salt on icy roads. It dissolves into the wet film on the ice, the salt water it makes stays liquid, and the ice it touches melts into slush. Salt lowers the temperature water freezes at; it does not heat the ice.

Does dissolved salt really vanish? A balance can tell. Weigh the water, the salt and its dish together, then stir the salt in until it can't be seen and weigh everything again. The balance shows the same mass as before, because the salt is still in the water in bits too small to see, and those bits still have mass. So 150 grams of water and 10 grams of salt make 160 grams of salt water.

Freezing keeps mass too. Cap a bottle of water, mark the water line, weigh it and freeze it overnight. The ice weighs just what the water did, but it stands above the mark. Water swells by about 9 percent as it freezes, so its volume, the space it takes up, grows while its mass stays the same. That is why ice floats: it takes up more room for its mass than water does.

Some changes do make something new. An iron nail left out in the rain for a few weeks grows a crust of reddish-brown rust. That rust is a new substance made from the iron. The iron has joined with oxygen from the air, helped by water, and rust is crumbly and weak because it is not iron any more. Rust is not just iron with a new colour, and no drying or picking apart turns it back into iron.

pushes-pulls-and-gravity.title: Pushes, Pulls and Gravity
pushes-pulls-and-gravity.context_blurb:
Every time you kick a ball, open a door or tug on a sock, you use a force. Forces start things moving, speed them up, slow them down, turn them and stop them. One force works without touching you and never lets go: gravity, the pull that holds you to the ground.

A force is a push or a pull that one thing gives another. The wind pushes a beach ball along the sand, and a fence pushes back to stop it. A force is not energy or motion, and no object carries a store of force inside it.

Every force points a certain way, and a push moves a thing the way the push points. Picture a hockey puck gliding north across the ice. To make it swerve west, a player must tap it on its east side, so that his stick pushes it toward the west. A tap from behind would only speed it up.

In a tug-of-war, two teams haul on one rope in opposite directions. While their pulls are equal, the forces are balanced, and balanced forces do not change how a thing moves, however hard or long both teams pull. The rope starts to move only when one team pulls harder than the other. Then the forces are unbalanced, and the rope slides toward the stronger team.

Kick a ball across a grassy field, and it slows bit by bit until it comes to rest. It has not run out of force: a kick is a push that ends when the foot leaves the ball. What slows the ball and stops it is friction pushing against its motion. Friction is a rubbing force between two surfaces, here the grass and the ball, and the air pushes back on the ball too.

Rough surfaces make more friction than smooth ones. Roll a toy car down a ramp onto smooth, bare wood, and it coasts a long way. Send it down onto a deep, shaggy carpet, and the thick fibres drag on its wheels. The car's run is shorter on the carpet, which makes more friction. Nothing pushes the car along once it leaves the ramp, so the carpet's grip can only slow it.

Friction can also keep a thing from starting to move. A boy can push a heavy crate with all his might and not shift it, yet his push is still a force. The floor pushes back on the crate just as hard, through friction, so the two forces are balanced and the crate stays still. A harder push, or a few friends pushing with him, would get it sliding.

Earth's gravity pulls every object toward the middle of the planet, so down always means toward Earth's centre, wherever you stand. People live all over the round Earth, even on the part a globe shows hanging upside down. Those people never fall off into space, because a pull toward Earth's centre holds them to the ground, just as it holds you.

Gravity keeps pulling when a thing sits still, too. A book that has sat on a shelf for a year is pulled down just as hard as if it were falling. It stays put only because the shelf pushes up on it just as hard, so the forces balance.

When nothing holds a thing up, gravity's pull is unbalanced, and an unbalanced force keeps changing a thing's speed. Drop a rock off a tall ladder, and it speeds up all the way down. Every second it falls, it goes almost 10 metres per second faster. The air holds back a rock only a little, but it soon stops leaves and snowflakes from gaining speed, so they drift down gently.

energy-changes-form.title: Energy Changes Form
energy-changes-form.context_blurb:
Flip on a flashlight, and something stored in its battery comes out as a beam of light. That something is energy. Energy lights rooms, spins fans and plays music, and it can change from one form into another again and again. Follow the energy through a machine, and you can see how the machine works.

Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. Whatever moves something, warms it, lights it up or makes it sound is using energy. Scientists sort it into forms: chemical, electrical, mechanical, light, heat and sound. A force is a different thing, only a push or a pull. Fuel is not energy either: wood and coal are stuff that stores energy.

Chemical energy is energy stored in substances, and food is full of it. A sandwich in your lunch box holds chemical energy, and your body releases it to move and to keep warm. Wood, coal and gasoline store chemical energy too, and so does a battery. A new battery lying unused in a drawer keeps its energy as chemical energy, in the substances packed inside it. Many people think a battery is full of electricity, but it makes electricity only when it is put to work.

A flashlight shows energy changing form. When the switch goes on, the battery's chemical energy becomes electrical energy, which flows through the wires to the bulb. The bulb turns that energy into light and heat. Every bulb warms up. An old-style bulb glows by heating a thin wire, and most of its energy comes out as heat. Hold a hand near one (never on it), and you can feel the warmth. A modern LED bulb wastes far less, but it still gets warm. None of the energy flows back to fill the battery up again.

Anything that moves has mechanical energy, the energy of motion. Inside a fan, an electric motor changes electrical energy into motion, and the motion spins the blades. A generator does the reverse: spin it, and it makes electrical energy. Big dams send water plunging through pipes to spin giant bladed wheels called turbines. It is the rushing water's mechanical energy that turns the turbines. The water itself holds no electricity. The turbines drive generators, and those make the electrical energy that reaches our homes.

A phone's speaker turns electrical energy into sound. A thin cone or sheet inside it shakes back and forth very fast, and that shaking makes the sound you hear. Rest a fingertip lightly on a speaker playing loud music, and you can feel it shake. The microphone does the opposite job, changing your own voice into an electrical signal.

A solar panel changes light into electrical energy, straight from sunlight, with no heating step in between. Many people guess that panels run on the Sun's heat, but heat does not help them. A hot panel works a little worse, and a cold, bright day suits it well.

Wind and coal both carry energy. The wind gets its energy from the Sun, which warms some parts of Earth's surface more than others, and that uneven heating sets the air moving. Coal formed long ago from ancient plants, and those plants had stored energy from sunlight. So if you trace the energy in wind and coal back far enough, nearly all of it began in the Sun. Earth's own inner heat is a real source of energy too, but it is tiny beside the Sun's.

electric-circuits.title: Electric Circuits
electric-circuits.context_blurb:
Flip a switch, and a lamp lights at once. Electricity reaches it through wires, but only along a path that runs all the way round and back again, like a toy train on a closed loop of track. Learn how that path works, and you can explain a flashlight or a doorbell, and stay safe near electricity.

Electricity flows only round a complete loop with no gaps. It leaves one end of a battery, runs along a wire and through a bulb, then comes home along another wire to the battery's other end. That whole path, out and back, is called a circuit. The electricity moving round it is the current, and copper wire is a conductor, a material that lets electricity flow. Every circuit also needs a battery, or some other source of energy, to push the electricity round. The wires only give it a path, so a buzzer in a perfect loop of copper wire stays silent until a battery joins the loop.

Try a puzzle with one battery, one bulb and one wire. Join the battery's top to the bulb's metal base with the wire, and let nothing else touch. The bulb stays dark. The electricity has no path back to the battery, so none flows at all. Nothing gets used up, and no switch is needed to start it. Now keep the wire on the side of the bulb's base and press the tip of the base against the battery's bottom end. The loop is complete, and the bulb lights.

A switch is a gate in the loop. Switch a flashlight on, and two metal parts inside the switch touch: metal touching metal closes the circuit, so electricity can cross. Switch it off, and the parts move apart, leaving a gap: the circuit is open, and nothing flows. These words run opposite to a door's. An open door lets people through, but an open switch lets no electricity through.

A gap anywhere in a single loop stops the electricity all the way round. Suppose the wire running back from a glowing bulb slips off the battery. The bulb goes out at once, even though the gap is after the bulb. No electricity waits in the wire to keep it glowing. That is also why a switch works wherever it sits in the loop.

The metal inside a lamp's cord, and in the wiring hidden in a house's walls, is copper. Copper carries electricity better than every metal except silver, which costs many times as much, and copper bends round corners without cracking. Around the copper is a coat of plastic. Plastic is an insulator, a material that does not let electricity pass. The coat keeps the current inside the metal and away from a person's hand on the cord. A cord with cracked plastic and bare wire showing is dangerous to touch.

Metals are not the only conductors. Tap water is not pure: it carries dissolved minerals. Those minerals let tap water pass electricity through it, though perfectly pure water barely lets any through. Water makes no electricity of its own, but it carries any that reaches it. So keep anything with a plug away from a bath, a sink or a pool, and dry wet hands before you touch a switch.

The same rule explains birds on power lines. The thick lines strung between tall towers are bare metal, with no plastic coat. A small bird perched on a single line touches nothing else, so the electricity has no path through its body, and almost none flows through it. But if a big bird's wings or feet touch two lines at once, its body completes a loop between them, like a bulb set between a battery's two ends, and electricity rushes through it. Touching a line and a tower at once is just as dangerous.

how-light-travels.title: How Light Travels
how-light-travels.context_blurb:
Switch on a flashlight in a dark room, and a beam shoots across to the far wall. Light is always on the move. It bounces off things, bends as it passes into water or glass, and gets soaked up by dark things. Everything you see, you see by light.

Light travels in straight lines, and it never curves round a corner on its own. Test it with a flashlight and three cards. Punch a small hole in each card and stand them one behind another between a wall and the flashlight, with all three holes lined up. A bright dot appears on the wall. Nudge the middle card a little to one side, and the dot disappears from the wall. No straight path runs through all three holes any more, and light cannot bend round the card.

Straight lines explain shadows too. A cardboard cat held in a lamp's beam blocks the light that hits it, while the light just missing its edges flies straight on to the wall. A shadow has the same shape as the thing that casts it, because light travels in straight lines. It is simply a place the light cannot reach.

The Sun and a lamp give out their own light, but most things give out none. A chair or a book is seen only because light bounces off it, and some of that light travels straight into your eyes. Your eyes send out no light; they only take it in. In a room with no light at all, you would see nothing.

Light that bounces off a thing is reflected, and nearly everything reflects some light, not just shiny things. A mirror is so smooth that it sends light back in neat order, so you see a sharp image in it. White paper is rough on a tiny scale, covered in bumps too small to see. Paper reflects plenty of light, but its bumps bounce that light off in every direction, so no picture forms. That scattered light is how you see paper, and almost everything else.

Light can bend, too. It travels more slowly in water and glass than in air, so it changes direction as it passes from one into another. This bending is called refraction. A straw in a glass of water, seen from the side, seems to snap in two where it enters the water. Light from its underwater part bends as it goes from water into air on its way to your eye, which shifts where that part seems to be. Lift the straw out, and it is perfectly straight. A lens is a piece of curved glass that bends light by refraction, and a magnifying glass is one: a small beetle seen through it looks bigger than it is.

Sunlight looks white, yet it is a mix of many colours. A prism, a block of clear glass with slanting sides, bends each colour by a different amount, so it spreads sunlight into a band of colours from red to violet. Isaac Newton turned a second prism the other way, and it gathered the colours back into white light: they had been in the sunlight all along, not added by the glass. Red, yellow and blue are only the painters' colours for mixing paint; sunlight holds every colour from red to violet.

Light can also be soaked up, or absorbed, and absorbed light turns into heat. Dark things absorb most of the light that falls on them, while white things reflect more of it away. So on a sunny day, a black T-shirt grows warmer than a white one, because it absorbs more of the sunlight. The air around both is just as warm. Lay a black cloth and a white one in the sun for an hour, then feel the difference for yourself.

how-plants-make-food.title: How Plants Make Food
how-plants-make-food.context_blurb:
Look at a tree, a lawn or a pot of basil on a windowsill. Not one of them ever eats. Green plants make their own food instead, right in their leaves, with the help of sunlight. The energy in your lunch began this way too, caught from the Sun by a plant.

A plant's way of making its own food from water and air, powered by sunlight, is called photosynthesis. The word comes from Greek: photo means light, and synthesis means putting together, so photosynthesis is putting together with light. A photograph is named for the same Greek word, because it is a drawing made with light.

A plant needs three things to make its food. Sunlight gives the energy. Water comes up through the roots. From the air, the plant takes in carbon dioxide, a gas that makes up only a tiny part of the air. Plants take in some oxygen too, but they use it to break their food down for energy, not to make it. Inside the leaf, the plant uses the light's energy to build sugar out of the water and carbon dioxide, and that sugar is its food. The sugar feeds every part of the plant, and any spare is stored as starch, a plant's packed-away food.

Leaves are the plant's food factories, because a plant can make food only where light reaches its green parts. Think of a potato plant. The potatoes sit underground, stuffed with food, but they did not make it, for no light reaches them down in the dark soil, and none reaches the roots either. The leaves above ground make sugar in the sunlight, and it travels down the plant to the potatoes, where it is stored as starch.

You can watch a plant making food. Set a sprig of pondweed in a jar of water in bright sunshine, and tiny bubbles soon gather on its leaves and drift upward. As the pondweed makes its food, its leaves give off oxygen, and the oxygen rises in the bubbles. Carry the jar into the dark, and the bubbles soon stop. The oxygen that plants give off is the same oxygen people and animals breathe.

Now for the biggest surprise. A little acorn can become an enormous oak, so where does all that wood come from? Many people guess the soil, but the soil gives a tree only small amounts of minerals. A tree builds its wood mostly out of air and water: carbon dioxide from the air, and water from the ground. Sunlight supplies the energy for the building, but none of the stuff itself. About four hundred years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont planted a small willow in a pot holding 200 pounds of dried soil and gave it nothing but water for five years. The willow gained over 160 pounds, yet the soil lost only about two ounces. He thought the water had built it all, and never guessed how much came from the air.

The Sun's energy does not stop at the plant. As grass makes its food, it catches energy from sunlight and stores that energy in its sugar. A cow grazing in a field takes that energy in, and it lets her move about and stay warm. The soil, the rain and the air give the grass things to build with, but no energy at all. So the cow runs on energy that was once the Sun's light, and so do you.

roots-stems-leaves-and-flowers.title: Roots, Stems, Leaves and Flowers
roots-stems-leaves-and-flowers.context_blurb:
Snap a celery stick or sniff a rose, and you are handling the parts of a plant. A flowering plant works like a team. Its roots work underground, its stem holds it up, its leaves catch light, and its flowers make seeds. Together, the parts keep the plant alive and start new plants.

Roots grip the soil so the plant stays put. Roots also take in water and minerals from the soil, soaking them up like a sponge. Tiny hairs near each root's tip give it a far bigger surface for drinking. Minerals are not food, though. Roots live in the dark, and a plant makes its food up in its leaves, where light reaches.

A stem holds the leaves up toward the light. Inside it run bundles of tiny tubes. One set of tubes, called xylem, carries water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves and flowers. A second set, called phloem, carries sugar made in the leaves to the rest of the plant. Stand a white carnation in water tinted with blue food dye, and by the next day its petals show blue streaks, because the dyed water climbed up through the xylem.

To make food, a leaf needs carbon dioxide, a gas from the air. Under a microscope, a leaf's underside shows tiny holes called stomata, from the Greek word for mouths. Two bean-shaped cells sit around each hole like a pair of lips, opening it or pressing it shut. Gases pass through the stomata: carbon dioxide comes in, while oxygen and water vapour go out. Light needs no hole, because it shines straight through the leaf's clear skin.

Flowers are the parts that make seeds. Bright petals, sweet scents and nectar draw in visitors. When a bee sips nectar, a fine powder called pollen sticks to its fuzzy body, and some of it brushes off on another flower of its kind. Carrying pollen to a flower of the same kind is called pollination, and it must happen before seeds can form. Butterflies, birds, bats and the wind carry pollen too. Spreading the seeds is a different job that comes later.

After pollination, part of the flower grows into a fruit around the new seeds. To a scientist, a fruit is any part that grows from a flower and holds seeds, so an acorn, with its seed inside a hard shell, is the fruit of an oak. Acorns and maple helicopters are not sweet, but both grew from flowers. A pine cone holds seeds too, yet pines have no flowers, so a cone is not a fruit.

A fruit also helps its seeds travel, so they need not fight the parent plant for water and light. Dandelion seeds float off on fluffy parachutes, and hooked burrs catch in animals' fur. A coconut goes to sea: its husk is full of air pockets, so it floats, and ocean currents carry it to far shores while the seed inside stays alive for months. Animals eat the sweet flesh of berries and spread the seeds, which pass through them unharmed and drop out in their droppings, often far away. The sweet flesh is there to tempt the animals, not to feed the parent plant.

Every seed holds a tiny young plant, a store of food and a tough skin, the seed coat. Soak a dry bean overnight and peel it, and it splits into two fat halves around a tiny plant. These halves are the bean's seed leaves, packed with food that the parent plant stored there. They feed the young plant as it starts to grow, until its own leaves can make food in the light.

To watch a seed sprout, wrap a bean in a wet paper towel inside a glass jar. Within a few days the bean swells and its coat splits. The young root comes out first and grows down, ready to anchor the seedling and drink in water. Only then does the shoot, the young stem with its first leaves, climb toward the light.

food-chains-and-food-webs.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
food-chains-and-food-webs.context_blurb:
Every living thing needs food, and nearly every living thing is food for something else. Grass feeds a rabbit, and the rabbit feeds a fox. Follow these links through a meadow, a pond or the open sea, and you find that they tie everything together, so a change to one member is felt by many others.

Every food chain starts with a producer, a living thing that makes its own food. Green plants and algae are producers, powered by the Sun's light. Even the moss on a forest rock is a producer, because moss is a small green plant, and like other plants it makes its own food from sunlight. A mushroom may look like a plant, but it is a fungus. It cannot make food, so it feeds on dead wood and leaves, as one of the decomposers. Animals such as snails and beetles are consumers: they must eat other living things.

Consumers are named for what they eat. A herbivore is a plant-eater, and a wild rabbit is a true one, living on grass, leaves, bark and twigs and nothing else. Deer and most caterpillars are herbivores too. A carnivore eats other animals. In a field, grasshoppers eat grass, frogs eat grasshoppers, and snakes eat frogs. Both the frog and the snake are carnivores, because both eat animals. It does not matter that the frog is eaten in its turn. The grasshopper eats plants, so it is a herbivore.

An omnivore eats both plants and animals, as bears and people do. In a forest where mice eat seeds and also caterpillars, the mice are omnivores, since seeds come from plants and caterpillars are animals. There, the deer and caterpillars eat only plants, and the owls eat only animals.

On paper, a food chain is a line of living things joined by arrows: grass → rabbit → fox. Each arrow points toward the living thing that eats, showing which way the food's energy travels. Many students draw the arrows backwards, so read each one as "is eaten by". The eater is not always bigger, either: a wolf pack can bring down a moose several times heavier than any one wolf.

A real pond is messier than one chain, because few animals stick to one kind of food. Frogs snap up many kinds of insects, and both snakes and herons hunt frogs. All the food chains of one place, joined where they overlap, make up a food web. Overlapping chains form a web, not one longer chain.

In a web, a change to one member spreads far. Picture a marsh where herons hunt frogs, and frogs eat the insects that chew the plants. Then a sickness wipes out nearly all the frogs. With the frogs gone, hardly anything eats the insects, so the insects multiply and there are more insects than before. They eat more of the plants, and the herons, short of food, dwindle.

The links pull both ways. If far more rabbits than usual are born in a meadow one spring, they eat the grass faster than it can grow back, so less of it is left. Grass makes its own food and regrows, but not fast enough for so many hungry mouths.

Far out at sea, where the water is miles deep, light reaches only the top part, so producers must live near the surface. Most of the ocean's producers are tiny floating algae called phytoplankton, each too small to see on its own, drifting in the sunlit water. Tiny drifting animals, which are consumers, graze on them. No seaweed grows on the dark seabed miles down, and the few floating seaweed mats make only a small share of the ocean's food.

decomposers-and-recycling-matter.title: Decomposers and Recycling Matter
decomposers-and-recycling-matter.context_blurb:
Every autumn, forests drop great piles of leaves, and every day plants and animals die. Yet the world is not buried in dead things. Living things called decomposers break dead matter down. They are nature's recyclers, handing the stuff of dead things back to the soil and the air for new life to use again.

Rotting does not happen by itself. An apple lying in the grass turns brown and shrinks because tiny living things, mostly bacteria and moulds too small to see, are feeding on it and breaking it down. Worms and insects help. Rain, wind and sunshine cannot rot an apple alone, and neither can old age: an apple sealed away from every living thing would never rot.

Decomposers do this to feed themselves. Moulds and mushrooms are fungi. A fungus pours digestive juices onto dead matter, then soaks up the softened food. Earthworms, woodlice and millipedes chew dead leaves into bits, which speeds up the bacteria and fungi. An earthworm swallows soil and dead plants as it tunnels. The worm's droppings, called castings, are richer in nitrogen and phosphorus than the soil around them, so the droppings make the soil richer for plants. Its tunnels let in air and water, too.

Bigger animals help with dead bodies. Vultures, burying beetles and carrion beetles soon gather at a dead deer. Animals that eat dead animals they did not kill are called scavengers. By eating a body, scavengers help it break down far sooner.

Decomposers need water and warmth, so they work fastest where it is warm and wet. On a warm, damp forest floor, such as a rainforest's, a fallen leaf can be gone within a year or two, far sooner than on a cooler forest floor. Heat alone is not enough: in a dry desert the decomposers lack water, and cold slows them too.

Gardeners put decomposers to work in a compost heap of peels, grass clippings and dry leaves, kept as damp as a wrung-out sponge. After a few days, a thermometer pushed into the middle shows the heap is hot. The heat comes from bacteria and fungi breaking the scraps down: as they feed, they give off heat, enough to warm the heap's centre to 55 to 70 degrees Celsius.

When something rots, its matter does not vanish. A rotting pumpkin's matter goes into the air and the soil. Decomposers turn it into carbon dioxide gas and water, which drift into the air, and into minerals, which stay in the soil. None of it is destroyed or turned into energy. A rotting pumpkin sealed in a jar would weigh the same at the end as at the start. Plants then take that matter up and use it again.

Under the fresh leaves of a forest floor lies dark brown, crumbly earth. This layer is humus, made by decomposers from dead plants and animals, and it holds nutrients and water for plant roots. It is nothing like sand, which is just tiny bits of rock.

A fallen log can take decades to rot, with fungi doing most of the work. Seedlings often sprout right on it. Besides water, those young trees take in nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, set free from the wood by the decomposers, through their roots. The log gives them no energy and no food, because a plant makes its own food in its leaves, using sunlight. So the dead tree feeds the young trees with matter, while the energy comes fresh from the Sun.

ecosystems-living-and-nonliving.title: Ecosystems: Living and Nonliving Parts
ecosystems-living-and-nonliving.context_blurb:
Step into a forest and look around. Trees, birds, beetles and mushrooms live there. So do things that were never alive: rocks, soil, water, air and sunlight. Every part acts on the others, and each living thing depends on the rest. Knowing how the parts fit together shows us what keeps a place healthy, and how people can harm it or help it.

All the living things in a place, together with the nonliving things around them, make up an ecosystem, with every part acting on the others. Ecosystems come in all sizes. At low tide, the sea leaves small pools in the rocks along the shore. Peer into one and you find a complete tiny ecosystem: snails, crabs, seaweed and small fish, with seawater, stone and sunshine.

Scientists sort an ecosystem's parts into two groups. An ecosystem's living parts, its plants, animals, fungi and bacteria, are called its biotic factors. Pine trees, deer and even the bacteria in soil are all biotic factors. An ecosystem's nonliving parts, such as sunlight, water, air, soil, rock and temperature, are its abiotic factors.

Living things need the nonliving parts as much as they need each other. Visit a pond on a cool, sunny morning, and you may see turtles lined up on the rocks. A turtle gets its body heat mostly from its surroundings, so it climbs out to soak up the warmth. A turtle warming itself on a sunny rock is using two abiotic factors at once: the sunlight and the stone. A hawk catching a mouse is using a biotic factor instead: another living thing.

Every living thing also needs a habitat. A habitat is the place where a living thing makes its home and finds everything it needs: food, water, shelter and space. A forest gives its deer and owls all of these: food, streams, thick brush to hide in and room to wander. So the forest is their habitat. A den or a nest gives shelter, but shelter is only one part of a habitat.

A healthy ecosystem usually holds many different kinds of living things, and scientists call that variety biodiversity. An ecosystem with many kinds of living things usually stands up better to trouble, such as a drought or a disease. Once, a disease killed most of the chestnut trees in some great forests. The forests lived on, because plenty of other kinds of trees grew there as well. Predators belong in a healthy ecosystem, too. Take them away, and a whole food web can be thrown out of balance.

People can harm an ecosystem or help it. Tree roots grip the soil and bind it together. Clear every tree off a steep hill, and that grip is lost. With the trees gone, no roots hold the soil together, so heavy rain washes it down the slope. After a storm, the streams below run brown with mud.

Pollution can harm a lake in a sneaky way. Farmers spread fertilizer to help their crops grow, but rain can wash it off the fields and into a lake. There the fertilizer feeds algae, tiny green living things that grow in water. The algae spread so fast that the lake turns green. When the algae die, bacteria break them down and use up the oxygen in the water. Fish need that oxygen to breathe, so when it runs low, many of them die. The green colour is not what kills them; the missing oxygen is.

People can help a lake too. One of the best ways is planting shrubs and tall grasses along the shore. This strip of wild plants catches soil and fertilizer before the rain can wash them into the lake, and its deep roots hold the bank in place. A mowed lawn cannot do this job, because its grass roots reach down only a few centimetres.

adaptations-built-for-a-place.title: Adaptations: Built for a Place
adaptations-built-for-a-place.context_blurb:
Why does a duck have webbed feet, while a cactus has a fat green stem covered in spines? Every living thing has a body suited to the place where it lives. Walk from a pond to a desert to an icy sea, and the bodies change with the place. Look closely at a body, and you can often tell where it lives and what it eats.

A body feature that helps a living thing survive in its surroundings, and that is passed down from parents to young, is called an adaptation. The hard shell of a turtle keeps it safe from hunters. The sharp, hooked beak of a hawk rips meat. Even the spines of a cactus are adaptations.

Water birds such as ducks and geese have skin joining their toes, which turns each foot into a paddle. A duckling inherits its webbed feet from its parents. The webs take shape while it is still growing inside the egg, so it has them before its very first swim. No animal can grow an adaptation because it wants one, or by working a body part hard. Adaptations build up over many generations instead, because the young born with them survive and have young of their own more often.

Cold places call for warm coverings. Fur keeps an animal warm by trapping a layer of still air against its skin. Many sea mammals, such as seals and walruses, have blubber, a thick layer of fat beneath the skin. Blubber is thickest in the seals and walruses of icy polar seas, where it holds body heat in against the freezing water. Animals of cold mountains live on land and stay warm mainly with thick, woolly coats, not blubber.

Colour can be an adaptation too. Camouflage is colouring that matches an animal's background, so a hunter's eyes pass right over it. A lizard as brown as the desert sand can lie in plain sight while a hawk hunts above, and the hawk never sees it. Like other adaptations, camouflage is passed down from parents to young.

You can often tell what a bird eats just by looking at its beak. Seed-eating birds such as finches have stout beaks shaped like a cone, built for cracking open hard seeds. A beak like this works like a strong nutcracker.

Teeth tell a story too, and you can learn to read a skull like a clue. Plant-eaters such as horses have broad, flat teeth at the back of the mouth, with ridges that grind tough grass and leaves. Meat-eating hunters such as foxes have sharp, pointed teeth for gripping their prey. An animal that eats both, such as a bear, has flat back teeth as well as long, sharp front teeth. So a skull with only flat, grinding teeth belonged to a plant-eater.

Desert plants have adaptations of their own. A cactus may go for months with no rain at all. A cactus stores its water in its stem: the thick, fleshy green body of the plant, which works like a water tank. Its folds let it swell after rain and shrink in dry months, like an accordion. Most cacti have no ordinary leaves. Their spines are a special kind of leaf that guards the plant from hungry animals.

Trees in lands with cold winters face a different problem: winter thirst. Leaves let water escape into the air. When the ground is frozen, the roots can take in little water to make up for it. So many of these trees drop all their leaves each autumn and stand bare. With its leaves gone, a tree loses far less water, so it saves water through the frozen months. Look at a bare twig in winter and you will find small buds. Next spring's leaves are already tucked inside, made back in late summer.

born-knowing-or-learned.title: Born Knowing or Learned
born-knowing-or-learned.context_blurb:
Some things you could do on the day you were born, and some you had to learn. A behaviour that no one has to teach is an instinct: a living thing is born with it, and every member of its kind does it the same way. A learned behaviour comes from experience, such as practice, watching others or a reward. Both kinds help living things survive.

People are born with instincts. Press a finger into a newborn baby's palm, and her tiny fingers curl tight around it. She can grip like this from her very first day, with no lessons at all. This grip is a reflex, an action the body does by itself, and it fades by about six months.

Some reflexes last a lifetime and keep you safe. A sneeze blasts dust from your nose, a cough clears a crumb from your throat, and your hand jerks back from a hot pan before you can think. Looking both ways before crossing a road is a learned skill instead: grown-ups teach children to look both ways, and then once more, before stepping into the street.

Many animals have instincts as well. A garden spider's mother dies in late autumn, soon after laying her eggs. In spring her young hatch, drift off on silk threads, and each spins a wheel-shaped web of its own. No one teaches a young spider, and it has never watched a web being made, yet its web works: it was born knowing how.

A mother sea turtle lays her eggs in a beach nest at night, covers them with sand and goes back to the sea. The eggs hatch about two months later. Because the mother left long before her babies hatched, no one is there to show them the way. Each hatchling crawls toward the brightest part of the sky, which on a dark beach lies over the water.

Learned behaviours are different. When a pet dog learns to sit or give a paw, its owner hands it a treat or praise each time it does the trick, until it does the trick whenever it is told. The dog's puppies are not born knowing the trick, because a learned behaviour is not inherited.

Learning has one more strength. Milk once came to the door in glass bottles, with the cream on top under a thin foil cap. Blue tits, which are small birds, learned to peck through the foil and sip the cream. No instinct could have prepared them for that, yet the trick spread from bird to bird to more than two hundred places. An instinct stays the same, but learning lets animals change their ways as the world around them changes.

Some traits come from genes, passed down to every child from both parents. Eye colour is one of these inherited traits, so a girl adopted as a tiny baby and raised in a faraway land still has eyes coloured by her birth parents' genes. Her language comes from the family who raised her, a skill comes from practice, and a scar from an old fall. Things gained during life are not passed on to children. The scientist August Weismann tested this: he cut the tails off mice, and their young were never born with short tails.

the-bodys-main-organs.title: The Body's Main Organs
the-bodys-main-organs.context_blurb:
Right now, as you read, your heart is beating and your lungs are filling with air. These are organs: body parts that each do one main job. Working together, they keep you alive, and you can feel some of them at work if you know where to look.

Lay two fingertips on the inside of your wrist, just below your thumb, and you will feel a steady throb. That throb is your pulse, and each one comes from a single beat of your heart. The heart is a muscle about the size of a fist, and with each beat it squeezes and pumps blood around the body. The throb in your wrist is that push of blood arriving. Count the throbs for one minute: for most children your age, the number lands between 70 and 110. The heart does not make blood, though. New blood is made in the soft marrow inside your bones.

Blood travels through a huge network of tubes that reaches every part of you. Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and digested food in the small intestine, and it brings both to every part of the body. On the way back, it carries wastes away.

One waste comes from your cells themselves. When cells use oxygen to break down food for energy, a waste gas called carbon dioxide is left over. The blood brings it back to the lungs. There, through the thin walls of tiny air sacs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood, while carbon dioxide passes out the other way, and you breathe it out. Carbon dioxide is not the same as carbon monoxide, a poison gas given off when fuel burns badly in stoves and engines.

Each swallowed mouthful travels down the food pipe to the stomach, a stretchy bag of muscle that can swell to hold a meal. Inside the stomach, strong acid juices soak the food while the muscular walls squeeze and mix it, until it turns into a thick, soupy mush.

Next the mush moves on to the small intestine, a narrow tube that lies coiled in loops in the belly. It is called small because it is narrow, not because it is short. Its lining is covered in tiny finger-like bumps called villi. Most of the digested food passes through the villi into the blood, which carries it all over the body. What is left moves on to the large intestine, which takes out water and forms solid waste.

Your brain is in charge of the whole body, and it needs a way to send orders and get news. Nerves are thread-like bundles that branch out from the brain and spinal cord to every part of the body, carrying messages both ways. Some nerves bring news in from your eyes, ears and skin. Others carry the brain's orders out to your muscles.

Bones give the body its frame. An adult has about 206 of them, and together they hold you upright and give your body its shape, the way poles hold up a tent. Some bones also guard soft organs. The skull, made of 22 bones joined together, forms a hard case around the brain. Your ribs make a cage around your heart and lungs.

Muscles move bones by pulling on them. The biceps sits on the front of your upper arm. When the biceps works, it gets shorter and pulls the forearm up through a tough cord called a tendon, so the elbow bends. A muscle can pull, but it can never push. So muscles work in pairs: to straighten the elbow again, the triceps on the back of the arm does the pulling. Grip your upper arm and bend your elbow, and you can feel your biceps at work.

Which organ is the biggest? Most people never think of the skin as an organ, but it is one. The skin is the largest organ of all: an adult's skin weighs nearly 4 kilograms, more than twice as much as the biggest organ inside the body. It wraps the whole body, keeps germs out and water in, and lets you feel heat, cold and touch.

the-sun-and-its-planets.title: The Sun and Its Planets
the-sun-and-its-planets.context_blurb:
On a sunny day, the warm light on your face comes from a star. The Sun is a giant ball of hot, glowing gas, and it sits at the centre of our solar system. Eight planets circle it, and Earth is one of them. The Sun's light and heat keep our world warm enough to live on.

The Sun is the nearest star to Earth. It outshines all the stars of the night sky because it is much closer to us than they are. Many stars are far bigger and hotter than the Sun. They are just so far away that they look like tiny points of light. A flashlight works the same way. Up close it lights a whole room, but far across a dark field it looks like a speck.

Why don't the planets fly off into space? The Sun's gravity, its pull, holds each planet on its path. Picture a ball on a string that you whirl around your head. The string pulls the ball toward your hand; let go, and the ball flies away. A planet is also racing forward all the time, so instead of falling into the Sun, it keeps curving around it. One trip all the way around the Sun takes Earth about 365 days, and that trip is what we call a year. A day is just one spin of Earth, and each of the four seasons lasts about three months.

Nearest the Sun are four small, rocky worlds. Mercury comes first, closest to the Sun of them all. Then come Venus, Earth and Mars. You might guess that Mercury, being so close, is the hottest planet, but it is not. It has almost no air, so its heat slips away into space. Venus is the hottest planet, because its thick air traps the heat like a heavy blanket. Its ground bakes at over 450 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Bright clouds wrap Venus and help make it the brightest planet in the night sky.

Earth, the third planet, is our home. As far as anyone knows, Earth is the only planet with living things on it. It is also the only one known to have liquid water on its surface. Other planets share some of Earth's features. Every planet has gravity. Mars and the giant planets have moons, and clouds drift over Venus, Mars and Jupiter. Earth's gravity keeps our Moon travelling around us, about once a month. The Moon shines brightly at night, yet it makes no light of its own. The Moon reflects light from the Sun: moonlight is sunlight that bounces off its rocky ground and travels on to us. A bike reflector works the same way, glowing only when a light shines on it.

On a clear night, Mars, the fourth planet, shines like a reddish star. Mars is red because rusty dust covers its ground. Its rocks and dust are full of iron, and the iron has rusted, like an old nail left out in the rain. Red does not mean hot here. Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth is. Even on a warm day, its ground reaches only about 20 degrees Celsius, about room temperature.

Past Mars lies the asteroid belt, a ring of rocky chunks. Beyond it are four giant planets, great balls of gas and ice. Jupiter, the nearest giant, is the largest planet of all. It holds more than twice as much matter as all the other planets put together. Next comes Saturn. Every giant has rings, but Saturn's are the bright ones, made of countless chunks of ice and rock. The ice shines in sunlight, so Saturn's rings show up even in a small telescope. The other giants' rings are faint and dark. Beyond Saturn lie two ice giants, Uranus and then Neptune, the most distant planet of all. Little Pluto, out past Neptune, is now called a dwarf planet.

day-night-and-shadows.title: Day, Night and Shadows
day-night-and-shadows.context_blurb:
Stand in the sunshine one morning and look at your shadow. Look again at lunchtime, and once more late in the afternoon. It will have shrunk, then stretched, and swung around to point a new way. The Sun seems to cross the sky, but the real traveller is the ground under your feet. Earth is spinning, and its spin makes day, night and the changing shadows.

Earth spins like a top. It turns around its axis, an imaginary line that passes straight through the middle of the planet, with the North Pole at one end and the South Pole at the other. Earth never stops turning, and one full spin takes about 24 hours. That one spin is a day. Earth also travels around the Sun, along a path called its orbit, but one trip around takes a whole year.

As Earth turns, it carries each town into the Sun's light and then around into darkness, again and again. At any moment, the half of Earth facing the Sun has day, and the half turned away has night. So day and night come from Earth spinning around, not from its yearly trip around the Sun. People long believed that the Sun circled a still Earth, because we cannot feel the ground move. In truth the Sun only seems to circle us.

That means two places on opposite sides of Earth have opposite times of day: when it is midday in one town, it is around midnight in the town on the exact other side, which faces away from the Sun. Half a day later, the two swap.

Because Earth spins toward the east, the Sun seems to rise in the east, climb across the sky and set in the west, so its daily path runs from east to west. It is like riding in a car: the trees outside seem to slide backward, though it is really the car that moves.

A shadow is the dark patch where something blocks the light. A shadow always falls on the side of an object away from the Sun. So if your shadow stretches out ahead of you, the Sun is at your back, and you are facing away from it.

As the Sun seems to move, shadows swing around. In the morning the Sun is in the eastern sky, so a stick's shadow points roughly west. By late afternoon the Sun has moved over to the western sky, and the same shadow has swung around to point roughly toward the east. A sundial tells the time by this swing, and people in ancient Egypt were telling time with stick shadows some 3,500 years ago.

Shadows change length too. The lower the Sun sits, the more its light comes in at a slant, and the longer the shadows it casts. So when a tree's shadow reaches far across a field, many times the tree's own height, the Sun must be low in the sky, near sunrise or sunset. A high Sun makes short shadows, and only a Sun directly overhead would leave a tree's shade lying right beneath it.

You can see the pattern for yourself: mark the tip of a pole's shadow once an hour, from morning till evening. The shadow starts out long just after sunrise, shrinks to its shortest around midday, when the Sun is highest, and grows long again toward sunset: long, then short, then long again. Far from the equator even the noon shadow never quite vanishes, because there the Sun never climbs directly overhead.

the-water-cycle.title: The Water Cycle
the-water-cycle.context_blurb:
Every drop of water on Earth is on a journey that never ends. It rises from the sea into the sky, falls as rain or snow, and runs over the land or sinks into it. This journey is called the water cycle, and it brings the rain that fills rivers and waters crops.

The Sun powers the water cycle. Its heat warms oceans, lakes and wet ground. As water warms, some of it changes from a liquid into water vapour, a gas you cannot see, and floats up into the air. This change is called evaporation. The water does not need to boil: evaporation goes on quietly at the surface, with no bubbles. Almost all of the rising water comes from the oceans.

Wet clothes on a sunny washing line dry the same way: their water evaporates and goes into the air as water vapour. The water has not vanished. It is still there, mixed into the air, but water vapour is invisible. Tiny drops of liquid would show as a mist, the way a cloud shows.

Warm, damp air drifts upward, and the higher it climbs, the colder it gets. Cooling turns water vapour back into liquid water, a change called condensation: it is evaporation running backward. The new droplets are so small that rising air holds them up. Millions of them crowd together, and that crowd is a cloud.

Water that falls from a cloud, as rain, hail, sleet or snow, is called precipitation. Inside a cloud, the tiny drops bump together and join, so a drop grows bigger and heavier. Once it is too heavy for the rising air to hold up, it falls as rain. It takes millions of cloud droplets to make one raindrop. Thunder does not shake rain loose: it is only the sound of lightning, and many clouds rain for hours without it. And though most of it rose from the salty sea, rain falls as fresh water.

The Sun lifts water up, and gravity, Earth's pull, brings it back down and makes it run downhill. When rain lands, some soaks into the ground. The rest flows over the surface into creeks and rivers, and that water is called runoff. Rain cannot soak into pavement at all, so on a paved parking lot nearly all of it runs off into drains and streams. Bare, ploughed soil soaks up some rain. Where grass and trees grow, roots and fallen leaves slow the water down and help it sink in.

Rain that soaks deep down becomes groundwater, filling tiny spaces and cracks in soil and rock. Groundwater does not stay put: it creeps along slowly, often only a few centimetres or metres a year, and seeps into the beds of rivers, lakes and seas, or flows out at springs. Deep groundwater may stay down for thousands of years, but in the end it gets out.

In all this travelling, no new water is made and none is destroyed. The cycle only moves water around and changes its form. So Earth has about the same amount of water today as it had in the days of the dinosaurs. Today's rain is the same water, used over and over for millions of years.

Oceans cover about seven tenths of Earth's surface. But they hold far more than seven tenths of the water: about 97 drops of every 100 are in the salty sea, so nearly all of it is ocean water. The oceans can hold so much because they are deep, more than three and a half kilometres on average. Only about two and a half drops in every hundred are fresh water. Most of that fresh water is frozen as ice in ice caps and glaciers: about 69 of every 100 drops of fresh water are ice. Most of the rest is groundwater. Lakes and rivers, where fresh water is easiest to see, hold only a tiny part of it.

wind-water-and-ice-shape-the-land.title: Wind, Water and Ice Shape the Land
wind-water-and-ice-shape-the-land.context_blurb:
A mountain looks as if it will last forever, but it is slowly wearing away. Rain, rivers, wind and ice break rock into bits and carry the bits off, grain by grain. Over thousands and millions of years, that slow work carves out valleys, heaps up hills of sand and builds new land where a river meets the sea.

Scientists split this work into two jobs. Weathering is the breaking: rock cracks and crumbles into smaller pieces right where it sits. Erosion is the carrying: running water, wind, ice or gravity moves the pieces somewhere else. In short, weathering breaks rock up, and erosion carries it away.

Freezing water is a mighty rock-breaker. Rain trickles into cracks in rock, and when the cold comes, the water freezes. Water takes up nearly a tenth more room as ice, so the ice shoves the crack a little wider. When the ice melts, water seeps deeper, ready for the next freeze. So rock splits fastest where it freezes and thaws again and again, as on high mountains. Rock that stays frozen all year cracks far more slowly, however bitter the cold.

Living things break rock too. When a tree grows out of a crack in a rock, its roots creep down into the gap and thicken every year. Like a wedge tapped in very slowly, the roots push the crack wider until the rock splits. In loose soil, roots hold the ground in place, but in solid rock they pry it apart.

Rivers carve the land. The sand and stones in a river scrape its bed like sandpaper, cutting it a little deeper every year. Over millions of years, a river can slowly saw its way down through solid rock and leave a deep, narrow canyon with steep walls. An earthquake cracks the ground, but it does not open a canyon.

On an ordinary day a mountain stream rolls along only sand and little pebbles, but a storm can turn it into a flood that rushes far faster than usual. The faster water flows, the bigger the rocks it can push and carry, so a racing flood can sweep along boulders that sit still on a calm day. The boulders never float, because ordinary rock is two to three times as heavy as the same amount of water.

Where a river runs into the still sea, it slows down. Slow water cannot carry as much, so the river drops the mud and sand it carries. This dropping is called deposition. Over thousands of years the mud piles up into a broad, flat plain of new land at the river's mouth: a delta, named after the Greek letter delta, a triangle, the shape a delta often takes.

Wind works on dry, sandy ground. It bounces sand grains along close to the ground and drops them wherever it slows, heaping them into hills. These hills are sand dunes, built by the wind in deserts and along beaches.

Ice carves the land as well. A glacier is a huge mass of ice that creeps slowly downhill, and it carves a valley shaped like a U. Stones frozen into its bottom grind the rock as it goes. Because it scrapes a valley's sides as well as its floor, it leaves steep sides and a broad, rounded bottom. A river cuts mostly downward instead, leaving a narrower valley shaped like a V.

Glaciers, rivers and wind mostly work slowly, over thousands of years. A few changes are fast: in a landslide, gravity drags a mass of rock and soil down a steep hillside, and the quickest landslides are over in seconds or minutes. Heavy rain soaking the ground, or an earthquake shaking it, often sets one off.

rock-layers-and-fossils.title: Rock Layers and Fossils
rock-layers-and-fossils.context_blurb:
Split open the right rock, and you might find a shell, a leaf or a fish bone from long, long ago. Many rocks are built in layers, laid down one after another like the pages of a book. Those layers hold fossils, and fossils are clues to what the land was like long ago.

A muddy river carries sand, mud, crumbs of rock and broken shells. When it flows into a calm lake or sea, it slows down, and the bits sink to the bottom. Bits like these, carried along by water, wind or ice and dropped somewhere else, are called sediment. Year after year, new sediment settles on top of the old, so it builds up in layers.

Given thousands to millions of years, buried sediment hardens into rock. The weight of the upper layers presses down on the lower ones, squeezing the grains tightly together and pushing out the water between them. Minerals in that water then stick the grains to one another, the way cement holds a sidewalk together. So the grains are pressed together and glued by minerals: sand becomes sandstone, and mud becomes shale, a rock that splits into thin, flat sheets. Mud that only dries in the Sun has not become rock. Rock made in layers this way is called sedimentary rock.

Some rock is made from living things. In warm, shallow seas, the shells of sea creatures and bits of coral heap up on the bottom, and over ages the heap hardens into limestone. Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, the hard stuff of shells and corals, so it is often packed with fossil shells.

A fossil is any remains, print or trace of a living thing from long ago, usually more than ten thousand years old. Bones, teeth and shells are fossils, and so are footprints, burrows and the prints of leaves. When a fern leaf falls in soft mud and rots away, its outline can stay pressed in the rock that the mud becomes. That print counts as a fossil, because a living thing left it. A shape in a rock that no living thing made is not a fossil.

Few living things ever become fossils. A body left out in the open is eaten by scavengers or rots away. A dead fish has its best chance when mud and sand bury it quickly. The cover keeps scavengers off and slows rotting, so the hard bones last long enough to be saved.

That is why most fossils are found in sedimentary rock, built from layers of sand and mud: the layers bury remains gently, without great heat. Rock that forms from melted rock, such as cooled lava, almost never holds a fossil, because the melted rock wipes the remains away.

Now and then a tiny creature is saved whole. Amber began as resin, a thick, sticky liquid that oozes from some trees. An insect that landed in fresh resin stuck fast and was sealed in, and over millions of years the buried resin hardened into amber, often clear and golden, with the insect still inside. Many books call the resin sap.

Fossils show how places have changed. Corals and starfish live only in the sea, never in lakes or rivers. So a rock layer full of their fossils under a dry field shows that an ocean once covered the land.

Buried life can even become fuel. Most oil formed from trillions of tiny living things, algae and plankton, that drifted in ancient seas, then died, sank to the sea floor and were buried in mud. Deep underground, heat and pressure slowly changed them into oil, and natural gas often formed alongside. Oil does not come from dinosaurs; that is a myth. Coal formed mostly from the plants of ancient swamps. Because coal, oil and natural gas all formed from the buried remains of living things, they are called fossil fuels.

earths-resources.title: Using and Protecting Earth's Resources
earths-resources.context_blurb:
Water, soil, sunlight, wind, forests, metals, coal and oil all come from nature, and people use them every day. They are called natural resources. Some come back soon after they are used, the way a forest grows again. Others take so long to form that, once they are used, nature will not make more for ages.

If nature replaces a resource within the span of a person's life, it is renewable. If nature takes far longer, it is nonrenewable. Coal is nonrenewable: it takes millions of years to form underground, so the coal burned today will not be replaced within anyone's lifetime. Oil and natural gas are nonrenewable for the same reason. Trees grow back within decades and a new corn crop grows every year, so firewood and fuel made from corn are renewable. The moving water that turns a dam's wheels is not used up at all, since rain and snow keep the river full.

Metals come from rock as well. Copper, the metal in many water pipes and wires, is dug from rocks called ores. Copper is nonrenewable, like other metals, because nature takes millions of years to make new copper ore, far too slowly for any human life. Used copper can be recycled again and again, as good as new. That makes the copper already dug up last longer, but it does not make copper renewable. Copper does not rust, either: over many years it grows a thin green coat that protects the metal beneath.

Soil is a resource too. Topsoil is made of rock broken down into tiny grains, mixed with the rotted remains of plants and animals. Nature makes it very slowly: a layer one inch deep, about two and a half centimetres, takes hundreds of years to form, from a few hundred to about a thousand. That is far longer than a human life. Rain and wind often carry topsoil away faster than it forms.

Plastic is made in factories, not found in nature. More than ninety percent of plastic is made from oil and natural gas, so most plastic comes from nonrenewable fuels. Less than one percent comes from plants.

Aluminium, the metal of drink cans, comes from a rock called bauxite. Making aluminium from old cans takes only about five percent of the energy needed to make it from bauxite, so recycling saves almost all of it, about ninety-five percent. Each tonne of recycled aluminium also leaves about four tonnes of bauxite in the ground.

Paper is made of tiny fibres from trees, and every time paper goes through recycling, its fibres get a little shorter and weaker, so it slowly wears out. In the end, fresh fibres must be mixed in; people often say this happens after about five to seven trips. Glass and metals are different: they are melted and remade, and they can go round again and again without wearing out. Thin kitchen foil tears as easily as paper, but it is aluminium, remade just like a can.

People speak of three Rs: reduce, reuse and recycle. Reducing means using less of something. Reusing means using a thing again just as it is, without breaking it down, such as filling an empty jam jar with buttons. Recycling means breaking a used thing down and making its material into something new, the way old cans become new ones.

Conserving a resource means using less of it and wasting less, which is the same as reducing. A family that fixes a dripping tap, takes showers rather than baths and sweeps the steps rather than hosing them is conserving water, because each of those jobs uses less.

Plastic left outdoors lasts a long time. Bacteria and fungi break down almost none of it, so it does not rot away like old leaves. Instead, sunlight makes it brittle, and the weather cracks it into tiny bits of plastic. Two scientists, Imogen Napper and Richard Thompson, tested this: they left plastic bags out in the open air, and within nine months every bag had fallen to pieces. The bits can last for decades or even centuries. More than 700 kinds of animals have been found to swallow plastic, often mistaking it for food.

weather-and-climate-basics.title: Weather and Climate
weather-and-climate-basics.context_blurb:
Step outside and look up. Is the sky blue or grey? Is the air warm or cold, calm or windy? All of that is the weather: what the air is doing in one place at one time. It decides whether you need a coat today, and simple tools let anyone measure it.

Weather is not the same as climate. Weather changes from day to day. Climate is a place's usual weather, the pattern it shows year after year. To work out a place's climate, weather scientists average its daily records of heat and rain over about 30 years. One year is far too short, because the weather jumps around so much. Over 30 years, one odd year hardly moves the average.

A desert gets very little rain in most years, so its climate is dry. Now and then a rare storm soaks it anyway, sending water down its dusty streets. Such a storm is just one day's weather, and one day's weather can differ from the climate. Once the storm passes, the desert is as dry a place as ever.

Weather watchers measure several things about the air. Humidity means how much water vapour the air is holding. Water vapour is water as an invisible gas. On a muggy day the air holds a lot of it, and it feels sticky on your skin.

Air has weight, too. A column of air kilometres high sits on every patch of ground and leans on it. That push is called air pressure, and a barometer is the tool that measures it. The pressure rises and falls as the weather changes, so weather watchers keep an eye on their barometers.

Wind is moving air. An anemometer is a set of small cups on short arms that spin on top of a pole. The wind catches the cups and whirls them round, and the stronger the wind, the faster they turn. So the spinning cups measure how fast the wind blows.

Beside the cups there is often a wind vane. A wind vane's arrow swings round until it points into the wind, toward the place the wind is coming from. So a north wind is one that blows from the north. Many people guess that the arrow points where the wind is heading, but it points the other way.

Clouds are weather you can see: countless tiny drops of water or bits of ice, floating in the air. In 1803 a man named Luke Howard gave the main kinds of cloud Latin names, and we still use them.

Cumulus is Latin for 'heap'. Cumulus clouds are the fluffy white heaps you might draw in a picture of a sunny sky, flat underneath with round, puffy tops. They form when the Sun warms the ground and warm, damp air rises. Small ones mean fair weather, but one may keep growing into a cumulonimbus, a dark storm tower full of rain, thunder and lightning.

Stratus comes from the Latin for 'spread out'. A stratus cloud is a low, even layer of grey that can cover the sky from edge to edge, like a lid. It brings dull days and drizzle, and a stratus cloud resting on the ground is fog.

Cirrus is Latin for 'curl of hair'. Cirrus clouds are thin white wisps high in the sky, usually more than 6 kilometres up. The air up there is so cold that they are made of tiny ice crystals.

At the seaside on a hot day, a cool breeze often blows in off the water. This sea breeze comes because the Sun warms the land faster than the sea. You can feel it: hot sand stings bare feet while the water still feels cool. The warm air over the land rises, and cooler air from the sea rushes in to take its place. At night the land cools faster, and the breeze turns round to blow out to sea.
