measuring-and-the-fair-test.title: Measuring and the Fair Test
measuring-and-the-fair-test.context_blurb:
Scientists learn about the world by measuring it, and you can too. A ruler, a thermometer or a timer turns words like long, hot and fast into numbers that anyone can check. But a number is only worth trusting when it comes from the right tool, read the right way.

Length is measured with a ruler, in centimetres and metres. Temperature is read from a thermometer, in degrees Celsius. Volume, the space something takes up, comes in litres and millilitres. Mass, the amount of matter in something, is found with a balance, in grams and kilograms. So a reading in kilograms, such as 6 kilograms for a big pumpkin, is always a mass.

A spring scale measures force, which is a push or a pull. Clip one to a brick and tug, and the spring inside stretches. The harder the pull, the farther the spring stretches, so the pointer shows how hard the brick is pulled. Force is counted in newtons, after Isaac Newton.

Liquids are measured in a graduated cylinder, a narrow glass tube marked in millilitres. Water clings to the glass and creeps up its sides, so the surface sags in the middle. Read the level at the bottom of that curve, with your eye level with it. Looking down from above lines the water up with the wrong mark.

Pour sand into a cup on a balance, and the reading is for the cup and the sand together. To find the mass of the sand alone, take away the mass of the empty cup. Setting the empty balance to zero first is no help, since the cup's mass still ends up in the reading.

Bacteria are living things too small for any eye to see on its own. A hand lens makes things look at most about 10 to 20 times bigger, not nearly enough. To see bacteria, a scientist needs a microscope, which makes things look from about 40 to hundreds of times bigger.

Science also needs fair tests. Say some students wonder whether a large parachute takes longer to float down than a small one. In a fair test, only one thing changes: here, the size. The load, the drop height and the timing all stay the same for both, so if one parachute takes longer to land, only the size can cause that difference. Change two things at once, and nobody can tell which one mattered.

Even a fair test needs more than one try. Drop a ball from the same height again and again, and the bounces will not all match. Each drop comes out a little different, because of small slips such as letting go a bit too high or reading the metre stick at a slant. So scientists repeat the very same trial and compare the results, or average them.

A bigger magnet is not always the stronger one: a small neodymium magnet can out-pull a much bigger magnet of a weaker kind. When careful, repeated tests go against a prediction, the honest move is to change your idea to fit the results, not the results to fit your idea. A test that proves an idea wrong has not failed; it has taught you something true.

Not every question suits a fair test. A fair test can answer whether bean plants grow taller in sun or in shade: grow some in each, keep everything else the same, and measure them. Counting the pebbles in a jar is useful, but nothing is changed and compared, so it is not a fair test. And no test can settle a matter of taste, like which song is prettiest, or what people ought to do.

Scientists record their numbers in tables and graphs. Picture temperatures read every hour from morning till evening. A line graph joins those readings with a line, so you can see at a glance how the temperature climbs and drops through the day. A bar graph compares separate groups instead, and a tally chart counts how often something happens.

particles-in-motion.title: Particles in Solids, Liquids and Gases
particles-in-motion.context_blurb:
Everything, from a gold ring to the air you breathe, is made of particles, tiny pieces far too small to see. Whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas depends on how tightly its particles are packed and how fast they move. That one idea explains why ice holds its shape, why water pours and why a mirror fogs up.

In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and held in fixed places, like students squeezed into a crowded class photo: nobody can swap places, but everybody fidgets. That is why ice keeps its shape. Yet the particles are never still, not even in the cold of a freezer: each one vibrates, shaking back and forth on its own spot, packed close against its neighbours.

In a liquid, the particles stay close together, so the liquid keeps its volume, the amount of room it takes up. A liquid's particles stay close but slide past one another all the time, so the liquid flows into the shape of whatever holds it.

In a gas, the particles are far apart, and they move fast and freely in all directions. Each one zooms in a straight line until it hits another particle or a wall, then bounces off. Nothing holds gas particles together, so their own motion carries them into every corner of any container. They do not shove one another apart from a distance; they meet only when they bump into each other.

Because gas particles are so far apart, most of a gas is empty space. Air's particles are far apart, with empty space all around them, so squeezing air pushes them closer together. A diver's tank holds only about eleven litres of water, yet a pump can force some two thousand three hundred litres of air into it, and that air is still a gas. Water can hardly be squeezed at all, because its particles already touch. Try it with a plastic syringe: block the tip, and the plunger pushes a long way into trapped air but hardly moves against trapped water.

Heating gives particles more energy, so they move faster; cooling slows them down. In a jeweller's furnace, the particles of a gold ring vibrate harder and harder. At the melting point, the temperature where a solid turns to liquid, the gold's particles have enough energy to break free of their fixed places. No particle melts or goes soft; only the way the particles are held together changes.

Heat a flask of water and its particles speed up too. At the boiling point, particles all through the water gain enough energy to pull away from one another. They gather into bubbles of water vapour, which is water in the form of a gas, and the bubbles rise and escape. Many people guess those bubbles are hydrogen and oxygen, but every particle that leaves is still a whole water particle.

The water particles in ice, in liquid water and in vapour are the very same ones, and the size of each particle never changes. What changes is how fast they move and how strongly they hold on to one another. When a heated thing swells, it is the space between its particles that grows.

Cooling runs the story backwards. After a hot shower, the air is full of water vapour. When the vapour touches the cool mirror, the glass takes energy from it, so its particles slow down and come close together, clinging to one another as a liquid. That change, a gas turning into a liquid, is called condensation: the reverse of evaporation.

pure-substances-and-mixtures.title: Pure Substances and Mixtures
pure-substances-and-mixtures.context_blurb:
Much of what you touch is a mix. Seawater, soil, air and brass are each several substances mingled together. Chemists sort all matter into two big groups, pure substances and mixtures, and knowing which is which tells them how a material will behave and how its parts can be pulled apart.

A pure substance is just one substance, with the same make-up and the same properties wherever it comes from. It comes in two kinds. An element, such as gold or oxygen, is made of only one kind of atom, the tiny building block of matter, and it cannot be broken down into anything simpler. A compound is two or more elements joined chemically in a fixed ratio, making a new substance. Only a chemical reaction, a change that makes new substances, can split a compound apart.

The ancient Greeks counted water as an element, beside earth, air and fire. In 1800, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle passed an electric current from a battery through water, and it split into two gases, hydrogen and oxygen. Since electricity breaks water into simpler substances, water is a compound of the two. The bubbles in boiling water are different: they are only water vapour, water as a gas.

Charcoal is mostly carbon, and as it burns, its carbon joins chemically with oxygen from the air. The two always combine in the same fixed ratio, so burning charcoal gives off carbon dioxide, a compound of carbon and oxygen: one new gas, not the two old elements simply mingled. Carbon dioxide is also one of the gases you breathe out.

In a mixture, the substances are not joined. They mingle in any amounts, and physical means such as filtering or settling can sort them out again. A homogeneous mixture is the same all the way through, like air or salt water. Brass, the golden metal of many wind instruments, is a homogeneous mixture: copper and zinc melted together, with the zinc spread evenly all through the copper. A heterogeneous mixture is uneven, and you can often see its different parts, like the coloured grains in a speckled rock.

Soil is a heterogeneous mixture you can test yourself. Shake a few handfuls with water in a clear jar until it is all mud-brown, then leave it alone for two or three days. Its grains of sand, silt and clay do not dissolve, so they settle out by size: sand, the biggest, within a minute, silt within a couple of hours, and the tiny clay grains last, over a day or more. So the jar ends up in layers, with sand at the bottom and clay on top, under clear water.

A thermometer can tell a pure substance from a mixture. A pure substance boils at one fixed temperature: at sea level, pure water always boils at 100 degrees Celsius. A mixture's boiling point depends on what is in it. Dissolved salt raises the boiling point, so seawater, with salt dissolved in it, boils a little above 100, at about 100.6 degrees.

Panning for gold separates a mixture by density, which means how heavy a material is for its size. Gold is many times denser than sand: about seven times denser than quartz, the main mineral in sand, and about nineteen times denser than water. So as the panner swirls water through the gravel, the lighter grains wash out over the edge while the gold sinks and stays. A tiny gold flake weighs far less than a pebble; it stays because gold is so heavy for its size.

In everyday talk, pure can mean that nothing was added, but to a chemist a pure substance is one single substance. Water from a mountain spring has seeped through rock underground and dissolved calcium, magnesium and other minerals from it. With rock minerals dissolved in it, spring water is a mixture, however clean and natural it is.

metals-nonmetals-and-metalloids.title: Metals, Nonmetals and Metalloids
metals-nonmetals-and-metalloids.context_blurb:
Everything is built from elements, 118 basic substances that cannot be broken into anything simpler. Chemists list them on one chart, the periodic table, and sort them into three families: metals such as gold and iron, nonmetals such as oxygen and sulfur, and metalloids, which fall in between. An element's family tells you how it behaves: whether it shines, bends or shatters, and whether electricity flows through it.

Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, and many come straight from the English name: H for hydrogen, O for oxygen. A few look like a puzzle. Lead is Pb, from plumbum, its name in Latin, the language of ancient Rome; plumbum is also the root of our word plumbing. Iron is Fe from ferrum, silver is Ag from argentum, and gold is Au from aurum. The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius drew his symbols from the elements' names in Latin around 1814, so that the same letters would stand for an element in every language. Einsteinium, named after Albert Einstein, simply follows its English name: Es.

About four in five elements are metals, so they fill most of the periodic table, from the left side all across the middle, along with the two long rows printed underneath. The nonmetals crowd into the top right corner, all except hydrogen at the top left. The metalloids sit on a zigzag staircase line between the two.

Metals are shiny, carry heat and electricity well, and bend instead of breaking. Gold is the champion of malleability, a metal's power to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without cracking. A goldbeater can pound a single gram of gold into a sheet about a metre long and a metre wide, so fine that light glows greenish blue through it. Ductility is a close cousin: the power to be drawn out into wire.

Most nonmetals are gases: of the seventeen, eleven are gases at room temperature, among them oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, helium and neon. Bromine is the only liquid, and the other five, among them carbon, sulfur and iodine, are solids. Every metal but mercury is a solid, and so is every metalloid, so every element that is a gas at room temperature is a nonmetal.

Solid nonmetals are mostly dull, they crumble or snap instead of bending, and heat and electricity pass through them poorly. Sulfur, a pale yellow crystal, breaks to crumbs under a hammer and barely carries electricity at all. Like most nonmetals, sulfur sits on the right side of the periodic table, far from the metals. Simple tests like these are how a chemist sorts an element into its family: a look at its shine, a hammer blow and a wire to a battery.

A metalloid usually looks like a metal but acts much like a nonmetal. Germanium shines grey like a metal, yet it is brittle, which means it breaks rather than bends. A hard hammer blow that would only flatten a lump of gold or lead shatters germanium into small pieces.

Silicon, the best-known metalloid, is shiny and brittle too, and it is found in sand and quartz. It is a semiconductor, a material in between for electricity: it carries electricity far less easily than copper but far more easily than glass, and adding tiny amounts of other elements changes how much it carries. With the right tiny additions, silicon can be made to carry electricity or to block it. A computer chip holds billions of tiny silicon switches, called transistors, that turn the flow of electricity on and off.

density-float-or-sink.title: Density: Why Things Float or Sink
density-float-or-sink.context_blurb:
A pebble sinks in a pond, yet a cargo ship of steel stays afloat with a full load. What decides is not size or weight alone but how heavy a thing is for its size, which scientists call density. Comparing densities explains floating ships, rising balloons and lakes that freeze only on top.

Density is how much mass, the amount of matter, is packed into each bit of volume, the space a thing takes up. It belongs to the material, not to the size of the piece. A chip broken off a big quartz crystal has far less mass, but it takes up far less room too, in just the same proportion, so its density is the same, since it is the same quartz.

A thing floats in a fluid, any liquid or gas, when it is less dense than that fluid, and sinks when it is denser. The fluid's upward push on a floating thing is called buoyancy.

Even a metal can be the fluid. Mercury is the only metal that stays liquid at room temperature. An iron bolt floats on mercury because mercury is denser than iron. Size is not the reason: the same bolt sinks at once in water. Gold, denser than mercury, sinks in it.

Steel is nearly eight times as dense as water, so a lump of steel sinks straight down. A ship's steel, though, is spread thin around a huge hollow hull full of air. What counts is the whole ship, steel and air together, and its air-filled hull makes it less dense than water, so it floats. Try it with clay: a ball of clay sinks, but the same clay pressed into a boat shape floats.

The fluid's own density matters too. Salt dissolved in seawater adds mass without adding as much volume, so salt water is denser than fresh water, and a swimmer lying on her back floats higher in the sea than in a freshwater lake. The denser the water, the less of it a floating body must push aside to be held up. In the Dead Sea, about ten times saltier than the ocean, people float with no effort at all.

Water holds one more surprise. For most materials the solid form is denser than the liquid, but ice is less dense than the water it freezes from, because freezing locks its particles into an open pattern that takes up more room. So ice floats as a lid on a lake, slowing the lake's loss of heat to the cold air, and the water below stays liquid for the fish. If ice sank like most solids, each new layer formed at the cold surface would drop and pile up on the bottom, with no lid to hold the warmth in, and a shallow lake could freeze from the bottom up.

Air is a fluid too, so the same rule works in the sky. A helium balloon rises because helium is far less dense than air, only about a seventh as dense. Helium does have weight, yet a balloon of it, rubber and all, still floats up. Not every gas rises: carbon dioxide is denser than air and flows along the ground into low places.

signs-of-a-chemical-change.title: Signs of a Chemical Change
signs-of-a-chemical-change.context_blurb:
Some changes only reshape a thing: ice melts, paper tears, a rock is crushed to dust. Others make something brand new. That is a chemical change, or chemical reaction: atoms, the tiny building blocks of all matter, rearrange into a new substance with new properties. Atoms are far too small to watch, so scientists look for clues.

A physical change alters only a thing's shape, size or state (solid, liquid or gas) and makes nothing new. The signs of a chemical change are a gas given off, a change in temperature, a solid appearing in a liquid, a new colour, light and a new smell. Each sign is a clue, not proof, since physical changes can show some too.

Take bubbles. Drop an antacid tablet into cool water and, once it is wet, two of its ingredients react and make carbon dioxide, a gas that was not there before. Boiling water bubbles hard too, but its bubbles are only water turned into a gas. Of the two, only the bubbles from the tablet hold a new substance, since boiling is a change of state that makes nothing new.

A change in temperature is another clue. A hand warmer is a cloth pouch of damp iron powder and salt, sealed in an airtight wrapper. Open the wrapper and oxygen from the air reaches the iron. Rusting is a chemical change that gives off heat, and the salt speeds it up, so the iron rusting very fast is what heats the pouch. An iron gate rusts too slowly for its heat to be felt; powder, with far more iron touching the air, rusts fast.

A burning log gives off heat, but some reactions take in heat instead. Stirred together in a flask, two white powders, barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride, react into new substances, ammonia gas among them. The reaction draws heat from everything around it, so the flask drops to about twenty degrees Celsius below zero and freezes a wet wooden block to its glass. Cold is not a thing that flows out of the powders: the flask feels cold because heat is leaving whatever touches it.

A third clue is a precipitate, a solid that appears in a liquid. Limewater is clear water with lime, a chemical called calcium hydroxide, dissolved in it. Blow into it through a straw and it soon turns milky. The carbon dioxide in your breath reacts with the lime and makes calcium carbonate, the white stuff of chalk and limestone, which does not dissolve. Its tiny grains of solid hang in the liquid and turn it white.

A new colour can be a clue too. Shiny reddish-orange copper, left on a roof in rain and wind for years, turns pale blue-green. The green comes from the copper reacting with air and rain: oxygen, carbon dioxide and water slowly combine with it into a crust called a patina, a new substance with its own colour. The patina shields the metal beneath, so a copper roof can last more than a hundred years.

Yet colour can fool you. Shiny, steel-grey hematite, rubbed across an unglazed white tile, leaves a reddish-brown powder. That powder is the same mineral, ground very fine: rubbing only breaks the hematite into tiny grains, a physical change that makes nothing new. Many minerals give a powder of a different colour from the lump; geologists call that colour the streak and use it to tell minerals apart. So a new colour alone is never proof.

Light can be a clue as well. Bending a glow stick snaps a thin glass vial inside, and shaking mixes the vial's liquid with the one around it. The two liquids react as they mix and give off light with very little heat, so the stick shines for hours with no battery. A glow-in-the-dark toy only soaks up light and gives it back slowly; a glow stick needs no light first.

Last comes a new smell. Fresh sweat, mostly water with a little salt and fat, hardly smells at all. Bacteria living on the skin feed on sweat and break it down into new, smelly substances, which is why a runner's shirt reeks at the armpits after a long, hot race.

forces-and-net-force.title: Forces and Net Force
forces-and-net-force.context_blurb:
A force is a push or a pull, and forces start things moving, speed them up, slow them down or turn them. Every force has a size, how strong it is, and a direction, the way it acts. Add up the forces on anything, from a sled to a skydiver, and you can tell what it will do next.

Forces come in two kinds. Contact forces act only where two things touch: friction, the rub between surfaces that works against sliding, and the normal force, a surface's push back on whatever rests on it. Gravity and magnetism pull across a gap instead: Earth pulls a falling apple, and a magnet tugs a paper clip, before anything touches. So whether a force acts only where things touch is what sorts it into one kind or the other. Earth's gravity pulls everything straight down, toward the planet's centre.

In a force diagram, every force acting on an object is drawn as an arrow pointing the way the force acts. The arrow's length shows how strong the force is: the longer the arrow, the stronger the force. The arrows stand for forces, not motion, so a book lying still on a table gets two arrows of equal length, gravity's pointing down and the table's pointing up.

Add all the forces together, minding their directions, and you get the net force: forces acting the same way add, opposite forces take away from each other, and the net force points the way of the stronger push or pull. When the net force is zero, the forces are balanced and the motion does not change: a still thing stays still, and a moving thing keeps the same speed in a straight line. When the forces are unbalanced, the motion changes in the direction of the net force.

A brick on a soft mattress makes a dip; on a stone floor it leaves no mark. Yet the brick sits still on both, so on both the surface's push up exactly matches gravity's pull down, and the two normal forces are equal. Stone is squeezed too, far too little to see, and pushes back like a very stiff spring, while the mattress only sinks further before its push matches the load.

A sled resting on flat snow is balanced, the snow pushing up as hard as gravity pulls down. Then a girl pulls it to the right, harder than friction holds it back. With her pull bigger than friction, the net force points right, so the sled starts moving right and speeds up, and it keeps speeding up for as long as she out-pulls friction.

Balanced forces do not mean a thing is still. A car cruising at a steady speed on a level road has balanced forces: since its speed is not changing, the engine's forward force exactly equals the backward push of friction and the air. A bigger forward force would speed it up; a smaller one would slow it.

Air resistance, or drag, is the air's push against anything moving through it, and it grows the faster the thing goes. A girl pedalling hard on a level road speeds up at first. But the air pushes back harder as she speeds up, and once its push matches hers, the forces are balanced and her speed holds steady.

A skydiver falls faster and faster until the air's upward push matches gravity, then drops at a steady speed. Her parachute's wide canopy catches far more air, so the moment it opens, the upward push beats gravity. The net force now points up, against her motion, so she keeps falling, but more slowly. She never rises: as she slows, the air's push weakens until it matches gravity again while she is still moving down, and she drifts down at five to eight metres a second. Films seem to show her shooting up only because the camera, carried by another skydiver, is still falling fast.

action-and-reaction.title: Action and Reaction: Newton's Third Law
action-and-reaction.context_blurb:
Stand on a skateboard and shove a wall, and you roll away from it, as if the wall had shoved you back. It did. A force is a push or a pull, and every force has a partner: whenever one thing pushes on another, it gets pushed back. That rule explains swimming, rockets and the bug squashed on a windshield.

Isaac Newton wrote the rule down in 1687 as his third law of motion: when one object pushes or pulls on a second, the second pushes or pulls back on the first, just as hard and the opposite way. A pair is always the same two objects acting on each other. When a hammer pounds a nail, the partner of its push down on the nail is the nail's push up on the hammer. The board pushes on the nail as well, but that push belongs to another pair, between the nail and the board.

The two forces of a pair begin together, too: a girl leaning on a heavy door feels it press back on her hands from the moment she starts to push on it, however gently, before it has moved at all. The word "reaction" makes the second push sound like a later reply, but neither comes first.

A pair is equal however different the objects are. When a bug hits a speeding truck's windshield, the bug pushes on the truck exactly as hard as the truck pushes on the bug. The same push changes a light thing's motion a lot and a heavy thing's hardly at all, so the bug splats while the truck barely slows.

Gravity comes in pairs too: Earth pulls a falling apple down, and the apple pulls Earth up just as hard. Mass is how much matter a thing holds. Earth is so massive that the apple's pull barely moves it, so nobody sees Earth rise to meet the apple.

Why don't two equal, opposite forces cancel out? Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, like two teams pulling equally hard on one rope in a tug-of-war that goes nowhere. A force pair never cancels, because each one acts on a different object: the bat's push acts on the baseball and sends it flying, while the ball's push acts on the bat.

A girl and a boy on skates grip the two ends of a rope on smooth ice; she tugs hard, and he only holds on. Both of them slide toward each other, because by holding his end he pulls back, so the rope pulls him toward her as it pulls her toward him. The two pulls act on two different skaters, so they do not cancel.

Swimming works by a pair, too: a swimmer's hands push the water backward, and the water pushes back on her hands, forward, and that push from the water moves her along. Her arms cannot move her by pulling on her own body, since forces between the parts of one body cancel out. Nor does she store up force with each stroke: a force lasts only while two things act on each other.

A rocket's engine pushes hot gas out of the back, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. Even in airless space, a spacecraft that fires its engine speeds up, pushed forward by the gas it blasts out. A rocket never needs air to push against; it works even better in a vacuum, a space with no air, where its exhaust escapes freely. A blown-up balloon let go is a rocket you can try: the air rushing out of its neck pushes it the opposite way.

People once doubted that. In 1920 a New York Times editorial mocked the rocket pioneer Robert Goddard, claiming a rocket needed something better than a vacuum to push on. In July 1969, during the flight of Apollo 11, the paper printed a correction, saying it regretted the error.

kinetic-and-potential-energy.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
kinetic-and-potential-energy.context_blurb:
A rock perched on a cliff and a rock tumbling down it both hold energy, what it takes to make something move, heat up or change. The falling rock's energy is in its motion; the perched rock's is stored, waiting. Following energy as it changes form explains roller coasters, bows and swings.

Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: a thing standing still has none, and the faster it goes, the more it has. A girl cycling on a flat road would have more kinetic energy only by riding the same bike much faster. Feeling well rested adds none: it is the motion that counts.

Mass, the amount of matter in a thing, counts too. A Wiffle ball is a hollow plastic ball full of holes, about as big as a tennis ball but far lighter. Thrown at a wall equally fast, the tennis ball carries more kinetic energy because it has more mass, which is why it stings far more. Bounciness has nothing to do with it.

Potential energy is stored energy, ready to turn into motion. Gravitational potential energy is stored by height, and it grows the higher a thing is lifted. Carry a backpack up to a third-floor classroom, and its gravitational potential energy is greater than on the ground floor, because the pack is now higher up. That energy came from your food, and the pack keeps it even sitting still on a desk, ready to become motion if it falls.

Elastic potential energy is stored in something stretched, squeezed or bent out of its resting shape, like a rubber band or a spring. When an archer pulls the string back and holds it, the energy that will launch the arrow is in the bow itself, bent out of shape. Her muscles did the bending, but the energy now sits in the bend, and the arrow holds none of it yet. Let go, and the bow springs back toward its resting shape and passes the energy to the arrow as kinetic energy.

Chemical potential energy is stored in the way atoms, the tiny pieces all matter is built from, are joined. Gasoline, a granola bar and a fresh battery all hold it, yet left alone they give off hardly any. Fuel, food and batteries let their stored energy out only when they react and become new substances. Gasoline burns into carbon dioxide and water, your cells break down the bar's sugars, and a battery's chemicals react in a circuit. Crushed into crumbs, a bar is still the same substance, with the same store.

Energy is never created or destroyed; it only changes form or passes from one thing to another. A motor's chain drags a roller coaster up the first hill; at the top, highest of all, the train holds the most gravitational potential energy, and from there it runs on gravity alone. As it dives, gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy, so the lower it gets, the faster it goes. It trades height for speed, then speed back for height on the next climb.

A pendulum, a weight swinging on a rope, trades energy the same way, and one classic demonstration trusts a teacher's face to it. With his head to a wall, he holds a bowling ball hung from the ceiling at the tip of his nose and lets it go with no push. Out it swings, then back, and it halts a hair from his face. He is safe because the ball cannot gain more energy than it began with, so it can never climb higher than where it started. At the far end it stops for an instant, its energy stored as height. A push would add energy, and then it could hit him.

A real swing slows down. Stop pumping, and each arc is lower than the last until you hang still. Friction, the rubbing at the swing's hooks, and the push of the air changed its energy, a bit on every arc, into heat, also called thermal energy. The warmth is too thin to feel, but the energy still exists.

Energy can also pass from one object to another. When a cue ball driven dead straight into a resting pool ball stops almost on the spot, most of its kinetic energy has passed into the ball that it struck, which rolls off nearly as fast. Only a little becomes the click's sound and heat.

waves-carry-energy.title: Waves Carry Energy
waves-carry-energy.context_blurb:
Toss a pebble into a pond and rings of little waves race outward. Clap, and a friend across the room hears it. Both are waves. A wave is a disturbance, a wiggle or a squeeze, that carries energy from place to place. The surprise is what it leaves behind: the water, rope or air it passes through stays put.

The stuff a wave travels through is its medium. Ripples carry the splash's energy all across a pond, but they do not carry the water with them. A floating leaf shows it: as ripples pass, it bobs and ends up almost exactly where it started, because the water under it mostly moves round in small loops.

Waves come in two kinds, sorted by how the medium moves. Tie a ribbon halfway along a long rope and flick one end up and down, sending humps along it. The ribbon rises and falls in one spot while each hump runs on past it. Each bit of rope moves at right angles to the way the wave travels, and a wave like that, with the medium moving across its path, is called transverse. A wave's high points are its crests, and each low dip between two crests, like the dips between the ridges of a lake's waves, is called a trough.

In the other kind, the medium moves back and forth along the wave's own path. Lay a spring toy on the floor and shove one end in and out along its length, and tight bunches of coils race along it. That is a longitudinal wave, because the coils move back and forth along the line the wave travels. Where the coils crowd together is a compression; where they spread apart is a rarefaction. Shaken from side to side instead, the same spring's coils move across the wave's path, so its ripples are transverse: the kind of wave depends on how the medium moves.

Sound is a longitudinal wave. Strike a drum and its skin snaps outward and inward. Each push outward crowds the air particles, the tiny bits air is made of, into a compression. Each pull back inward leaves a rarefaction, a region where the air particles are spread apart. As a school bell's ring travels down a hallway, the air particles move back and forth, each near its own place, every one pushed a little way along the sound's path and springing back to pass the push on. The air never flows down the hall, and the sound does not slip through the gaps between particles: with no particles to push, there is no sound.

A glass jar shows what sound depends on. Seal a switched-on buzzer and a small lamp inside and pump the air out bit by bit: the buzz dies to a faint whisper, though the buzzer keeps shaking, while the lamp stays just as bright. Sound needs matter to travel and light does not, so with nearly all the air gone, too little is left to carry the buzz out. A school pump never takes out every last bit of air, so the buzz fades almost to nothing rather than to perfect silence. Light needs no matter at all, which is how sunlight crosses the nearly empty space to Earth.

Light is a wave too, and a transverse one: what vibrates in it runs across the way the light travels. So when a flashlight shines on a spring wiggling from side to side, the spring's ripples and the light are both transverse waves.

Sound also travels through liquids and solids, wherever there are particles to pass the push along, and water carries it well over long distances. Scientists listen to the sea with a hydrophone, an underwater microphone. A hydrophone can hear a distant ship's engine humming because the sea water around it carries the sound. The waves rolling on top of the sea are a different kind of wave, not sound.

cells-the-building-blocks-of-life.title: Cells: The Building Blocks of Life
cells-the-building-blocks-of-life.context_blurb:
Your body is built of cells, the way a house is built of bricks. A cell is the smallest living unit, and most cells are far too tiny to see without a microscope. Plants, animals, mushrooms and bacteria are all made of cells, and everything a living thing does, from growing to healing, is cells at work.

In 1665, in his book Micrographia, Robert Hooke described a thin sliver of cork seen through his microscope. It was full of little box-shaped rooms, like the cells of a honeycomb, and he called them cells. Cork cells are dead, so their insides were long gone, and all Hooke could see of each one was the cell wall, holding air. A plant cell's stiff wall outlasts the living cell inside it.

Cell theory sums up what microscopes have shown since then in three big ideas. First, every living thing is made of one or more cells. A single bacterium is one whole living cell that does all the jobs of life by itself, while a person is built of around 30 trillion cells. A virus is not a cell at all, and molecules are the far smaller pieces that cells are built from. Second, the cell is the basic unit of life. Third, every new cell comes from a cell that already exists.

That third idea explains how a scraped knee heals. The scab is dried blood that shields the wound, and it never turns into skin. The new skin comes from living skin cells around and beneath the wound. Cells at its edges and deep in its floor split again and again. They creep across under the scab, which falls off once the new skin is done.

Cells come in two great kinds. Eukaryotes, which include amoebas as well as plant and animal cells, keep their genetic instructions, called DNA, inside a nucleus. Bacteria are prokaryotes, with no nucleus at all. A bacterium keeps its DNA in a loose clump in its cytoplasm, the jelly that fills the cell. Every cell is wrapped in a thin membrane. The membrane is the cell's gatekeeper: it controls what enters and leaves the cell, letting in water, oxygen and food and letting out wastes. In a plant or animal cell, the nucleus is the control centre. It holds the DNA and uses those instructions to direct the cell's work, such as making proteins. Mitochondria, found in plant and animal cells alike, release the energy stored in food.

A green leaf cell has extra parts. A leaf cell's chloroplasts make its food: they use the energy in sunlight, with water and carbon dioxide, to build sugar. Green chlorophyll inside them colours the leaf. Your cheek cells have none, so they cannot make food. Yet a leaf cell needs mitochondria too. Chloroplasts make the sugar, and mitochondria release the energy stored in that sugar so the cell can use it. A plant cell also has a stiff wall outside its membrane, for shape and support. One big central vacuole, a store of water, can fill most of a grown plant cell. When the central vacuole is full, it presses the cell out against its stiff wall, and that keeps the plant firm. Forget to water a potted plant and its vacuoles shrink, so it droops; water it and they swell and stand it up again. Animal cells have only small vacuoles, or none.

In a body of many cells, similar cells doing one job together form a tissue. Cardiac muscle, which squeezes with every heartbeat and makes up most of your heart, is a tissue of muscle cells. Two or more kinds of tissue make an organ, such as the heart itself. The heart, the blood vessels and the blood together make up an organ system, the circulatory system.

one-cell-or-many.title: One Cell or Many
one-cell-or-many.context_blurb:
Put a drop of pond water under a microscope and it comes alive: tiny cells swim, crawl and hunt, and each one is a whole living thing. Your own body is built the other way, from a great many cells that each do one job. Living things also differ in how they get their food.

A unicellular, or one-celled, living thing is a single cell that does every job of life by itself, from feeding and growing to getting rid of wastes. The amoeba crawls by pushing out arms of itself called pseudopods, or false feet. To eat, it surrounds its prey with those arms until the tips meet, closing the meal inside a bubble called a food vacuole, where it is digested. It has no mouth. The paramecium, shaped like a slipper's sole, moves by beating thousands of tiny hairs called cilia, which ripple like rows of oars. To back away from an obstacle, it reverses the beat.

In a multicellular, or many-celled, body the cells specialise: each kind does one job and depends on the others. A muscle cell cut from an arm soon dies alone, though it has a membrane, several nuclei and thousands of mitochondria, the parts that release energy. What it has lost is the blood, pumped by the heart, that brought it food and oxygen. An amoeba finds both by itself.

Nerve cells carry signals, and some are astonishingly long. One nerve cell's fibre can run a metre or more, from the base of the spinal cord, low in the back, down to the foot, so it carries signals along the whole leg. Even the longest muscle cell, which shortens to pull on bones, falls far short of that.

A red blood cell, as it ripens in the bone marrow, throws out its nucleus and most other parts. That leaves more room to carry oxygen, because the emptied cell fills with haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body. With no nucleus it cannot divide, and it lives only three or four months. It has no stiff wall either: it is a soft disc that bends through the narrowest blood vessels.

An autotroph makes its own food; the auto in its name means self. Euglena, a green pond cell that swims with one whip-like tail called a flagellum, is one. Keep a jar of pond water by a sunny window and the Euglena gather on its brightest side, because each one makes its own food from light in tiny green parts called chloroplasts, and swims to where the light is best. Its red eyespot cannot see prey; it only tells the cell which way the light lies. In the dark, Euglena can take in food from the water instead.

Even a plant that eats flies is an autotroph. Each trap of a Venus flytrap is one leaf with two halves that snap shut in about a tenth of a second, yet the plant's green leaves make its food from sunlight, and it can live without ever catching a fly. It grows in wet, boggy ground poor in nitrogen and phosphorus, and its catch supplies the nitrogen that is scarce in its soil.

A heterotroph, whose name means other feeder, cannot make its own food and must take in food made by other living things. Every animal is a heterotroph, and so is every fungus. Linnaeus filed mushrooms and moulds among the plants, but a fungus has no chlorophyll, the green colouring that catches light, and in 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed a kingdom for the fungi alone. Fungi have since proved closer kin to animals than to plants. Many feed on dead remains, but others feed on living plants or animals.

A mould digests its food outside itself and then absorbs it: on old bread, its fine threads pour digestive juices into the slice, break the starch into simpler food and soak that food up. Mould needs damp to grow, but water is not its food, and its tiny spore held far too little to feed it.

Yeast is a one-celled fungus, kin to the many-celled mushrooms and moulds. Wild yeast dusts fruit skins and lives in soil. Unlike a bacterium, a yeast cell has a nucleus, and like every fungus it cannot make its own food. No animal is ever made of just one cell.

variation-and-survival.title: Variation and Survival
variation-and-survival.context_blurb:
No two members of one species are exactly alike: they differ in size, colour, shape, speed and much else. These differences are variations. They matter because the world changes, and a storm, a drought or a new disease can turn a small difference into the one that decides who lives.

Many variations are inherited, carried in the genes that parents pass to their young. A paper strip soaked in a chemical called PTC reveals a hidden one: roughly three students in four find it bitter, and the others taste nothing. The difference lies in the genes each student inherited, above all one gene called TAS2R38. The whole tongue senses bitterness; the old map of taste zones is a myth.

Other variations come from the surroundings. A bigleaf hydrangea blooms blue in acid soil, where its roots can take up aluminium, and pink in alkaline soil, the opposite of acid, where they cannot. A cutting has the same genes as its parent bush, so if a blue bush's cutting blooms pink in a friend's garden, the soil in the friend's garden changed the colour. A difference made only by the surroundings is not passed on to the young.

Here is how a helpful variation spreads. Picture green and brown beetles on brown soil, where the green ones stand out to hungry birds. Fewer brown beetles are eaten, so more of them live to breed and pass their colour on, and since colour is inherited, their young are brown too. No beetle changes colour to suit the soil, and parents cannot give their young a colour because the young need it: the helpful variation must already be there.

In 2017 Colin Donihue's team had just measured the anole lizards on two islands of the Turks and Caicos when two hurricanes struck. Weeks later, the survivors' toe pads were bigger on average, and their bodies smaller, so the biggest had not done best. The biologists' best explanation was that lizards with bigger pads held on in the wind and lived, while the storms changed no lizard's feet. They could not rule out other causes, such as lizards blown in from another island. A year and a half later, lizards hatched since the storms had pads as big as the survivors'.

On a Galápagos island, a drought in 1977 left finches mostly big, hard seeds, which suit thick beaks, so thick-beaked birds came through best. Heavy rains from the end of 1982 then brought a flush of small, soft seeds. A thinner beak eats small seeds more efficiently, so after the rains the thin-beaked birds grew faster and raised the most young, and within a few years the average beak had shrunk. A variation that helps in one setting can hurt in another.

Cliff swallows often nest under highway bridges, where cars kill some of them. For thirty years in Nebraska, Charles Brown and Mary Bomberger Brown collected the road-killed birds, whose wings were a few millimetres longer than the rest. A shorter wing lets a swallow rise and swerve from a car faster, so short-winged birds lived to raise more young. Over those years the swallows' wings have grown shorter on average, and far fewer of the birds now die on the road. Charles Brown has said other causes may play a part too.

Variety can also carry a species through a disease. Ash dieback, caused by a fungus, has killed millions of ash trees across Europe, yet a few trees stay green among the dying. Those healthy trees inherited a resistance to the fungus, and their seedlings can inherit it from them. In one English wood, the young ash were already more resistant, on average, than the old. Resistance does not spread like a cold, and young trees without it die fastest.

A crop with no variety shows the danger. Until the 1950s, the Gros Michel was the banana on the ships to Europe and North America. Bananas are grown from shoots of older plants, not from seeds, so every Gros Michel was a copy of the same plant, with the same genes and the same weakness. Panama disease was neither new nor quick: its soil fungus creeps in through the roots and takes months to kill. Yet with no plant able to resist, it laid waste to vast tracts of plantations in Central America. Its successor, the Cavendish, resists that fungus, but it is a copy too, and a new strain now threatens it.

competing-for-resources.title: Competing for Resources
competing-for-resources.context_blurb:
Every living thing needs things from its surroundings: light, water, food, a place to live, shelter and a mate. Ecologists call these resources. When one runs short, living things compete for it, and the contest settles which of them thrive. You can watch it in any crowded garden row.

Competition happens only when there is not enough of a resource for both. Where there is plenty, sharing costs no one anything, however close together the neighbours live. Members of one species often compete hardest, since they need exactly the same things, but different kinds compete too.

Competing needs no fight, and not even a meeting. Desert harvester ants go seed-hunting by day, and kangaroo rats collect the same kinds of seeds after dark. Seeds are scarce, though, and each seed one side eats is lost to the other, so the two compete without ever crossing paths. When ecologists fenced rodents out of some desert plots, the number of ant colonies there rose by 71 percent, and where the ants were removed, the rodents increased.

Plants compete too. A plant makes its own food, but it needs light and water to make it, and nutrients from the soil to grow. Scatter carrot seed thickly, leave every seedling, and the crowded plants all reach for the same light, water and soil nutrients. Most of them end up smaller than carrots given room, because they must share that light, water and nourishment, and many twist around one another. That is why gardeners thin their rows.

In 1934 Georgy Gause raised two kinds of paramecium, the slipper-shaped pond cell, both of which feed on bacteria. Grown in tubes of their own, both kinds did well. Sharing a single tube and a limited food supply, one kind kept growing and thrived while the other dwindled and died out. Two kinds that need exactly the same scarce resource cannot share it for long, and kinds living side by side in nature often use different foods or places.

Ecologists call anything that holds a population down a limiting factor: often a resource in short supply, such as food, water or places to nest, but sometimes a predator or a disease. Great tits and other small birds that breed in tree hollows show how it works. Where felling had left few hollows, ecologists hung up nest boxes, and more of the birds bred there, because the shortage of holes had been keeping their numbers low.

For a crop, the limit is set by the scarcest thing it needs, not by the total. Wheat draws two nutrients from the soil, nitrogen and phosphorus. If a field is rich in nitrogen but short of phosphorus, adding more nitrogen does nothing, because the phosphorus, the scarcer of the two, sets how much the wheat can grow. Carl Sprengel stated the idea first, in 1828, and Justus von Liebig made it famous in 1840. It is often pictured as a barrel built of wooden strips of different heights, which holds water only up to its shortest strip.

A place's limiting factors set its carrying capacity, the largest population it can keep fed and housed year in and year out. A population let loose in a rich new home grows faster and faster at first. As it fills the place, its members compete harder for what is left, so its growth slows down before it reaches the carrying capacity, and its numbers level off near it. Drawn as a graph of numbers against time, that makes an S-shaped curve. A population that does shoot past the carrying capacity shrinks back, but it does not usually die out.

The reindeer of St. Matthew Island made a famous crash, and biologists still argue over its cause. In 1944 the Coast Guard set twenty-nine reindeer ashore there. With no wolves or hunters, the herd swelled to some six thousand by 1963, grazing away much of its winter lichen. Then the herd crashed: nearly all of the reindeer starved when deep snow buried the last of the lichen in the hard winter of 1963 to 1964. Only 42 were left by 1966. David Klein, the biologist who counted the herd, judged that it had outgrown what the island's lichen could feed. Frank Miller and two colleagues, reading the records again in 2005, argued that the herd was still growing fast and breeding well, and blamed that savage winter most of all.

predators-partners-and-parasites.title: Predators, Partners and Parasites
predators-partners-and-parasites.context_blurb:
Look closely at a meadow or a forest and you will find living things tangled together: a bee in a flower, a tick on a deer, a lynx chasing a hare. Biologists sort these meetings with one simple test: what does each side gain, and what does it lose?

Biologists call it symbiosis when two different species, two kinds of living thing, share their lives closely over a long stretch of time. In everyday talk the word often means a partnership where both sides win, but to a biologist it covers three types. What sorts them is whether each partner is helped, harmed or neither. In mutualism both gain; in commensalism one gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed; in parasitism one partner, the parasite, gains at the cost of the other, its host.

A honeybee visits a flower to drink its nectar, a sweet juice. While it feeds, pollen, the fine dust a flower makes, catches in the hairs on its body. At its next stop some of that dust brushes off, and the carried pollen lets that plant make seeds. The bee gets food and the plant gets its pollen delivered, so both gain: mutualism.

Trillions of bacteria, living things far too small to see, live in your large intestine, the last stretch of your gut. They digest fibre, the tough part of plant food your body cannot break down, and many make vitamins such as vitamin K. In return they get a home and a share of the food.

Pull up a clover or a bean plant and you will find little lumps on its roots, each crowded with bacteria. Air is mostly nitrogen gas, which plants need but cannot use as it is. The bacteria in the lumps take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form the roots can soak up, and the plant pays them with sugar from its leaves.

High in a rainforest, an orchid perches on a branch to reach the light. Its roots grip the bark and drink in rain and mist, and it takes no water or food from inside the tree. The orchid gains a sunny perch, and the tree is neither helped nor harmed: commensalism. Biologists admit it is hard to prove the tree is truly unaffected, since a tiny cost could go unseen.

In parasitism one side pays. A tick fastens onto a deer and feeds on its blood for days, then drops off once it is full. The tick gains a meal and the deer loses blood, and a heavy load of ticks can wear an animal down, so this is parasitism. It is not predation: a predator kills and eats its prey, while a parasite feeds on a host that usually lives on.

A tapeworm hooks onto its host's gut wall and soaks up digested food for years, giving nothing back. Yet a tapeworm rarely kills the person it lives in, because it needs a living host to feed and spread. A host killed quickly would leave the worm no time to send its eggs on to new hosts.

Even a green plant can be a parasite. Mistletoe's leaves catch sunlight and make part of its food, yet a root-like part of it grows into the branch to take water and minerals that the tree carries up from its roots. Unlike the orchid, it gains at the tree's cost, and a heavy load can stunt or kill a tree.

Predation, the fourth way species meet, is not counted as symbiosis at all. For nearly a century, trappers sold lynx furs to the Hudson's Bay Company in Canada, which counted them each year, and hare records cover the same span. Side by side, both counts rise and fall in waves about ten years long. Lynx live mostly on snowshoe hares, so their numbers can climb only after the hares have grown plentiful, and the lynx peaks come a year or two after the hares peak.

Why, then, do the hares never vanish? As hares grow scarce, lynx grow fewer too. With little left to catch, many lynx starve and few of their kittens live, and with fewer hunters about, the last hares breed back up and the cycle begins again. Food for the hares plays a part as well.

populations-communities-ecosystems.title: Populations, Communities and Ecosystems
populations-communities-ecosystems.context_blurb:
Ecologists, the scientists who study how living things fit together with one another and with their surroundings, sort nature into levels, like boxes packed inside bigger boxes. One fox, all the foxes of a valley, everything alive in a pond, the whole living planet: each is a different level. Knowing which level you are looking at tells you exactly what to count.

The smallest level is the organism, one single living thing, such as a fox, a maple tree, a mushroom or one bacterium. An ecologist who weighs one red fox every month of a winter and tracks how far it roams is studying an organism.

One step up is the population: all the members of one species living in one area. A species is one kind of living thing, such as the sugar maple. So in a hardwood forest of maples, beeches and birches, every sugar maple growing there, young and old, makes up one population. Maples and beeches together are two populations side by side. A tadpole is a young frog that lives in water and breathes with gills, yet it is the same species as its parents and belongs to their population.

Where one population ends depends on who can meet to breed. Picture two ponds a long way apart, with dry ground between that no bullfrog ever crosses. The frogs of one pond never breed with those of the other, so there are two populations, one in each pond, tadpoles included.

Next comes the community: all the populations of living things in one area, of every kind, from plants and fungi to animals and bacteria. Algae make food from sunlight as plants do, and bacteria, too small to see, crowd the mud at the bottom of a pond; both are as alive as the frogs. So a student who lists only the birds, fish, frogs and insects of a pond has left out its plants, algae and bacteria.

Add the nonliving parts, such as sunlight, water, mud, soil and air, and the community becomes an ecosystem. Follow nitrogen, a nutrient that plants need, around a forest. Tree roots pull it from the soil; it waits in the leaves until they fall; then fungi and bacteria rot the dead leaves and hand it back to the soil. That loop links living things with a nonliving part, the soil, so an ecologist who traces it is studying the ecosystem.

People fit into the levels too. The people of a town are one species, so they are one population, and with the pigeons, dogs, lawns, oaks and soil bacteria they form the town's community. Its roads and houses belong only to its ecosystem. In everyday speech a town's people are its community, but to an ecologist a single species is never a community.

At the top sits the biosphere: all of Earth's ecosystems together, the whole zone where life is found. Microbes, living things too small to see, have been found high in the sky, tens of kilometres above the ground, and small shrimp-like animals live at the bottom of the deepest trench in the sea, almost eleven kilometres under the waves. A biome, such as a desert or a rainforest, is smaller: one great region of similar ecosystems inside the biosphere.

Each step up adds something different. From organism to population you add more members of one species, from community to ecosystem you add the nonliving surroundings, and the biosphere takes in the whole planet. Only the step from population to community adds more kinds of living things, and that step needs no extra land. A single rotting log can shelter a salamander, pill bugs, beetles, ants and fungi in a patch about a ruler's length across, and that tiny crowd is a community. Gray squirrels counted over a whole forest are still one species, one population, so the log's group sits higher, since it holds many species.

the-bodys-defences.title: The Body's Defences Against Germs
the-bodys-defences.context_blurb:
Every day, germs try to get into your body on your hands, in your food and in the air you breathe. Germs, such as bacteria and viruses, are far too small to see, and they can make you ill. Your body fights back in layers: walls to keep them out, guards to hunt down the ones that slip through, and a memory for old enemies.

The first wall is your skin. Its outer layer is made of dead cells, tough and dry, and a cold virus cannot get through it, pores and all. A cold virus picked up from a doorknob does no harm on your fingers, but it takes hold once a fingertip carries it to the moist lining inside your nose. That is why touching your face with unwashed hands spreads so many colds.

The nose and the windpipe, the tube that carries air to your lungs, are coated with sticky mucus that traps dust and germs. Under it, cilia, tiny hair-like parts on the lining, beat together ten to twenty times every second, like rows of oars. The beating cilia sweep the dirty mucus up the windpipe to the throat, where you swallow it or cough it up.

Food brings germs too. Your stomach's juices hold hydrochloric acid, strong enough to kill most of the bacteria that come in with food and drink, so most are dead long before the meal reaches the intestines.

Past the walls wait the guards: white blood cells, which travel in the blood. When bacteria get into a cut, white blood cells slip out of the tiny blood vessels nearby and reach them within hours. Many of these guards, called phagocytes, wrap themselves around a germ, swallow it and digest it.

You can see this fight on your own skin. Leave a splinter in a finger for a few days and the skin around it grows red and warm as extra blood flows in, and swollen as fluid and white blood cells leak out of the vessels. The thick, yellowish pus that gathers there is mostly dead and dying white blood cells, which crowded in to fight the bacteria and died there.

A fever is one of the body's own defences, not harm done by the germs. In an illness such as strep throat, chemicals from white blood cells turn up the brain's thermostat, the part that sets the body's temperature, and the body makes extra heat to reach the new setting. A thermometer shows the change: a healthy body sits near 37 degrees Celsius, and a fever runs above about 38. The extra heat is thought to slow how fast germs can multiply and to help white blood cells work faster, though much of the evidence comes from studies in labs and on animals. Sweating comes as a fever breaks and the body cools; it washes no germs out.

Now feel gently under your jaw, on both sides of your neck. Lymph nodes sit there: small, bean-shaped organs that filter a body fluid called lymph, trap germs and hold many white blood cells. During a cold, the white blood cells in them multiply to fight the germs and more crowd in, so the nodes swell into the tender lumps people call swollen glands.

Your defences also remember. Beating chickenpox leaves the body with memory cells, white blood cells that know that one germ, and antibodies, proteins made to lock onto it. If the same germ comes again, the body remembers the germ and stops it fast, before it can cause illness, which is why most people have chickenpox only once.

So why do colds keep coming back? Colds come from many different viruses, more than two hundred of them, and beating one protects only against that one, so a new cold is usually a virus the body has never met. The memory works on viruses as well as bacteria: measles, a virus, usually leaves protection for life.

Your hands can help: health experts advise scrubbing them with soap for twenty seconds or more. Soap loosens the grease and dirt that germs cling to, and with the rubbing it lifts the germs off your skin so the water can rinse them away, soap and all. Soap removes far more germs than water alone, warm water works about as well as cold, and teaching people to wash this way cuts the number who catch colds or come down with diarrhoea.

why-we-have-seasons.title: Why We Have Seasons
why-we-have-seasons.context_blurb:
Every year the world turns from warm to cold and back: summer evenings stay light past bedtime, winter afternoons go dark before supper, and snow, blossom and falling leaves come round in turn. The seasons rule what farmers plant and what you wear, and their cause is a lean you can see on any classroom globe.

Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, and that axis leans. Stand a pencil straight up on the flat plane in which Earth circles the Sun, and Earth's axis tips about 23.5 degrees away from that pencil. Measured from the plane itself, the axis stands at about 66.5 degrees, so the two numbers add up to 90.

What makes the lean matter is that the axis keeps pointing the same way all year, wherever Earth is on its trip. Polaris, the North Star, shows it: the axis's northern end aims almost straight at that star, and the star hangs in the same spot in the northern sky all year. On one side of the trip, the Northern Hemisphere, the half of Earth north of the equator, leans toward the Sun; six months later, on the far side, it leans away. The seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, which turns each half of the planet toward the Sun and then away from it, once a year. Carry a tilted ball round a lamp, its tilt always aimed at the same wall, and first its top half, then its bottom half, leans toward the light.

So the two halves of Earth always have opposite seasons. In late December, while snow settles over Canada and the north has winter, the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and its summer is beginning. In Australia, Christmas comes in early summer, a day for barbecues and the beach.

Many people believe summer comes when Earth swings closer to the Sun. That is wrong. The gap between Earth and the Sun changes by only about 5 million kilometres out of some 150 million. Earth passes closest to the Sun in early January, at about 147 million kilometres, and is farthest in early July, at about 152 million. The north has its winter while Earth is nearest the Sun.

The leaning half warms for two reasons. First, its noon Sun climbs high. A low winter Sun sends its light in at a slant, and a slanting beam spreads the same sunlight over a wider patch of ground, so each patch gets less warmth. Shine a flashlight straight down on paper, then tip it: the spot of light grows bigger and dimmer. Second, its days are long and its nights short, so the Sun has more hours to warm it.

At the equator, day stays close to 12 hours all year round. In late June, with the North Pole tipped toward the Sun, more of each spin keeps the far north in sunlight, so the days grow longer the farther north you travel. North of the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set at all, giving 24 hours of daylight: the midnight sun.

Around June 21 comes the June solstice, when the north leans most toward the Sun and has the most daylight of the year, its longest day, while the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest. The main line of Stonehenge, in England, points at that day's sunrise.

Midway between the solstices come the equinoxes, around March 20, when spring begins in the north, and around September 22, when autumn does. Earth's axis is still tilted then, but it leans neither toward the Sun nor away from it. Day and night are then about equal almost everywhere on Earth, close to 12 hours each; only at the North and South Poles does the Sun stay up for a few days, skimming along the horizon. Equinox comes from Latin words for equal night.

Yet the hottest weeks come later than the longest day. Far north of the equator, a thermometer read every afternoon for a year shows the warmest weeks in July and August, a month or two after the noon Sun stood highest. The oceans cover most of Earth and are slow to warm up, so the air over land and sea goes on warming for weeks after the solstice. This delay is called the lag of the seasons.

the-tides.title: The Tides
the-tides.context_blurb:
Twice a day on most coasts, the sea climbs the beach and then slides away again. These rises and falls are the tides, and fishermen, sailors and swimmers plan their days around them.

Many people guess that the wind drives the tides. It does not: a storm wind can pile water against a shore, but wind changes from day to day and could never keep the tides' steady timetable. Tides come mainly from the pull of the Moon's gravity. The Moon tugs on Earth's oceans and draws the water up into a broad bulge, and as Earth turns, each coast is carried into the high water and out of it again.

Strangely, there is high water on the far side of Earth at the same time. The Moon pulls hardest on the near side of Earth and most weakly on the far side. So as the whole planet is drawn toward the Moon, the water on the far side is left behind, rising into high water there too: a second bulge. The low tides lie in the low places between the bulges. Earth spins through both bulges, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides each day.

A tide table, the timetable of the tides that sailors and fishermen carry, shows the rhythm. On most coasts the high tides come about 12 hours and 25 minutes apart, with low water about halfway between. Two such gaps add up to a day and 50 minutes, so each day's high tide comes about 50 minutes later than the day before's. The Moon moves on along its path around Earth, travelling the same way that Earth spins, so when Earth has made one full turn the Moon has crept ahead. The coast needs about 50 minutes more to turn back under the Moon.

The Sun raises tides as well, but they are only about half the size of the Moon's, though the Sun outweighs the Moon some twenty-seven million times over. The Sun loses out because it is much farther away from Earth, nearly 400 times farther than the Moon. A tide comes not from the pull itself but from how much harder a body pulls on Earth's near side than on its far side, and that difference fades with distance even faster than the pull does.

Around new moon, when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, and around full moon, when it sits on Earth's far side from the Sun, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up. The Sun's tide then adds to the Moon's: the bulges grow taller, and the extra water heaped into them comes from the low places between, so the tide table shows higher high tides and lower low tides. These are spring tides, and they come twice a month, all year round. Many people think the name belongs to the season of spring, but it does not; it comes from the water springing up.

About a week after each spring tide comes a quarter moon, first or third, when the Moon looks half lit and stands at a right angle to the Sun as seen from Earth. The Sun's pull then works across the Moon's and partly cancels it, so the tidal range, the gap in height between high and low water, is the smallest of the month: these are neap tides. Lay a tide table beside a calendar of the Moon's phases and you can check the pattern for yourself.

moon-phases-and-eclipses.title: Moon Phases and Eclipses
moon-phases-and-eclipses.context_blurb:
Watch the Moon for a month and you will see it change: a thin curved sliver, then a half circle, then a bright round disc, and back again. These shapes are the Moon's phases, and the same line-ups of Sun, Moon and Earth that make them also make eclipses.

The Sun always lights one half of the Moon, the half facing it. As the Moon travels round Earth, a bigger or smaller part of its sunlit half faces Earth, and that changing slice is the phase. Many people think Earth's shadow makes the phases, but it does not: Earth's shadow touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse. In a room lit by one lamp, hold a ball at arm's length a little above your head and turn slowly round: you will see crescent, half and full, though your shadow never touches the ball.

At new moon the Moon lies between the Sun and Earth. Its sunlit half faces away from us, so the side we see is dark, and the Moon is lost in the daytime glare near the Sun. Just then the Moon's far side is lit all over by the Sun. People often call the far side the dark side, but it gets just as much sunlight as the near side.

From new moon the lit part grows, and a growing Moon is waxing. First comes a thin waxing crescent, less than half lit; then first quarter, a half circle; then the waxing gibbous Moon, more than half lit; and about two weeks after new moon, the full moon. After full moon the lit part shrinks, and a shrinking Moon is waning: it passes through waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent, and so back to new moon.

At full moon the Moon is on Earth's far side from the Sun, so its whole sunlit half faces us. That is why a full moon rises at sunset and stays up all night: as the spinning Earth turns your home away from the Sun in the evening, it turns you toward the Moon. The Moon takes about 27 days to go once round Earth, and in that same time it turns once on its own axis. Because it spins once for each trip round Earth, it always keeps the same face toward us. Walk once round a chair while facing it, and you turn round once yourself without ever showing it your back.

In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light from part of Earth, and it can do that only when it stands between the Sun and Earth, which happens at new moon alone. The Sun's width is some 400 times the Moon's, but the Sun also lies about 400 times farther away, so the two look about the same size in our sky. A coin held close to your eye can hide a distant house the same way. By the time it reaches Earth, the Moon's darkest shadow has narrowed to a strip rarely more than a few hundred kilometres wide, and only inside it is the Sun fully hidden.

Still, most months pass with no eclipse at all. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's path round the Sun, so at most new moons the Moon slides just above or below the Sun, and its shadow misses Earth. Only when a new moon falls where the two paths cross does an eclipse happen, a few times a year. A Moon farther away than usual still makes an eclipse, leaving a bright ring of Sun round its edge.

A lunar eclipse is the other way round. Earth's shadow points straight away from the Sun, and the Moon can drift into it only at full moon, when it sits beyond Earth with its whole sunlit face turned toward us. At every other phase the Moon passes off to one side of the shadow. When the whole Moon is inside, it does not disappear but turns a deep coppery red: a blood moon. Earth's air bends some sunlight round the edge of the planet and into the shadow, and on the way the air scatters away most of the blue light, the same reason sunsets look red. So the red glow is sunlight bent through Earth's air. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.

earths-four-spheres.title: Earth's Four Spheres
earths-four-spheres.context_blurb:
Step outside and you stand in four great parts of Earth at once. Under your feet lie rock and soil; around you is air; rain, rivers and the sea are water; and you, the grass and the birds are alive. Scientists call these four parts Earth's spheres. They never work alone: each one keeps changing the others.

The geosphere is the solid Earth: its rock, sand and mud, down to the hot rock deep inside the planet. Soil belongs in the geosphere too, because most of it is tiny grains of weathered rock, rock that rain, ice and wind have slowly broken into bits. It also holds water, air and living things, but rock grains come first.

The hydrosphere is all of Earth's water, in every form and every place: the sea, rivers and lakes, ice and snow, clouds, the water vapour in the air, which is water as an invisible gas, and water underground. Rain that sinks into the earth gathers in the gaps between sand grains and in cracked rock, where a well can reach it. That groundwater is part of the hydrosphere: the sand and rock around it belong to the geosphere, but the water held inside them does not.

The atmosphere is the layer of gases around Earth: the air. Many people think air is mostly oxygen, the gas we breathe to stay alive, but it is not. Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of dry air and oxygen only about 21 percent, so there is nearly four times as much nitrogen as oxygen. The amount of water vapour ranges from almost none in dry air to about 4 percent in very damp air. The biosphere is all of Earth's living things, people included.

Now watch the spheres work on one another. The sea soaks up most of the sunlight that reaches Earth's surface, then hands much of that heat back to the air. Warm sea water heating the air above it is the hydrosphere at work on the atmosphere.

The air works on the sea in return. As wind blows across the sea, it drags on the surface and heaps the water up into ridges, so most waves are made by the wind: the atmosphere at work on the hydrosphere. Blow gently across a bowl of water and you can raise tiny waves of your own. The Moon does not make the waves that break on a beach; its pull makes the tides.

Living things work on rock as well. A pine tree growing from a crack in a cliff shows the biosphere and the geosphere at work on each other: its thickening roots pry the rock apart, so the crack widens year after year.

A volcano links the spheres too. Deep underground, magma, which is melted rock, holds water and other gases dissolved in it, squeezed in by great pressure. As the magma rises, the pressure drops and the gases bubble out, the way bubbles rush up in a fizzy drink the moment you open the bottle. Most of a volcano's gas is water vapour, usually 60 to 90 percent of it, with carbon dioxide next. So an eruption is the geosphere pouring water into the atmosphere.

Volcanic ash is not the soft ash of a campfire but tiny bits of broken rock and glass. Over many years that ash weathers into soil rich in the minerals plants need, so the geosphere feeds the biosphere, and that is why farms climb the sides of volcanoes that could one day erupt again.

The higher you go, the thinner the air. Near the top of the highest mountain, the air pressure, the push of the air around you, is only about a third of what it is at sea level, so each breath holds far less oxygen. That is why climbers there breathe from bottled oxygen. Many people guess that high air holds a smaller share of oxygen, but moving air keeps its gases well stirred, so even on the peak the air is still about 21 percent oxygen, as at the seashore.
