earths-layers.title: Earth's Layers
earths-layers.context_blurb:
Cut a hard-boiled egg in half and you will see a thin shell, a thick white and a yolk in the middle. Earth is built in layers in much the same way. Its centre lies about 6,400 kilometres below your feet, far deeper than anyone has ever dug, and its layers explain why deep rock is hot and why Earth has a heart of iron.

Earth has four main layers, one inside another. From the outside in, they are the crust, the mantle, the outer core and the inner core.

The crust is Earth's outer skin of solid rock, less than 1 percent of the planet's volume, the space it takes up. The crust is thinnest under the floor of the open ocean, usually only 5 to 10 kilometres thick. Under the continents, the great masses of land, it is far thicker, often 30 to 50 kilometres, and thickest of all beneath high mountains.

The record drill hole, bored into a continent's solid rock over some two decades, reached just over twelve kilometres down. The crust there is about 35 kilometres thick, so the drill got only about a third of the way through the crust, and barely 0.2 percent of the way to Earth's centre. No drill has yet bored down through the whole crust into the mantle beneath it, let alone to the core.

Going down, the rock grows hotter. Earth is very hot at its heart, and heat flows up from deep inside Earth toward the cooler surface, so the deeper the rock lies, the warmer it is. In the deepest mine on Earth, some four kilometres down, miners work beside rock at around sixty degrees Celsius and need ice sent down to cool the air. The Sun cannot be the cause, for its warmth reaches only the top 20 metres or so of the ground.

Pressure, the squeeze on the rock, rises with depth as well, because every layer of rock presses down on the layers below, so deep rock carries the weight of all the rock above it. Think of the bottom book in a tall pile, which bears the weight of every book on top. Only five kilometres down, the squeeze is already more than a thousand times the push of the air at the surface, and at Earth's centre it is millions of times greater.

Under the crust lies the mantle, which reaches down to about 2,900 kilometres. The mantle is by far the thickest layer, and it fills about 84 percent of Earth's volume, more than the other three layers put together. Almost all of the mantle is solid rock, yet it flows very slowly: it is so hot that over long ages it creeps along, about 1 to 10 centimetres a year. Many people picture the mantle as a sea of melted rock, but only small parts of it are even partly melted.

Below the mantle comes the outer core, about 2,200 kilometres thick. The outer core is not rock but liquid metal: melted iron, about 85 to 90 percent of it, with some nickel and a little of a few lighter elements.

At the very centre sits the inner core, a solid ball of iron and nickel about 2,400 kilometres across. Temperature keeps rising all the way down, so the inner core is hotter than the outer core around it: it is the hottest layer of all, more than 4,000 degrees Celsius, about as hot as the surface of the Sun. So why is the hottest layer solid? At the surface, iron turns liquid at a little over 1,500 degrees Celsius. Squeezed by the enormous pressure deep inside Earth, iron needs far more heat than that to melt, so the inner core stays solid.

Long ago the newborn Earth was so hot that much of it was molten. Iron is much denser than rock, which means more matter is packed into the same space, so in the melted young Earth the iron sank toward the centre while the lighter rock rose above it. That is why Earth's layers are sorted by density, with the heavy metal core at the centre and the light rock of the crust on top. Shake oil and water in a jar and let it stand, and you can watch the same sorting: the lighter oil rises to the top.

the-rock-cycle.title: The Rock Cycle
the-rock-cycle.context_blurb:
Every stone you pick up has a long past. The pebble in your hand may once have been melted rock, then sand on the sea floor, then rock squeezed deep underground. Earth keeps turning one kind of rock into another, so slowly that a single change can take millions of years. That endless remaking is called the rock cycle.

Geologists, the scientists who study rocks, sort every rock into one of three great kinds, and what decides its kind is how the rock formed, not how it looks. Igneous rock, named from the Latin word for fire, forms when melted rock cools and hardens. Sedimentary rock forms from sediment, loose bits of rock, sand and shell, pressed and cemented together. Metamorphic rock forms when an older rock is changed by heat and pressure. Colour can fool you: a dark rock might be igneous basalt, sedimentary coal or metamorphic slate.

Melted rock underground is called magma; once it pours out at the surface it is lava. Look closely at granite and you can pick out its crystals with your bare eyes, pale grains and dark specks, while the crystals in dark basalt are far too small to see. The difference comes from how fast the melted rock cooled, because crystals need time to grow.

Granite's magma cooled slowly, kilometres underground, over hundreds of thousands of years, so its crystals grew large. Basalt's lava cooled quickly at the surface, so its crystals stayed tiny. Basalt is the commonest igneous rock at Earth's surface, and most of the solid rock under the open ocean is basalt, from lava that welled out onto the sea floor and hardened there. Granite, by contrast, is common in the crust of the continents. Some lava cools so fast that it hardens into obsidian, a glossy black natural glass with almost no crystals at all.

Granite hardens kilometres down, so how do whole cliffs of it come to stand in the open air? Over millions of years the land is slowly pushed up while rain, rivers and ice wear away the rock on top of the granite, until rock that hardened far below lies bare. Granite does not come out of volcanoes: it is magma that stayed below and hardened there.

Heat and pressure deep underground can remake a rock without melting it. A rock turns metamorphic while it stays solid: the heat and pressure make its crystals regrow, often larger than before, and the rock comes out denser and more compact. Many people think metamorphic rock melts along the way, but it does not; rock that melted would become magma, and then igneous rock.

Where hot magma forces its way into limestone, a rock built from the shells and coral of warm, shallow seas, the heat bakes the nearby limestone into marble. Its small crystals grow larger as it bakes, and marble has been a favourite stone for statues and buildings for thousands of years.

Slate begins as shale, a sedimentary rock made of hardened mud. Mild heat and pressure turn and regrow its flat flakes of clay until they all lie the same way, which is why slate peels apart into smooth, thin sheets, good for roofs and for the writing slates of old schoolrooms.

In granite, pale and dark crystals are sprinkled through the rock with no pattern at all. Buried deep for ages, granite can become gneiss (said like "nice"), a metamorphic rock with stripes. Deep heat and pressure sort granite's light and dark minerals into separate layers, and those layers show as bands.

Rock travels around the cycle by many paths, in no fixed order: any of the three kinds can become either of the other two, through melting, weathering, or heat and pressure. Far beneath a mountain range, metamorphic rock can heat up until it starts to melt, and the molten part creeps upward and sets as granite. Whatever a rock was before, anything that hardens from melted rock is igneous, so here metamorphic rock has become igneous rock.

For basalt, or any rock, to become sedimentary rock, it must first be worn down by weathering: rain, ice, waves and wind break it into bits called sediment, which can then be buried, pressed and cemented into new rock.

caring-for-air-water-and-soil.title: Caring for Air, Water and Soil
caring-for-air-water-and-soil.context_blurb:
A brown haze over a city, a muddy river after a storm, a field stripped bare by the wind: each shows air, water or soil being dirtied or lost. Scientists measure where the harm comes from and test what stops it, from treatment plants and rows of trees to the light bulb in a lamp.

Pollution is anything harmful added to the air, the water or the soil. Burning fuels such as coal, gasoline and wood, in engines, power plants, factories and stoves, makes about 85 percent of the dirty air that people breathe. Farms, mines, dumps and everything else add a much smaller share.

Smoke is a mix of gases and solid specks. The finest specks of soot and ash are the worst danger to health: about 30 times thinner than a hair, they slip past the nose and throat deep into the lungs, and some reach the blood. Bigger flakes rarely get that far. Carbon monoxide, a poison gas, is a danger near the flames, but very little of it is found a short way off.

Rain and melting snow wash drips of oil from leaking cars, roads and parking lots into rivers, which carry it to the sea. In 2022 the National Academies, a group of leading American scientists, ranked this runoff from the land first among the sources of oil in North America's seas. Seeps from the seabed came second, and oil spills, the source most people picture, only third.

A drinking-water plant cleans river water in steps. First a chemical called alum makes dirt stick together in heavy clumps that sink, and filters of sand and gravel catch much of the rest. Near the end, a small dose of chlorine kills any germs the filters missed. Germs are living things too small to see, and some cause disease, so water can look clear and still be unsafe. A little chlorine stays in the water to keep killing germs in the pipes.

Untreated sewage, the dirty water from toilets and drains, spreads diseases such as cholera, and as it rots in a river it uses up the oxygen that fish need. At a sewage plant, heavy solids first sink in tanks of still water. Then bacteria feed on the waste and break it down, and like people these bacteria need oxygen, so pumps keep bubbling air through the tanks. Bacteria are not all harmful: the plant keeps these alive.

Soil carried off by water or wind is lost to erosion. Raindrops hit bare soil hard enough to splash specks loose, and the specks clog the surface into a crust, so less rain soaks in and more runs off, carrying soil away. Straw and stalks left on a field after the harvest take the blow of each falling raindrop, so the surface stays open and more rain soaks in. The straw is a shield, not a weight.

On steep hillsides, farmers build terraces, turning one long slope into a row of short, flat steps propped up by low walls. Rain landing on a flat step slows down and has time to soak in, and any soil it carries settles on the step instead of rushing downhill. On average, terraces cut soil loss about eleven times.

On flat plains, a row of trees along a field's edge, called a windbreak, slows the wind by half or more just behind it, and slower wind cannot lift and carry off dry soil. Its roots reach only a narrow strip near the row, so they are not what saves the field. After the dust storms of the 1930s, about 220 million trees were planted in such rows across the American plains.

Efficiency is how much of a machine's energy goes into its real job. An old incandescent bulb makes light by heating a thin wire until it glows, so more than 90 percent of its energy leaves as heat and only about a tenth or less becomes light. An LED, a light-emitting diode, wastes far less as heat: a 9-watt LED gives about as much light as a 60-watt old bulb. Energy is never used up; it only changes form, here from electricity into light and heat.

hypothesis-theory-and-law.title: Hypothesis, Theory and Law
hypothesis-theory-and-law.context_blurb:
Scientists give three words exact meanings: hypothesis, theory and law. In everyday talk people mix them up, as when someone waves an idea away as just a theory. In science each word does a different job: a hypothesis is an idea to test, a law sums up a pattern, and a theory explains why nature behaves as it does.

A hypothesis is a testable idea about what will happen, and it is often, though not always, put in the form "If..., then...". A boy who guesses that longer wings carry a paper plane farther can test his hypothesis by folding planes with short and long wings and measuring their glides.

Some observation must be able to show whether a hypothesis is right or wrong. The astronomer Carl Sagan once imagined telling a friend that his garage held a fire-breathing dragon. Each time the friend proposed a test, Sagan had an excuse: the dragon is invisible; it floats, so flour on the floor would keep no prints; its fire is cold, so a heat camera would show nothing. Because every test meets a new excuse, no test could ever show the claim to be wrong, and that is why it is not a scientific hypothesis. Sagan asked how such a dragon differs from no dragon at all.

Ideas about the past can be tested too, by the traces the past left behind. Fine-grained rock in China has kept the feathers of small meat-eating dinosaurs as fossils: Sinosauropteryx, described in 1996, was the first, and more than 30 feathered kinds are now known. Asking other scientists would be no test: however many agree, only the evidence can show whether an animal had feathers.

When tests turn out the way a hypothesis predicted, the results support it, even before anyone can explain why it holds. Science never calls an idea proven for good, since a later test under other conditions could still find where it fails.

In everyday talk a theory can be a hunch. To a scientist, a theory is a well-tested explanation of how nature works, backed by evidence from many tests over many years. Germ theory, which explains that tiny living things called germs cause many illnesses, has more than a century of evidence behind it, from Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch onward.

A law sums up a pattern found again and again, often as an equation, and it says what happens without saying why. Hooke's law, stated by Robert Hooke in the 1670s, says that each equal weight hung on a spring adds an equal stretch, until the spring is stretched past its limit.

Isaac Newton's law of gravity, from 1687, tells how hard two masses pull on each other and how the pull fades with distance. Yet Newton later wrote that he had not been able to discover what causes gravity's pull, and he refused to make up a guess. Over two centuries later, Albert Einstein's general relativity, a theory, explained gravity as mass bending space and time.

Boyle's law goes back to Robert Boyle's measurements of 1662: squeezed into less room at the same temperature, a trapped gas presses harder. Boyle himself called the pattern a hypothesis; the name law, for a statement that describes a pattern, came later. The particle theory of gases explains it: a gas's tiny moving particles keep hitting the walls of their container, and crowded closer they hit the walls more often. A law describes a pattern and a theory explains why it happens, so the two do different jobs, and neither one ever grows into the other. The particle theory has equations of its own, yet after more than 150 years of tests it is still a theory.

Many people trust a law more than a theory, as if a law were proven and a theory were not. In fact laws and theories both rest on a great deal of evidence, and both are among the best-tested knowledge in science. Newton's laws of motion describe how forces change motion, and cell theory explains how living things are built. Neither is proven forever: Newton's laws give way to Einstein's relativity for things moving close to the speed of light.

measuring-like-a-scientist.title: Measuring Like a Scientist
measuring-like-a-scientist.context_blurb:
Scientists measure things so that anyone, anywhere, can check the work. That takes units everyone shares, careful notes, many tries at the same measurement, and honesty about the slips and leaks that throw a result off. In 1999 one mix-up of units cost a whole spacecraft.

Lockheed Martin, which built the Mars Climate Orbiter, wrote software that gave each thruster firing's push in pound-force seconds, an English unit, while the software of NASA's navigators expected newton-seconds, the metric unit. Nobody caught the mismatch, so the craft's path was worked out wrong, and it passed only about 57 kilometres above Mars and was lost. That is why scientists everywhere share one system of units, the International System, or SI: the modern metric system.

A metric prefix in front of a unit means the same thing on every unit, so a person who knows the prefixes can read a unit he or she has never met. Kilo- means a thousand, so a kilojoule is a thousand joules, just as a kilogram is a thousand grams. The joule is the metric measure of energy, and many food labels give energy in kilojoules. Milli- comes from mille, Latin for a thousand, but it means a thousandth, so a thousand millilitres fill a litre. Milli- sounds like million, but that is a trap: a millionth has its own prefix, micro-.

Data, the information a scientist records, come in two kinds. Qualitative data are descriptions in words, such as a colour, a smell or a texture, while quantitative data are measurements in numbers, such as a temperature in degrees Celsius. Both count as evidence.

Scientists repeat a measurement in several trials, because any single try can go wrong. A result far from all the rest is called an outlier. It may come from a slip, such as a misread tape measure or a toy car that clips a chair leg, so a careful scientist looks for the cause and runs that trial again. She keeps the odd result in her notes and says what she did with it, because quietly dropping data misleads, and averaging it in as it stands would drag her result far off.

When trials of the same measurement agree closely, the result can be trusted to come out the same way again. How far results differ from one another is called their spread. A pendulum, a weight swinging on a string, keeps nearly the same time swing after swing, so a wide spread in timing one comes from the measuring, such as a slip in counting swings. Even close agreement is no proof of a right answer, since a faulty tool can be off by the same amount every time.

An average of several trials beats any single one. Small chance slips make some times a little too long and others a little too short, so in an average they partly cancel, and no single slip sways the result much. The average does not show how far apart the times are, and no number of trials takes away every error.

A source of error is anything that pushes a result away from the truth, and a good scientist says which way it pushes. Evaporation, water drifting off into the air as an invisible gas called vapour, is measured from the water a dish loses. If the dish has a crack, the water that seeps out through it is lost too, so the dish seems to show more evaporation than really happened. Seeping is not evaporating: the water leaves as a liquid, and even a slow seep adds up.

When someone times a fall by hand, his or her reactions in starting and stopping the watch each take about a fifth of a second, and the delay differs a little every time. A ball dropped the same way from the same spot falls in the same time, because gravity holds steady in one place, and a quartz stopwatch drifts only seconds a month. That is why hand-timed trials are repeated, and why races are now timed electronically.

the-microscope-and-cell-theory.title: The Microscope and Cell Theory
the-microscope-and-cell-theory.context_blurb:
Every living thing is built of cells, most of them far too small to see. What we know of them began with lenses: a Dutch cloth seller's tiny ones in the 1600s, German scientists' microscopes in the 1800s, then a microscope that sees with electrons.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth seller in Delft, built his own microscopes, each a single tiny lens set in a brass plate. The compound microscopes of the time, such as Robert Hooke's, used two lenses in a row, yet Leeuwenhoek's one lens showed sharper detail. Every lens of that time blurred the picture a little and fringed it with colour, and in a microscope with two lenses the flaws of both added up. His lenses were tiny, most under 3 millimetres across, and for a microscope the smaller the lens, the more it magnifies: his best made things look over 250 times bigger, Hooke's about 50.

In 1676 Leeuwenhoek told the Royal Society in London, a club of leading scientists, that a drop of pepper water swarmed with over a million tiny living things. Some of its Fellows doubted him. Witnesses, drawings and counts all rested on Leeuwenhoek and his lenses, and he kept his methods secret. The doubters needed an observation that did not depend on him: one of their own Fellows seeing the creatures for himself, through a microscope of his own. After two failures, Robert Hooke did just that in November 1677, and the Society's records say no doubt was left.

In 1683 Leeuwenhoek stirred a pasty white film from his own teeth into rainwater that held no living things, and the mix swarmed with tiny moving ones. They were bacteria, and his letter about them is often counted as the first clear sighting of bacteria. His Dutch word for such creatures meant little animals; his English translators made it animalcules. They were single cells, not tiny many-celled animals like mites.

Plant cells are easy to pick out, since a thick wall surrounds each one, and in 1838 the German plant scientist Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plants are built of cells. An animal cell has no stiff wall, so its edges are faint. Schleiden held the nucleus, a cell's control centre, to be its most important part. Theodor Schwann reasoned that if plants and animals were built alike, the nucleus should turn up in animal tissue too, and his microscope found nuclei in tissue after tissue. In 1839 he showed that animal bodies are made of cells as well.

Both men thought new cells formed out of a fluid, the way crystals do. Robert Remak found the truth first. He watched the red blood cells of chicken embryos, chicks still growing in the egg, pinch in two, and published it in 1852, but few noticed. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow, a German doctor who had at first doubted that cells divide, made the idea famous with the Latin motto omnis cellula e cellula: every cell from a cell. His essay never named Remak, and the historian Paul Weindling says Virchow plagiarised Remak's idea, passing it off as his own. That rule is now part of cell theory.

In 1931, in Berlin, Max Knoll and Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope. It uses a beam of electrons instead of light, so it can show far finer detail.

A school microscope is a compound microscope: the eye looks through the eyepiece, and objective lenses of different strengths turn into place on the nosepiece, above a slide clipped to the stage. The diaphragm, under the stage, opens and closes to let more or less light up through the slide, and closing it a little cuts the glare so pale cells stand out.

The coarse knob makes big moves, right for finding a cell at low power, but a high-power lens sits so close to the slide that one big turn can crash it into the glass, scratching the lens and cracking the slide. The fine knob makes the small moves high power needs, and focusing never changes the magnification. The objective makes an enlarged picture of the cells, and the eyepiece enlarges that picture again, so the total magnification is the two lenses' numbers multiplied together.

elements-compounds-and-formulas.title: Elements, Compounds and Formulas
elements-compounds-and-formulas.context_blurb:
Everything you can touch, from beach sand to the air in your lungs, is made of atoms, particles far too small to see. Chemists write each substance as a formula: a row of symbols and small numbers telling which atoms it holds, and how many.

An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. Atoms often bond into small groups called molecules. The oxygen in air comes as molecules of two oxygen atoms, O2. Ozone, O3, has three to a molecule; it is a pale blue gas that irritates the lungs, yet high in the sky a layer of it soaks up nearly all of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light. Because ozone and ordinary oxygen hold nothing but oxygen atoms, they are two forms of one element, even though their atoms are bonded together.

A compound is two or more different elements bonded in a fixed ratio, and it seldom behaves like the elements that built it. Sodium is a metal soft enough to cut with a knife, and it reacts violently with water; chlorine is a choking yellow-green gas. Joined one to one, they make sodium chloride, the salt every human body needs. As a compound, salt has properties all its own: it is stable, unreactive and safe to eat in moderate amounts.

Halve a drop of water again and again, and even a droplet far too small to see still holds countless molecules. The halving ends at a single molecule of water, one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, the smallest particle that keeps water's makeup and chemical properties. There is no water atom: break the molecule, and only hydrogen and oxygen are left.

Each symbol is one or two letters, a capital first and any second letter small, so every capital starts a new symbol. Co, with a small o, is therefore one symbol for one element: cobalt, a hard, bluish-grey metal. CO, with two capitals, is carbon and oxygen, the poisonous gas carbon monoxide, and copper is Cu, from its Latin name, cuprum.

A small number after a symbol counts the atoms of that element alone, and a symbol with no number means one atom. Ammonia, the sharp-smelling gas of rotting matter, is NH3. Each of its molecules is one nitrogen atom joined to three hydrogen atoms, since the 3 belongs to the hydrogen alone. Glucose, the sugar that fuels the body's cells, is C6H12O6. Its formula holds only three symbols, so glucose is built from three elements, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; the numbers count its atoms, six, twelve and six, twenty-four in all. In quartz, the main mineral of sand, silicon and oxygen atoms link into one network through the whole crystal. So its formula, SiO2, gives a ratio, not a count: two oxygen atoms for every silicon atom.

A battery shows what water holds. A current passed through water splits it into its two elements, which bubble off at two wires into two tubes, and the hydrogen tube always gathers twice as much gas. The reason is the molecule: each water molecule holds two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom, so splitting water frees twice as much hydrogen. Both gases come as two-atom molecules, and, as Amedeo Avogadro proposed in 1811, equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules, however light or heavy the gas.

Around 1800 the French chemist Joseph Proust prepared copper carbonate himself and compared it with the same compound dug up as a mineral. Both held about five parts copper to one of carbon and four of oxygen by mass. A compound, Proust concluded, always holds its elements in fixed proportions, though the parts need not be equal. Claude Berthollet, another French chemist, argued that the makeup depends on how a compound forms, but by the 1810s the evidence had settled the debate for Proust.

In 1808 the English chemist John Dalton built such findings into a theory of atoms. Each element has its own kind of atom, he said, and atoms are never created, destroyed or changed into another element's atoms, though alchemists had long believed one metal could be turned into another. In Dalton's view, a bar of pure gold holds gold atoms only, all alike and all of the same weight. Later chemists found that most elements' atoms come in a few slightly different weights, though gold's really are all alike.

physical-or-chemical-change.title: Physical or Chemical Change
physical-or-chemical-change.context_blurb:
Burn a match, and its wood is gone for good; snap a glass rod, and every piece is still glass. Chemists sort every change in matter into two kinds, physical and chemical, by one test: has a new substance formed? Flashes and heat can fool the eye; the proof is in what is left.

A physical change alters a substance's shape, size or state, but the substance stays the same. A chemical change, or chemical reaction, turns substances into new ones with new properties, as atoms break their old bonds and form new ones.

Many people believe a change that is impossible to reverse has to be chemical, and they are wrong. A dropped beaker may never be whole again, yet every broken piece is still the same glass, so shattering is only a physical change. Melted down, broken glass makes new glass. Dissolving is physical too, and the proof is easy to try. Stir salt into water until it vanishes, then let the water dry away, and the same salt is left behind: it was there all along, in bits too small to see. An unchanged weight proves nothing, since mass is kept in every change, chemical ones included.

A new property is no proof either. Rub a magnet along an iron nail, always the same way, many times over, and the nail starts lifting paper clips. Iron holds tiny groups of atoms called domains, and stroking lines up their magnetism. No new substance forms, and the nail is still the same iron, so magnetizing it is a physical change. Light and heat are only clues as well. In an old-style bulb, a current heats a thin tungsten wire until it glows. Yet the wire stays tungsten the whole time it glows, and it is still tungsten when it cools, so the glow is a physical change. It cannot burn, because the bulb holds no air, only a vacuum or an unreactive gas.

Burning, though, is chemical. When a match burns down, its wood becomes carbon dioxide, water vapour and ash, and the black stick left is charcoal, mostly carbon: the wood has become new substances, which no change of shape or size could turn back into wood. A firework's black powder burns in a flash into new substances: mostly solid potassium salts, which hang in the sky as white smoke, and hot gases, chiefly carbon dioxide and nitrogen, whose sudden rush bursts the shell.

Even iron can burn. When a 9-volt battery touches fine steel wool, which is almost pure iron, its hair-thin threads glow, spark and leave a dark, crumbly lump. A nail rusting in the wet goes through the same kind of change, only far slower: in both, iron joins with oxygen from the air and becomes iron oxide. The dry wool takes seconds; the wet nail takes months, with no flame or light. Old silver slowly grows a black film of tarnish, but not from oxygen. Traces of sulfur gases in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide given off by wool and rubber, join their sulfur to the silver and make black silver sulfide, a new substance. Because the film is partly made of the silver itself, every polishing carries a little silver away.

Rocks change both ways as they weather, or slowly break down. Water freezing in a crack pries rock apart, but the pieces are the same minerals as before: physical weathering. Carbon dioxide from the air makes rainwater a weak acid, and over many years it reacts with the feldspar crystals in granite and turns them into kaolinite, a soft, white clay mineral that is easy to shape when damp. A new mineral means chemical weathering.

A candle shows both kinds of change at once, and Michael Faraday made it famous in his Christmas Lectures for young audiences at London's Royal Institution. The flame melts the wax, the liquid creeps up the wick, and the heat turns it to gas: changes of state, so the wax stays wax and can still burn. Only the burning is chemical, making carbon dioxide and water vapour, which cannot burn. Faraday showed where the fuel is: he blew a candle out, brought a light into the thin trail drifting up from the wick, and a flame raced down the trail and relit it. The trail was wax turned into a gas, the true fuel of every candle flame.

solutions-solute-and-solvent.title: Solutions: Solute and Solvent
solutions-solute-and-solvent.context_blurb:
Seawater, a bronze statue and the air you breathe are all solutions: mixtures so even that no separate bits can be seen, however close you look. Every solution has a solvent, the part that does the dissolving, and at least one solute, the part dissolved in it. How fast a solid dissolves, and how much of it can, are things you can test with a few beakers.

The solvent is the part a solution holds the most of, and a solute is spread evenly through it. A solution need not be a liquid. Bronze is mostly copper with a little tin, the two melted and cooled into one even solid. In bronze, copper is the solvent because there is more of it, and the tin is a solute dissolved in the copper. Tin does make bronze harder, but hardness never decides the solvent; only the amount does. Chemists call metal solutions like bronze and brass alloys.

Water earns the name universal solvent because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid. That is why rain, rivers and blood carry dissolved minerals and nutrients wherever they go. The oxygen end of a water molecule is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive, so water tugs on charged particles and pulls the sodium and chloride of salt apart. Still, water cannot dissolve everything: iodine dissolves so poorly in it that tincture of iodine, an antiseptic put on cuts, is made with alcohol.

Concentration is how much solute a given amount of solution holds. Seawater has about 35 grams of salt in every kilogram. At low tide a rock pool is cut off, and a hot sun evaporates water from it, but the salt stays behind. The same salt now sits in less water, so the concentration rises, and a sun-baked pool can reach 50 grams or more in a kilogram. Rain does the opposite: it dilutes the pool with fresh water, and the concentration falls.

How fast a solid dissolves can be tested with pairs of beakers, for water can only work on a solid where it touches it. Try halite, natural rock salt: one lump in a beaker, an equal mass of crushed grains in another. The grains are gone first, because crushing bares far more surface to the water, while most of the lump hides inside, away from it. Heat speeds dissolving too. Drop matching crystals of blue copper sulfate into cold water and into hot, and the hot one vanishes first. In hot water the particles move faster, strike the crystal more often and carry its particles off sooner. The crystal dissolves; it does not melt, for copper sulfate never melts at all.

The water right against a crystal of Epsom salt soon fills with dissolved salt and takes up more only slowly, so stirring speeds things up by sweeping that water away and bringing fresh water to the crystal. Stirring, crushing and waiting change only how fast a solid dissolves, never how much the water can hold. Keep stirring potassium nitrate, a white crystalline salt, into some water, and at last extra crystals lie undissolved on the bottom: the solution is saturated, holding all the solute it can at that temperature. Only warming the water makes room for more, since warmer water holds more of most solids. Water near boiling holds over seven times as much potassium nitrate as water at 20 degrees Celsius.

Gases go the other way. Heat helps dissolved gas escape, so warm water holds less gas than cold: fresh water at 20 degrees Celsius can hold about 9 milligrams of oxygen in a litre, but at 30 degrees only about 7.6. That is why hot, calm summers can leave pond fish short of oxygen. Pressure matters too: the harder a gas presses on a liquid, the more of it the liquid holds. At the bottling plant, carbon dioxide is forced into chilled water under pressure, and a tight cap keeps the pressure in. Twist the cap off, and the pressure falls to that of ordinary air, so less gas can stay dissolved, and the extra carbon dioxide streams up as bubbles. Those bubbles were dissolved in the water all along; no air has to get in to make them.

speed-velocity-and-motion-graphs.title: Speed, Velocity and Motion Graphs
speed-velocity-and-motion-graphs.context_blurb:
How fast is a bike, a bus or a storm going, and which way? Physics answers with three careful words: speed, velocity and acceleration. A tape measure and a stopwatch are enough to measure them, and a simple graph can turn a whole trip into one line you read at a glance.

Speed is how far something travels in a given time, in metres per second or kilometres per hour. A speedometer shows the speed at one instant. Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time, and every minute counts, even minutes spent standing still. A walker who covers six kilometres in two hours averages three kilometres per hour; if she also rests for an hour, the same six kilometres take three hours, and her average falls to two. A rest adds time but no distance, so it always pulls the average speed below the speed shown while moving.

Velocity is speed together with a direction: thirty kilometres per hour toward the east is a velocity, while thirty kilometres per hour alone is only a speed. A weather report that gives a storm's speed but not which way it is heading cannot tell a town whether the storm will reach it at all. Distance is the whole length of a path. Displacement is the straight-line change of position from start to finish, and average velocity is worked out from it, not from the distance. A lap of a running track ends on the very line where it began, so its displacement is zero, and so is its average velocity, however fast the runner went.

A distance-time graph draws a trip as one line, with time running along the bottom and distance climbing up the side. To make one, mark a hallway with tape every metre, call out the seconds while a friend walks along it, and plot which mark the walker reaches at each call. The slope of the line, its steepness, is the speed: a steeper line gains more distance every second, and a straight line means a steady speed. So when two riders set off together and one rider's straight line climbs more steeply than the other's, the steeper line belongs to the faster rider. A flat stretch means the clock runs on while the distance stays the same, so the walker was standing still in one spot. A curved line means the speed is changing. A line that keeps rising but grows less and less steep shows something slowing down: it is still moving forward, but it covers less ground each second. And a graph is not a picture of the road: a steep line means fast, not uphill.

Two runners on one straight track make two lines, and when one starts ahead but the other runs faster, the lines cross. A crossing point marks a moment when both runners are the same distance from the start line, which means they are side by side. At a crossing the two lines have different slopes, and the steeper belongs to the runner who has caught up and is passing. In 1980 the researchers Trowbridge and McDermott found that students who compared two moving things wrongly nearly always did so by judging speed from position, as if being in the same place meant going at the same speed.

Acceleration is any change in velocity: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. In everyday speech, to accelerate means only to speed up, but science counts all three. So a cyclist braking for a red light is accelerating, because her speed is changing; her acceleration simply points backward, against her motion. Everyday speech calls that deceleration. A car rounding a curved road at one steady speed is accelerating too, because its direction, and so its velocity, keeps changing. Going fast is a different thing: a car holding one speed along a straight road has an unchanging velocity, so its acceleration is zero, however fast it goes.

inertia-newtons-first-law.title: Inertia: Newton's First Law
inertia-newtons-first-law.context_blurb:
Kick a ball across a field and it soon rolls to a stop. For centuries most thinkers took that as proof that moving things need a push to keep going. Finding out why they were wrong gave us Isaac Newton's first law of motion, the law of inertia, at work every time a car brakes or turns.

The Greek philosopher Aristotle taught that things on Earth come to rest once nothing keeps them moving. Galileo Galilei tested that for himself. He rolled bronze balls along grooved wooden ramps, timing them with a water clock. A ball run down one ramp and on up a facing one rises nearly to the height where it began, however steep or gentle the far slope. Then Galileo imagined laying the second ramp flat and making it perfectly smooth. The ball could never climb back to its old height, so he concluded it would roll on forever at the same speed. Real balls stop because friction, the rubbing force between surfaces, and the air push against them; a ball on grass stops far sooner than one on smooth ice.

In his Dialogue of 1632, Galileo argued that a stone dropped from the top of a smoothly sailing ship's mast lands at its foot, not behind it, because the stone was already moving forward with the ship. Toss a ball straight up in a train running smoothly on a straight track, and the same thing happens: the ball keeps the train's forward speed and comes back down into your hand.

Isaac Newton made this a law in his Principia of 1687. His first law says that a thing at rest stays at rest, and a moving thing keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line, unless an unbalanced force, one not cancelled by another, acts on it. Inertia, from the Latin word for idleness, is that resistance to any change in motion; it is a property of matter, not a force. Far out between the stars, a space probe with its engines off has almost no force acting on it, so it keeps moving straight on at the same speed. Only a force, such as a rocket firing or a planet's pull, could change that.

How much inertia a thing has depends on its mass, the amount of matter in it, so a small iron weight is far harder to start than a big beach ball full of air. A NASA lesson pictures an astronaut struggling to push a one-ton satellite out of a space shuttle's cargo bay: weightless in orbit, it still has a ton of mass. So aboard a space station, where nothing registers on a scale, whichever floating object holds more mass is still the harder one to start drifting.

When a driver brakes hard, the brakes slow only the car, so an unbelted passenger's body goes on moving at the old speed until the dashboard or the windshield stops it. A seat belt slows him with the car, spreading the force across his hips and shoulder. When a car swings left, a box on the seat keeps going in a straight line while the car turns beneath it, so the right-hand door swings round to meet it. The outward push passengers seem to feel on a bend is not a real force. A ball whirled on a string circles only because the string pulls it toward the centre. If the string snaps, the ball flies off in a straight line, the way it was heading at that instant, along the edge of the circle.

In the old tablecloth trick, a performer jerks a silk cloth from under a table set with dishes, and they stay put. The cloth does rub on the dishes the whole time it slides, but a sharp yank is over so quickly that friction has too little time to get them moving, and their inertia keeps them almost where they stood. A slow pull gives friction time to drag them along. Try it small: lay a card across a cup with a coin on top, flick the card sharply away, and the coin drops into the cup. To tighten a loose hammer head, a carpenter bangs the end of the handle down hard on the floor, head up. The handle stops short, but the head, with only the wood's friction to hold it back, keeps going and slides farther on, wedging itself tighter.

heat-on-the-move.title: Heat on the Move
heat-on-the-move.context_blurb:
Hold your hands toward a campfire or grip a sun-baked railing, and you feel heat on the move. Heat is energy flowing from warmer things to cooler ones, and it travels in three ways: conduction, convection and radiation. Knowing which is which lets people trap heat or keep it out.

Left to itself, heat flows only from a warmer thing to a cooler one. It keeps flowing until the two things share one temperature, somewhere between where each began, and then the flow stops. Press a hot metal block against a cold one, with a thermometer in each, and the two readings move until they meet. The hot block is still warm then; what has gone is the difference in temperature that drove the flow.

Conduction is heat passing through matter by touch. In a metal rod with one end in a flame, the particles at the hot end jiggle faster and bump into their neighbours, passing energy along, while the metal itself stays put. Metals are good conductors; wood, plastic and still air are poor ones. In the late 1700s many scientists pictured heat as an invisible fluid called caloric, until Count Rumford's cannon-boring work in 1798 and James Joule's later experiments showed it to be energy on the move. Conduction runs in every direction, down as well as up. The saying that heat rises is a mix-up: what rises is warm air. So an ice pack propped under a sore ankle draws heat down out of it just as readily as a pack laid on top.

In convection, the second way, a liquid or gas carries the heat as it moves. Warmed fluid expands, grows less dense and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place; the loop is a convection current. To see one, let a few crystals of potassium permanganate, which turn water purple, settle near one side of a beaker, then gently warm the glass just under them. A purple streak climbs the heated side, drifts across the top, and sinks down the far side as it cools. Despite its name, a typical hot-water radiator gives off only about a quarter of its heat as radiation. Mostly it warms the air touching it, which rises and carries the heat round a chilly classroom in a convection current.

Radiation, the third way, needs no matter: it is energy carried by rays, mostly invisible infrared, which every warm thing gives off and which travel in straight lines, even across empty space from the Sun. Sit a few steps from a campfire and most of the warmth on your face arrives as these rays, spreading straight out from the flames in every direction. The fire's hot air rises straight up into the sky, and your back, in the shadow of your body, stays cold. A metal railing in bright sun is heated first by radiation, as the metal absorbs the sunlight, and then by conduction it passes that heat into any hand that grips it.

Insulators slow heat down. Still air is a poor conductor, but left free it carries heat by convection, so the best insulators trap air in spaces too small for it to flow. Fur, down feathers and fibreglass, a fluffy mat of fine glass threads laid in attics, all work this way. Solid glass passes heat about twenty times better than glass wool, so in a fibreglass mat the trapped air does most of the work.

In 1892, at the Royal Institution in London, the Scottish chemist James Dewar built a vacuum flask to keep his liquefied gases cold long enough to study them. Its glass is doubled, an inner bottle inside an outer one, and the air between them has been pumped away. Conduction needs particles to bump together and convection needs a fluid to flow, so the near-empty gap blocks conduction and convection alike. Radiation can still cross a vacuum, so the glass facing the gap is silvered like a mirror to reflect it back.

Shiny metal absorbs little radiation and reflects most of it. That is the secret of the space blanket, a thin plastic film with a shiny skin of aluminium, often wrapped round marathon runners after a race. Every warm body gives off infrared rays, and the aluminium reflects up to 97 percent of a runner's heat rays back toward him.

temperature-and-moving-particles.title: Temperature and Moving Particles
temperature-and-moving-particles.context_blurb:
Everything around you is made of particles far too small to see, and they never stop moving. Temperature tracks how fast they move on average. That one idea explains why bridges have gaps, why a stuck jar lid comes loose, why sweat cools you, and why there is a coldest possible cold.

A thermometer reads the average energy of motion of the particles it touches: the faster they move, the higher it reads. Because that is an average, the amount of water makes no difference. Warm a brimming beaker and one holding a spoonful of water until their thermometers agree, and the particles in both move at the same average speed, however long each was heated.

Thermal energy is the total instead: the energy of motion of all of a thing's particles added together. A mug of water fresh from the kettle is far hotter than a warm bath, yet the bathtub holds more thermal energy, because it holds far more water: its particles are slower, but there are vastly more of them. Even ice chilled to minus 80 degrees Celsius has thermal energy, since its particles never stop vibrating in place. Cold is not a substance that soaks in; the ice grew cold by losing energy, as heat flowed out of it.

Put a thermometer in crushed ice, warm it gently and stir: the reading sits at zero degrees for as long as any ice is left. The energy flowing in is busy freeing particles from the fixed places that hold them in the solid, not speeding them up, so the temperature holds still. Only when all the ice is water does the reading climb.

In a liquid, particles move at many speeds, and only the fastest at the surface can break free into the air. As the fastest particles escape, they carry energy off with them, so the water left behind is slower on average and colder, and it draws heat from whatever it wets. That is how sweat cools you. Weather observers hang a thermometer with a wet wick on its bulb beside a dry one; the wet one reads lower, and comparing the two tells them how damp the air is.

Heat also makes most things expand, or grow, and cooling makes them contract. A metal ball that drops neatly through a metal ring sits on the ring, too wide to pass, once the ball is heated in a flame. Inside the hot ball the particles jiggle harder and jostle one another a little farther apart, so the whole ball swells, though each particle stays the same size. Many scientists of the late 1700s explained this with caloric, an invisible heat fluid they pictured seeping between the particles; the idea was dropped in the 1800s, once heat was shown to be energy.

A long concrete bridge grows in summer heat, so its ends push into the gaps where it meets the road and narrow them; in winter's cold it shrinks and the gaps open wide. These gaps are expansion joints, spanned by meshing steel fingers; they let a bridge change length without buckling, and rails laid in separate lengths leave small gaps for the same reason.

Materials also expand by different amounts. Under a hot tap, a stuck jar lid comes loose because the metal lid expands more than the glass, and warms faster too, so it widens past the rim. Glass grows when warmed as well, only less.

In Padua in the 1590s Galileo built a thermoscope, which shows warming but has no scale: an egg-sized glass bulb on a long, narrow neck, set mouth-down in a bowl of water, with air trapped above the water in the neck. Air swells far more than water, so as the room warmed, the trapped air pushed the water down the neck, and as it cooled the water crept back up. A modern thermometer runs the other way: its liquid expands more than its glass and climbs the tube.

Cooling takes energy from particles and slows them. At absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, particles would have the least energy they possibly can, with nothing left to take, so nothing can be colder; even there a tiny quantum jiggle remains. Guillaume Amontons estimated that limit in 1703 from how the air in his thermometer pressed less as it cooled, and in the mid-1800s William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, worked out with James Joule the Kelvin scale, which starts counting there.

mendels-peas-and-inherited-traits.title: Mendel's Peas and Inherited Traits
mendels-peas-and-inherited-traits.context_blurb:
Why does a child look like his or her parents? The first real rules came from a monk. Between 1856 and 1863 Gregor Mendel grew and counted more than 28,000 pea plants in his abbey's garden in Brno, now in the Czech Republic. Those counts began genetics, the science of how traits are handed down.

Picture a blacksmith whose arms have grown powerful from years of hammering. His strength is an acquired trait, gained during his life. Strength built by work changes his muscles, not the genes he passes on, so his son inherits none of it. The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck taught that traits gained by use pass to the young; genetics found no way for that to happen. A child gets about half of his or her genes from each parent, but none of what a parent gains in life.

A pea flower pollinates itself, so a variety left alone breeds true. To choose a flower's father, Mendel had to stop that. Pollen is made by the anthers, at the tips of the stamens, and a pea's anthers burst inside the bud before it opens. So Mendel opened young buds and plucked out the anthers, the pollen makers, with fine forceps. The stigma, where pollen lands, and the ovary, where seeds form, were left in place. Then he dusted the stigma with pollen from the father plant he had chosen.

Mendel crossed pure tall plants with pure short ones. Most naturalists of the day expected blending, offspring halfway between their parents, like red and white paint stirred to pink. Instead, every plant of the first generation grew tall, and the short trait seemed to have vanished. Mendel called such a trait, one that shows in every hybrid, dominant. When he let those hybrids pollinate themselves, 787 plants of the second generation grew tall and 277 grew short. That is about three tall for every short one, so roughly one plant in four was short again. The short trait had only been hiding, and Mendel called a trait like that recessive.

Mendel explained this with separate hereditary factors, one from each parent, which the Danish botanist Wilhelm Johannsen named genes in 1909. Inside a tall hybrid, the tall factor and the short factor stay separate and unchanged, so the hybrid can pass its short factor on as whole as it came in. Blending could never explain that. We now call a gene's versions alleles. When a pea makes pollen or egg cells, each grain or egg gets just one of its two alleles for height, tall or short by chance.

One tall allele is enough to make a pea tall. So a pea with two tall alleles looks just like one with a tall and a short. The two share a phenotype, the trait that shows, but differ in genotype, the pair of alleles each carries. If two tall plants have a short seedling, each must carry one short allele, because a short plant needs one from both parents. A Punnett square, a grid pairing each parent's possible alleles, turns these rules into chances. Cross a hybrid with a short plant, and the short parent can give only short alleles. Two of the grid's four boxes then come out short-short, so about one half of the seeds should grow short. The famous one in four holds only for a cross of two hybrids, and the square gives chances, never an exact count.

Mendel read his paper to Brno's natural history society in 1865. Then the paper sat in a small society's journal, and few scientists took any notice of it, citing it only a handful of times before 1900. Even Charles Darwin seems never to have heard of it. Mendel died in 1884, and sixteen years later Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns, who had found the same patterns in their own crosses, brought his paper to light. Mendel is now called the father of modern genetics.

energy-through-the-food-web.title: Energy Through the Food Web
energy-through-the-food-web.context_blurb:
A food chain is the path energy takes as one living thing eats another: grass to rabbit to fox. Nearly every chain on Earth starts with sunlight caught by plants; a few, at deep-sea vents and in some caves, run on chemical energy instead. Following that energy explains why hunters like foxes are always fewer than the animals they eat.

Ecologists number the feeding levels from the bottom. Producers, the plants and algae that make their own food, are the first level, and consumers, the eaters, stack above them. In a desert, a seed-eating mouse is a primary consumer, a snake that swallows it is a secondary consumer, and an owl that snatches the snake is a tertiary consumer, at the fourth level. An animal that hunted owls would make a fifth level, a quaternary consumer.

People are omnivores, eating both plants and animals, so a person can change levels from meal to meal. A hiker snacking on wild berries feeds as a primary consumer; dining later on a rabbit, which eats nothing but plants, he feeds one level higher, as a secondary consumer.

Little of the energy at one level reaches the next. A rabbit, like any warm-blooded animal, spends nearly all the energy it absorbs on living: moving, breathing, mending its body and keeping warm, and that energy ends up as heat given off to its surroundings. Less than a tenth is built into its body, the only part a fox can get. Feel the warmth of a sleeping dog: that is food energy leaving as heat.

Ecologists sum this up in the ten percent rule: roughly a tenth of one level's energy passes to the level above. So of the energy in a meadow's grass, a tenth reaches the rabbits and a tenth of that tenth reaches the foxes, about a hundredth, because the shares multiply at each step. The tenth is only a rough guide, since measured shares often run from about a twentieth to a fifth.

An energy pyramid draws the levels as stacked bars, each as wide as the energy it holds. Counting creatures instead can flip the picture: one oak may feed some two thousand leaf-eating insects, which feed far fewer birds, so a pyramid of numbers stands on its point. Measured by energy, though, the tree is the widest level, because every bit of energy the insects and birds get came from the oak, and most of it is spent and lost as heat at each step. A pyramid of energy is never upside down.

Each step up leaves less energy, so top predators are always far fewer than the plant-eaters below them. A bird that catches seed-eating mice feeds one level nearer the plants than a bird of the same size that catches frogs, which live on insects that live on plants; more energy is left for it, so a marsh can feed more of the mouse-catchers. Eating meat-eaters gives a hunter no extra energy; it only puts the hunter a level higher, where less is left.

Weight tells the same story: a songbird outweighs a grasshopper many times over, but a grassland holds so many more grasshoppers that all together they far outweigh the songbirds. What counts is the weight of the whole level, its biomass, not the size of one animal.

Wild food chains seldom pass four or five levels, because so much energy is spent and lost as heat at every step that too little energy is left for another level. That energy is not destroyed; it has become heat, which no living thing can use as food. Matter is different: the atoms in food return to the soil, water and air for plants to use again, so matter cycles while energy flows through and out. Energy is the textbook reason chains stay short, but not the whole story: a study of lakes, from small ponds up to Lake Erie, found longer chains in bigger lakes.

Decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria, break down dead things. They feed on dead plants, droppings and dead animals from every level, top predators included, so they fit no single step, and ecologists usually leave them out of the count. They still take in a huge share of the energy: on land most plant growth is never eaten by plant-eaters while it lives, and the decomposers break it down when it dies. Tiny soil animals, such as springtails, feed on the decomposers in turn.

body-systems-supply-and-defence.title: Body Systems: Heart, Lungs, Gut and Kidneys
body-systems-supply-and-defence.context_blurb:
Press two fingers to the inside of your wrist and feel your pulse, the push of each heartbeat. Heart, lungs, gut and kidneys work as one supply line, bringing every cell oxygen and food and carrying its wastes away. Doctors long got it wrong, until measuring set them right.

Galen, a Greek physician of the Roman Empire, taught that the liver turns food into blood, which the body's flesh then uses up. In his book of 1628, the English doctor William Harvey tested that idea with sums: a heart holding about two ounces of blood beats over a thousand times in half an hour, so even a little per beat adds up to more than the body's whole supply. Food eaten could never make that much blood so fast, so Harvey reasoned that the same blood must travel round the body in a circuit, again and again.

Harvey also bound a person's upper arm tight, and the veins below swelled, with little bumps marking the valves, one-way flaps inside them. Pressing on a swollen vein, he could push its blood up the arm toward the heart but never back down, because the valves open only toward the heart. So veins carry blood back to the heart. His teacher Hieronymus Fabricius had described the valves; Harvey showed what they are for.

The heart, a fist-sized double pump, has four chambers: two atria on top take blood in, and two ventricles beneath squeeze it out. The right ventricle sends blood only the short way to the lungs, but the left ventricle pumps blood out through the aorta to the whole body, so it must squeeze much harder, and its wall is roughly three times thicker than the right one's.

An artery is any vessel carrying blood away from the heart, and a vein any vessel bringing it back, whatever oxygen the blood holds. So the pulmonary artery, running to the lungs, carries oxygen-poor blood just back from the body, where the cells took its oxygen and gave it their carbon dioxide.

Harvey never saw how blood crosses from arteries to veins. In 1661 the Italian doctor Marcello Malpighi found the link by looking at a frog's lung through an early microscope: capillaries, vessels too fine for the naked eye. Blood trades with the body's cells in the capillaries because their walls are only one cell thick, thin enough for oxygen and food to pass out and carbon dioxide and wastes to pass in.

The lungs' air tubes end in the alveoli, hundreds of millions of air sacs wrapped in capillaries. Together the sacs' thin walls spread over 70 to 80 square metres, far more than a few big sacs could offer, and oxygen enters the blood only through that wall. Emphysema, most often caused by smoking, destroys the walls between sacs, so they merge into fewer, larger ones. With less surface left for oxygen to pass into the blood, each breath brings in less oxygen and the person runs short of breath, though the air is as rich as ever.

The small intestine takes in most of the food; the large intestine, about a metre and a half long, mainly takes water and salts back from what is left, returning about nine-tenths of that water to the blood, so the waste firms up. When a stomach bug rushes the waste through, there is no time to reclaim its water, so it comes out runny, one cause of diarrhoea; waste that lingers too long dries and hardens.

Each day the kidneys strain about a hundred and eighty litres of fluid from the blood, then take about ninety-nine percent of its water and useful substances back into the blood. What remains is urine, a litre or two a day, stored in the bladder: a little water carrying wastes such as urea, which the liver makes from broken-down proteins.

When both kidneys fail, wastes such as urea pile up in the blood and, untreated, can kill. Dialysis, first made to work by the Dutch doctor Willem Kolff in 1943, cleans the blood through a filter outside the body, usually three times a week.

Run hard up a hill and your pulse races, as your heart's output climbs to three or four times its resting flow. Nerves narrow the vessels of the kidneys and gut, cutting their blood by up to three-quarters, so the kidneys get less than at rest, while the working muscles' vessels open wide.

body-systems-control-and-support.title: Body Systems: Bones, Muscles, Nerves and Glands
body-systems-control-and-support.context_blurb:
Kick a ball, and your body works as a team. Bones hold you up, and muscles pull on them. Two messenger systems give the orders: nerves flash electrical signals in an instant, while glands send slower chemical messages, called hormones, through the blood.

A newborn has close to three hundred bones, a grown-up only 206. Many start as separate pieces joined by cartilage, a firm, rubbery tissue. As the child grows, the cartilage hardens into bone and the pieces fuse into single bones, so none is lost.

Red marrow, a soft tissue inside bones, makes the blood cells. A baby's marrow is nearly all red, but much turns yellow with growth. In a grown-up, the hollow shaft of the thigh bone holds yellow marrow, made mostly of fat, which makes no blood cells. Adult blood comes from red marrow in the hips, ribs, breastbone, skull and backbone.

A muscle moves a bone by contracting, or shortening, to pull it; it can never push. So muscles work in pairs, one shortening while its partner relaxes. The quadriceps, down the front of your thigh, straightens the knee, and the hamstrings behind bend it. In a kick, the backswing is the hamstrings' work, and then the quadriceps shortens and the hamstrings relax. Straighten your leg with a hand on your thigh, and feel the quadriceps firm up.

Hair and nails grow from living roots in the skin, but the parts you see are dead cells packed with keratin, a tough protein, so trimming them does not hurt. A hair's root, though, is wrapped in nerve endings, so pulling one out stings.

In the eye, the clear cornea and the lens behind it bend light into a sharp, upside-down picture at the back of the eye. There, in the retina, light-sensing cells called rods and cones turn the picture into electrical signals, which the optic nerve carries to the brain. The coloured iris only sets the size of the pupil.

Step on a tack, and your foot jerks up in a reflex, a movement made without thinking. A sensory nerve, which carries news from the senses, takes the signal to the spinal cord, and a motor nerve, which carries orders, takes the cord's reply straight back to the leg muscles. The signal reaches the brain too, so the sting is felt a moment after the foot has moved.

Because the spinal cord carries signals both ways, news up to the brain and orders down to the muscles, a cut clean through it takes away feeling and movement below the injury. A patient hurt mid-back cannot feel or move the legs, though the legs are unhurt.

Glands release hormones into the blood, which carries them all over the body. The pituitary, a pea-sized gland under the brain, makes growth hormone and is called the master gland, since its hormones set other glands working. Robert Wadlow had an overgrown pituitary; at his death in 1940, aged 22, he stood 2.72 metres, the tallest person ever recorded. The extra hormone reached his leg bones by travelling in his blood, for nerves carry electrical signals, not hormones.

The thyroid, a butterfly-shaped gland in the neck, sets how fast cells burn the fuel from food. When it makes far too much hormone, cells burn food faster than it comes in, so a woman with the problem loses weight though she eats more, and she feels hot, with a racing heart.

Insulin, made by the pancreas, lets the body's cells take sugar in from the blood to use or store, so the blood's sugar level falls. In diabetes, too much sugar stays in the blood. In January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a boy of 13 or 14 dying of diabetes in Toronto, got the first insulin injection, made from animal pancreases by Frederick Banting and Charles Best. It caused an allergic reaction, but twelve days later James Collip's purer extract dropped his blood sugar from 520 to 120 within about a day, and he lived about thirteen more years.

A nerve signal acts within thousandths of a second and stops with the signalling, but a hormone works as long as it stays in the blood. In a fright, the adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys, pour out adrenaline, which speeds the heart and sends extra sugar into the blood. A girl startled by a firework jumps at once, but her heart pounds on for minutes, because the adrenaline keeps acting until her body clears it.

two-ways-to-make-offspring.title: Two Ways to Make Offspring
two-ways-to-make-offspring.context_blurb:
Living things make offspring in two ways. In asexual reproduction, one parent makes clones, offspring with exactly its genes. In sexual reproduction, cells from two parents join, and each offspring gets a new mix of genes. A bread bag, a pond and a garden show both at work.

Before a bacterium divides, it copies the loop that holds nearly all its genes, then splits in two, so both new cells have the same genes as the first cell, barring rare copying mistakes. At one split every 20 minutes, a single cell can become over a million in under seven hours.

Baker's yeast, a one-celled fungus, uses both ways. While food lasts, each cell buds off a little copy of itself. When food runs out, yeast can turn to sexual reproduction and form spores, shuffling its genes. Its offspring then vary, so if conditions change, some may cope better than the parent would; a new mix is not better by rule, only different. The spores are also tough resting cells, with thick walls that stand up to heat until food returns.

Moulds spread mostly by spores too small to see, which float in the air indoors and out. Mould turns up on a sealed loaf because spores drifting in the air settled on it as it cooled or was sliced, and each grew into a new mould, a copy of its parent. In the 1700s the Italian botanist Pier Antonio Micheli tested spontaneous generation, the mistaken old idea that fungi spring from food itself, by setting spores on melon slices: up came the very kind of fungus that had shed them.

A planarian, a small pond flatworm, is full of stem cells, which can build any missing part. Cut one in half across the middle, and the front half regrows a tail while the back half regrows a head, so each piece grows into a whole worm within a few weeks. Some planarians pinch in two on their own.

A strawberry spreads by runners, long creeping stems that root a little plant at each end. Grown from the parent's own stem, every runner plant is a clone with exactly its genes, which is how growers spread a good strawberry. Each seed on the berry, though, formed when a cell from a pollen grain joined an egg cell in the flower, so every seedling has a new mix of genes.

Cycads, cone-bearing plants, grow as separate males and females, and a seed forms only when a male's pollen reaches an ovule, a seed-to-be, on a female's cones. In 1895 the botanist John Medley Wood found one wild cycad at a forest's edge in South Africa, and no other has turned up. Gardeners have grown hundreds more from shoots at its base, but Wood's plant was a male and shoots are clones, so all are males, cloned from one male plant, and none can set seed.

In a flower, the stamens make pollen and the pistil holds the ovules in its ovary. Pollination, the carrying of pollen to the pistil, is often done by animals paid in sugary nectar. Bees see ultraviolet light, which people cannot. Photographed in ultraviolet, a meadow buttercup's yellow petals show dark near the flower's centre, where the nectar lies: a nectar guide, which steers a bee quickly to its reward. Bees cannot see red, though. Red, scentless tubes brimming with watery nectar suit a hummingbird, since birds find flowers by sight and have a poor sense of smell. Moth and bat flowers are mostly pale or dull and strongly scented, though such patterns are tendencies, not rules.

Wind carries corn's pollen from the tassel on top to the silks below, each the long tip of one tiny flower, joined to one future kernel. A kernel forms only where a pollen grain lands on its silk, sticks fast and sends a tube down to the ovule. In a single row, much of the pollen blows away from the ears, so too little reaches many silks and the ears come out gappy; garden guides advise a block of at least three or four short rows.

Once a cell from the pollen has fertilized, or joined, the egg cell in each ovule, the ovules ripen into seeds and the ovary swells into the fruit around them. So a pea pod, grown from the flower's ovary, is a fruit, and each pea is a seed; tomatoes and cucumbers are fruits too, sweet or not.

natural-and-artificial-selection.title: Natural and Artificial Selection
natural-and-artificial-selection.context_blurb:
Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, explained how living things change over generations. Breeders change them by choosing which ones breed: artificial selection. In the wild, those whose inherited traits best suit their surroundings leave the most young, so those traits spread: natural selection, as Darwin named it. It is settled science, and it can be watched at work.

In the Origin's fifth edition, Darwin adopted Herbert Spencer's phrase survival of the fittest, but to a biologist fitness means how many young an animal leaves, not its strength or speed. Among four stags in a wood, the fittest is the one that fathers the most fawns; a champion fighter that fathers none passes on nothing.

Darwin joined two pigeon clubs in London and kept every breed he could get, among them the fantail, fanning thirty or forty tail feathers where most pigeons carry twelve or fourteen. Fanciers believed each main breed had its own wild ancestor. Darwin concluded instead that all the breeds came from one wild species, the rock pigeon, reshaped by breeders choosing which birds to mate.

From wild cabbage, farmers chose big leaves for kale, the big tip bud for cabbage and the side buds for Brussels sprouts. Picking the plants whose flower buds grew in the biggest bunches gave broccoli, a crowd of unopened buds on thick stalks. All remain one species.

Teosinte, the wild Mexican grass that became corn, bears a dozen kernels at most per little ear, each locked in a stony case. A one-gene change leaves a kernel bare; it arose by chance, and no farmer could cause it. By planting seed from the plants with the change, season after season, farmers in southwestern Mexico made it common, starting about 9,000 years ago.

Selection can only choose among differences that already exist. For generations rose growers kept their bluest seedlings, yet got nothing bluer than lilac or purple. No rose has the gene needed to make delphinidin, the blue pigment of pansies, so there was no blue to choose. A bluish rose came later only by genetic engineering, with a pansy gene, and even it is lavender-mauve.

Robert Wayne's DNA studies in the 1990s showed that dogs descend from wolves, and every breed, from the Chihuahua to the Great Dane, was shaped from them by people's choosing. A breeder who allows only her tiniest dogs to have puppies is doing artificial selection, since a person chose the parents. Among strays in a hot city, where short coats survive better, the heat, not a person, decides which dogs breed: natural selection, though people built the city.

Each dose of an antibiotic kills the bacteria it can, and the few that resist it live and multiply, passing their resistance on, so an infection can come back resistant. No bacterium learns to resist, and a patient's body never becomes resistant, though three people in four believed it did in a 2015 survey.

Spraying with DDT, an insect-killing chemical, spread in the 1940s, and by 1947 houseflies in Europe were shrugging it off. Selection works one generation at a time, and a housefly can grow from egg to adult in about ten days, so flies pass through ten or more generations a year.

The peppered moth's dark form was rare until factory soot blackened England's woods; by 1895 it made up about 98 in 100 near Manchester. In 1953 Bernard Kettlewell released paint-marked pale and dark moths in a sooty wood near Birmingham and recaptured about twice the share of dark ones as of pale. In a clean Dorset wood with lichen-pale bark, he got back two to three times as many pale moths as dark. With no soot to blame and the result reversed, the cause was camouflage: matching the bark kept a moth alive, because birds hunting by sight, filmed by Niko Tinbergen, ate the moths that stood out.

Critics objected that Kettlewell's moths sat on bare trunks, packed more densely than in nature, so from 2001 to 2007 Michael Majerus re-ran the test in his garden outside Cambridge, setting twelve moths a night on branches, where the species usually rests, and watching for birds at dawn. Nine kinds of bird, robins and blue tits among them, took the dark moths more often than the pale, so Kettlewell's finding held up on the moths' natural resting sites. Published after his death, the work is the most direct evidence yet that camouflage and bird predation drive the change.
