classifying-living-things.title: Classifying Living Things
classifying-living-things.context_blurb:
Taxonomy, the science of naming and sorting life, gives each kind of living thing one name that scientists everywhere share. Then it files each kind into groups within groups, like books on the shelves of a library, and the groups show who is kin to whom.

Carl Linnaeus, a Swedish botanist who lived from 1707 to 1778, is called the father of modern taxonomy. Before him, a species, one kind of living thing, bore a long Latin phrase describing it; Linnaeus gave each a short two-word name, far easier to use. The first word is the genus, a group of close kin, written with a capital; the second picks out one species within it. So Apis mellifera and Apis cerana, the western and eastern honey bees, are two species sharing the genus Apis, while Bombus terrestris, the buff-tailed bumblebee, belongs to another genus, Bombus.

Linnaeus grouped living things by the features their bodies have in common, found by close study and dissection. In 1758 he put people, apes, monkeys and even bats in one order, Primates. He saw his groups as the plan of God's creation, and not until 1859 did Charles Darwin explain shared features by descent from common ancestors.

From biggest to smallest, the ranks run domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. The smaller the group two living things share, the closer their kinship. The rose family holds apples, pears and cherries as well as roses, so the apple tree, sharing that small group, is the rose's closest kin. The Christmas rose, despite its name, belongs to the buttercup family.

Common names can fool you. The cougar has over forty English names, a record, puma and panther among them. But its scientific name, Puma concolor, means one species in every land and language, so a puma in Chile and a panther in Florida are the same species. A South American black panther is a dark-coated jaguar, Panthera onca, another species.

Names ending in fish can fool you too. A true fish has a backbone, and the lungfish is a true bony fish that breathes with gills and also gulps air into lungs. The cuttlefish, kin to the squid, has no backbone; its so-called bone is a shell inside its body.

To name a living thing, biologists use a dichotomous key: a chain of steps, each with two contrasting choices that lead to the next step or to a name. Many tree keys start with the leaves. Opposite leaves grow in twos, facing across the twig; alternate leaves grow one at a time, staggered, each a little higher than the last. So a tree with staggered, deeply lobed leaves keys out as an oak; maple leaves are often lobed too, but they grow in pairs. Pick a twig and try it.

DNA, the molecule that carries genes, now tests groupings once made by eye. Linnaeus put the tomato in the potato's genus, Solanum, in 1753. Philip Miller of London's Chelsea Physic Garden soon named a new genus, Lycopersicon, for it, though in 1768 he moved the potato in too; later botanists kept Lycopersicon for the tomatoes alone for nearly two centuries. In the 1990s, DNA showed the tomato and the potato to be close cousins inside Solanum, so Linnaeus had been right: the tomato belongs in the potato's genus. Chili peppers and tobacco, also of the nightshade family, sit in other genera.

Methane-making microbes, found in marshes and cows' guts, look like bacteria: single cells with no nucleus, the walled-off store of a cell's DNA. They were counted as bacteria until two scientists in Illinois, Carl Woese and George Fox, compared the code of their ribosomal RNA, a molecule that every living thing carries, with other living things' code. In 1977 the two reported that the code set the methane-makers apart from bacteria, and from plants and animals as well: they were a separate branch of life, now called the archaea. Many scientists doubted it at first. In 1990 Woese and two colleagues proposed three domains above the kingdoms: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, the living things whose cells have a nucleus, though our own mature red blood cells lose theirs.

comets-asteroids-and-moons.title: Comets, Asteroids and Moons
comets-asteroids-and-moons.context_blurb:
Between and beyond the planets fly smaller worlds: moons, rocky asteroids and icy comets. Many are leftovers from the solar system's birth, 4.6 billion years ago, holding clues to how it formed, and some you can watch for in the night sky.

Jupiter and Saturn, the gas giants, are more than nine-tenths hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune, visited only by Voyager 2, are ice giants: only about a fifth of each is hydrogen and helium, and most of the rest is water, methane and ammonia. They are called ices because they froze as the planets formed, but deep inside they are a hot, dense fluid.

Under the bright, cracked ice of Europa, one of four moons Galileo Galilei found circling Jupiter in 1610, scientists think there lies an ocean of salty liquid water, perhaps twice as much as all Earth's oceans. A spacecraft named Galileo found the clue: Europa's magnetic field changes just as a buried layer of salty water, which carries electric current, would make it change. Life needs liquid water, so Europa is a prime place to look for it.

In 1801 Giuseppe Piazzi, in Sicily, found Ceres, the first asteroid, between Mars and Jupiter, where astronomers were seeking a missing planet. In 1802 Heinrich Olbers suggested such bodies were pieces of a shattered planet, a respectable idea since given up. The asteroids are now thought to be leftovers from the solar system's birth that never gathered into a planet, because Jupiter's gravity kept stirring them up.

The belt holds over a million asteroids a kilometre or more across, but on average they lie nearly a million kilometres apart, and spacecraft since Pioneer 10 have crossed it unharmed. Pack every asteroid into one ball and it would have only about 3 to 4 percent of the Moon's mass, a few hundredths of it, and Ceres alone would hold about a third of that.

A comet is a cosmic snowball of ice, rock and dust. Near the Sun, the Sun's heat turns its ice straight into gas, which carries dust out to form a glowing head, the coma, and a tail. Nothing is burning; the glow is sunlight on dust and light from the gas.

The tail points away from the Sun because the Sun pushes it: sunlight presses on the dust, and the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, sweeps the gas straight outward. So a comet heading back out travels tail first; the tail is no trail left behind.

The English astronomer Edmond Halley noticed in old records that the comets of 1682, 1607 and 1531 had followed nearly the same path. He concluded that they were one comet coming back about every 76 years, and he predicted its return in 1758. Halley died in 1742, but on Christmas night of 1758 a German farmer, Johann Georg Palitzsch, saw it return. It is due again in 2061.

Short-period comets mostly come from the Kuiper belt, a flat band of icy bodies beyond Neptune; long-period comets fall in from the Oort cloud, a vast round shell of icy bodies thousands of times farther out than Earth. Jan Oort reasoned in 1950, from comets' paths, that the cloud must exist; no one has seen it. So comet 67P, where Rosetta's lander Philae touched down in 2014, laps the Sun in about six and a half years and came from the Kuiper belt, while Hale-Bopp, which needs some 2,400 years, fell in from the Oort cloud.

Pluto, found by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930, stood as the ninth planet until a team led by Mike Brown found Eris, an icy world that outweighs it. The International Astronomical Union then defined a planet, in 2006: it must go round the Sun, be massive enough for its gravity to pull it round, and have cleared its neighbourhood of other bodies. Pluto meets the first two rules, but it shares its zone of the Kuiper belt with many other icy bodies, so it fails the third and is now a dwarf planet.

Meteoroids are chips of asteroids and dust from comets, drifting in space. When one dives into Earth's air, it burns, drawing a glowing streak across the sky: that streak is the meteor, or shooting star. Most burn up completely, so a meteorite, a piece that reaches the ground, is rare. Most meteor showers are comet dust, like August's Perseids, specks of comet Swift-Tuttle, though the Geminids come from the asteroid Phaethon.

gravity-and-orbits.title: Gravity and Orbits
gravity-and-orbits.context_blurb:
Gravity is the pull that every mass has on every other. It makes a dropped pen fall, holds the Moon on its path round Earth and keeps space stations circling overhead. Isaac Newton set out its law in 1687, in his great book the Principia.

Any two masses pull on each other equally hard, and bigger masses pull harder. So two bowling balls do tug on each other, but far too weakly to notice; only a mass as huge as a planet gives a pull you can feel. Henry Cavendish measured such a tiny pull between lead balls in 1797 and 1798, with a balance so delicate that he shut it in a case and read it through a telescope from outside.

A world's pull comes from its mass, and the Moon has only about one eighty-first of Earth's; being smaller also puts its surface nearer its centre, so the pull there is about a sixth of Earth's. That is why a pack that weighs an astronaut down at home rides lightly on the Moon.

Mass is the amount of matter in a thing, the same anywhere; weight is gravity's pull on it, which changes from world to world. Say a rock reads 2 kilograms on a spring scale and on a pan balance at home. On the Moon, the rock and the metal masses on the balance's other pan are both pulled about six times less, so the balance still reads 2 kilograms. The spring scale feels only the rock's weight, so it reads about a sixth as much, roughly a third of a kilogram.

A pull weakens with distance, yet gravity has no edge. As a probe coasts toward Mars, Earth's pull on it grows weaker and weaker, but it never ends. Far out, the Sun's stronger pull adds to Earth's rather than blocking it, and gravity needs no air: Earth's pull holds the Moon far beyond the air.

Near Earth, distance matters less than most people guess. The International Space Station flies about 400 km up, which takes it only from about 6,400 to 6,800 km from Earth's centre. Up there Earth's pull is still about nine-tenths as strong as at the ground, nearly as strong as down here.

Earth is some 81 times as massive as the Moon, so halfway to the Moon Earth still pulls a coasting craft 81 times as hard as the Moon does. The two pulls match only much nearer the Moon than Earth, about nine-tenths of the way, and past that point the Moon's pull wins.

Newton also saw how a thing can circle Earth without ever landing. He imagined a cannon on a very tall mountain, firing level, and asked us to picture Earth with no air. Each ball curves down to the ground, a faster one landing farther off; throw a ball level, softly and then hard, to see it. Fire one fast enough, Newton reasoned, and it would circle Earth. It still falls the whole time, but it moves forward so fast that the round Earth curves away beneath it as quickly as it drops. An orbit is a fall that never ends, and no push from the blast is needed to keep the ball going.

The space station, its crew and everything aboard are falling toward Earth in just that way, all the time, and since they all fall together, an astronaut's pen hangs beside her instead of dropping to the floor. Gravity has not gone, and NASA calls the phrase 'zero gravity' misleading.

An orbit can also fail. America's first space station, Skylab, circled empty after 1974, brushed by wisps of thin air. Slowed a little, it fell toward Earth slightly faster than the round Earth curved away beneath it, so it sank lower, into thicker air that slowed it still more. On 11 July 1979 it fell back through the atmosphere, scattering pieces across the Indian Ocean and Western Australia. The International Space Station sinks the same way, about 2 km a month, so docked spacecraft fire their engines to push it back up.

why-earth-supports-life.title: Why Earth Can Support Life
why-earth-supports-life.context_blurb:
Every living thing on Earth needs liquid water. To hold water and life, a world must be warm enough, have gravity enough to keep its air, and be shielded from the Sun's harshest rays. Earth has all three, and the Moon, Mars and Venus show why each one matters.

Around every star lies a habitable zone: the distances at which a planet would be neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water. A dimmer star gives off less light and heat, so a red dwarf, a small, cool star, has its habitable zone much closer in than Earth is to the Sun. The red dwarf TRAPPIST-1 has three planets in its zone, all nearer to it than Mercury is to the Sun.

The Moon shares Earth's distance from the Sun, yet it is nearly airless. The fastest molecules of a gas escape a weak pull: 2.4 kilometres a second frees one from the Moon, against 11.2 for Earth. The Moon's gravity is too weak to hold gas, so any air it had leaked away into space long ago.

Earth's surface averages around 15 degrees Celsius, thanks partly to greenhouse gases, a small share of the air that holds in some of the ground's heat. Without them, under the same Sun, Earth would average about -18 degrees Celsius, some 33 degrees colder and well below the freezing point of water.

Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, and it makes up nearly all the air of both Venus and Mars. Yet it heats Venus by hundreds of degrees and barely warms Mars, because Venus's air holds vastly more of it: its atmosphere is over ten thousand times as massive as Mars's.

Earth's volcanoes, like Venus's, have puffed carbon dioxide into the air since the planets were young. On Earth, rain dissolves the gas and slowly wears down rock, and rivers carry what dissolves to the sea, where it settles as carbonate rock. So most of Earth's carbon dioxide now lies locked in limestone and other carbonate rocks, which hold about as much of it as Venus's whole atmosphere does. Venus, with no liquid water, keeps its gas aloft.

Earth's oldest rocks show that its early air held almost no oxygen. The first oxygen came from cyanobacteria, microbes in the sea that make their food from sunlight, a process called photosynthesis, and give off oxygen as they do. At first it joined with iron dissolved in seawater, laying down striped, iron-rich rocks. Only about 2.4 billion years ago did oxygen build up in the air, some two billion years before plants grew on land.

Ozone, a form of oxygen with three atoms to a molecule, lies mostly in the stratosphere, the layer of air some 15 to 35 kilometres up. It absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light, invisible rays that burn skin and harm eyes, though a milder kind, UV-A, mostly passes. Where the layer thins, more ultraviolet light reaches the ground, so people below must guard harder against sunburn. In 1985 British Antarctic Survey scientists reported such a thin patch over Antarctica: the ozone hole.

Iron churning in Earth's liquid outer core gives the planet a magnetic field. The Sun blows out the solar wind, a thin stream of electrically charged particles, and Earth's field, which pushes on moving charges, steers most of them aside. Without the field, the solar wind would beat straight down on the top of the air. A few particles slip down near the poles and make the air glow as auroras. Light, which carries no charge, crosses the field unbent.

Mars lost its global magnetic field about 4.1 billion years ago. Since 2014 NASA's MAVEN spacecraft has measured the solar wind knocking about 100 grams of gas a second off the top of Mars's air, and the loss was likely far greater when the young Sun was stormier. In 2017 MAVEN's team reported that the solar wind had stripped most of Mars's air away into space.

The lower the air pressure, the push of the air above, the lower the temperature at which water boils; even high on a mountain on Earth, water boils below 100 degrees Celsius. Mars's air has less than one percent of Earth's air pressure, so water there boils at about its freezing point. Pour water onto warm Martian ground and it soon boils away, because the air is so thin; Mars's gravity, 38 percent of Earth's, still holds water down.

plates-at-work.title: Plates at Work
plates-at-work.context_blurb:
The ground under your feet is moving. Earth's stiff outer shell is cracked into giant slabs called plates, which creep along, carrying continents and sea floor. Where they part, collide or grind past each other, they build mountains and oceans and shake the land with earthquakes.

A plate is the crust plus the top of the mantle, the thick layer of hot rock below. Most plates move a few centimetres a year, from about one to ten, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow. GPS receivers fixed to bedrock measure the creep, and at five centimetres a year a plate travels fifty kilometres in a million years.

Heat from radioactive atoms deep inside Earth, and heat left from its birth, keep the mantle's solid rock churning very slowly, hot rock rising and cooler rock sinking. A plate's old, cold edge sinking back into the mantle is part of that churning, and its weight drags the plate along: the strongest force on a plate, far ahead of the push from the ocean ridges.

Where two plates move apart, hot mantle rock rises into the gap and partly melts. The magma, or melted rock, fills the crack and hardens into new ocean crust, so new sea floor is made there. This has built the mid-ocean ridge, Earth's longest mountain chain, which stands high because its new rock is still hot and swollen.

A plate can also split on land, opening a rift valley, a long sunken valley shaken by earthquakes and volcanoes. Over millions of years the valley floor sinks until the sea floods in, and magma welling up between the halves becomes the floor of a new ocean. The Red Sea is a young ocean opening this way.

Earth grows no bigger for all that new floor, because old sea floor sinks back into the mantle at the trenches, the ocean's deepest gashes, as fast as new floor forms at the ridges. Some geologists once argued that Earth must be swelling like a balloon, but in 2011 a NASA-led team under Xiaoping Wu measured Earth from space and found no measurable growth.

Density is how much mass is packed into a given space, and ocean rock is denser than the lighter rock of a continent, growing colder and denser still with age. So where ocean floor meets a continent, the ocean plate goes under, though its crust is actually the thinner of the two.

An island arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands beside a deep trench, marks a place where one ocean plate sinks beneath another. Water carried down with the sinking plate helps the hot rock above it melt, and the melted rock rises to build the islands, many of them active at once.

When the ocean between two continents has sunk away, they collide. Continental rock is too light to sink deep, so neither side goes under; instead the crust crumples, folds and stacks up to about twice its usual thickness, raising a range of high, folded mountains. The Himalayas rose this way.

Along California's San Andreas Fault, plates grind sideways past each other. The plates keep creeping, but friction locks the fault, the crack between them, so the rock on each side slowly bends and stores energy, like a stick bent in two hands. When this stress, the force building in the rock, grows too great, the fault slips all at once and the rock snaps back: an earthquake. Harry Fielding Reid worked this out from the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, which split a fence across the fault and shifted its halves some 2.6 metres.

Some volcanoes rise far from plate edges, over a hot spot, where unusually hot rock wells up from deep in the mantle. The hot spot stays nearly still and builds a volcano on the plate above; the plate carries that volcano off, and a new one grows in its place. In Hawaii the Pacific Plate creeps north-west, so the youngest island, which erupts most, lies at the chain's south-east end, and the islands grow older toward the north-west.

Plot the world's strong earthquakes and active volcanoes on a map, and most fall in narrow belts along the edges of Earth's plates, where the rigid slabs do their grinding, sinking and pulling apart. Many coasts, such as the Atlantic's, sit inside a plate and stay quiet. Young mountain belts follow plate edges too, while old ranges like the Appalachians now sit inside a plate.

fossils-layers-and-a-changing-earth.title: Fossils, Layers and a Changing Earth
fossils-layers-and-a-changing-earth.context_blurb:
Rocks keep Earth's diary. Each layer records the place where it formed, and fossils, the remains or traces of ancient living things kept in stone, show what lived there. Read with care, rocks show sea floors that became mountains, and lands now oceans apart that were once joined.

Mount Everest's summit is limestone, a rock formed on the sea floor, and it holds fossil crinoids, or sea lilies, animals of the sea alone. It formed about 450 million years ago in a warm, shallow sea. Long afterward, as the Himalayas were built, that old sea floor was thrust up kilometres high into mountains. Some 500 years ago Leonardo da Vinci already doubted that a flood had carried sea shells up into mountains, arguing that they were laid down in ancient seas.

Geologists read rock layers by superposition: in layers that lie as they formed, each settled on top of those already there, so the bottom layer is the oldest and the top one the youngest. Each rock also tells of its place: shelly limestone forms on a sea floor, coal from swamp-forest plants, and dune sandstone in a desert. So a cliff with shelly limestone at the bottom, coal above it and dune sandstone on top was first sea, then swamp forest, then desert. Read from the top down, the cliff tells its story backwards.

Sand and mud also settle in flat or nearly flat layers, as you can see by shaking them in a jar of water and letting it stand. Even the steepest slopes they build, on the fronts of river deltas and dunes, lean only about 20 to 35 degrees. So layers that now stand on end settled flat and were tilted later, by forces in Earth's crust.

A layer must exist before anything can break it, so a fault, a crack along which rock has slipped, is younger than every layer it cuts. Suppose a fault breaks the bottom four of six layers, shifting all four by the same amount, while the top two lie whole across it. Then it formed after the bottom four and before the top two, which settled later.

All this holds only for layers that lie as they formed. Squeezing can fold a stack so far that it turns upside down, putting the oldest layer on top, and a fault can shove older rock over younger. So before trusting the bottom layer to be oldest, a geologist makes sure the layers have not been flipped over, looking first for folds and faults. A layer worn away by erosion leaves only a gap; the order of the rest stays the same.

Fossils also match across oceans. Glossopteris, a seed fern, was no true fern but a shrub or tree with seeds and tongue-shaped leaves. Its fossils lie in rocks of one age in Antarctica, Australia, India, Africa and South America. Its big, heavy seeds could never have crossed thousands of kilometres of open sea, so it could spread over all five lands only while they were joined together.

The best evidence comes from living things that could not cross the sea alone; anything that swims, flies or drifts on the wind, as fern spores do, proves little. Lystrosaurus, a plant-eating reptile about the size of a pig, lived on dry land and could not have crossed an ocean, so its bones in South Africa, India and Antarctica show that those lands were once connected. Edwin Colbert's team dug it out of Antarctica's mountains in 1969 and 1970.

Coal is a black rock made of plants that piled up in waterlogged swamps and were buried, so each seam marks a place where swamp forests grew. Antarctic coal shows that swamp forests, many of them Glossopteris trees, grew there some 250 to 300 million years ago, in a climate far milder and wetter than today's.

Mountain ranges match too. The Appalachians, in eastern North America, share their rocks, their age and their folds with the ancient ranges of Norway and Scotland. They began as one long range, built over many millions of years before the Atlantic existed; when the land split apart, its pieces ended up on both sides of the new ocean. In the 1700s the German mineralogist Abraham Werner taught that one worldwide sea had laid down the same rocks everywhere, but field evidence led geologists to drop the idea.

watersheds-and-groundwater.title: Watersheds and Groundwater
watersheds-and-groundwater.context_blurb:
Rain that lands on a hill runs into creeks, soaks into the ground or waits in a marsh, and at last it reaches a lake or the sea. Whatever it washes off the land, from soil to fertiliser, rides along downstream.

A watershed is all the land that drains to one outlet, such as a bay. Nearness does not decide which watershed a place is in; the water's path does. The Susquehanna River rises in New York hills far closer to Lake Ontario, yet it flows south into the Chesapeake Bay. So a farm there whose creeks drain to that river lies in the bay's watershed.

A watershed's edge is its divide, the high ground where rain parts, flowing to this river on one side and the next on the other. Rivers and creeks run through the low middle, so in rugged land the edge mostly follows the tops of ridges and hills.

Groundwater is no hidden lake or river: it fills the pores, tiny spaces between grains, and cracks in rock, like water in a sponge. Below the water table, every pore is full. Porosity is how much of a layer is open space, and permeability is how easily water flows through it. Clay is more than half space, but its pores are so tiny and poorly linked that water barely moves. Gravel holds less water, yet its large, joined spaces let water flow easily, so a well in gravel refills fast. Silt passes water slowly, and solid granite only through cracks.

Pumping a well draws the water table down around it in a funnel-shaped dip called a cone of depression, deepest at the pump. A big well's cone can reach a shallow well nearby and drop the water table below its bottom, so the shallow well runs dry, though deeper ground stays soaked.

Water in the pores helps hold up the ground above, so when it is pumped out, the weight packs the grains tighter. Clay squeezes far more than sand or gravel, so clay layers thin and the land sinks, mostly for good. After decades of pumping for crops, parts of California's San Joaquin Valley had dropped some eight and a half metres by 1970.

A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up storm water and letting it out slowly, which keeps floods downstream lower. Drain and plough it, and the next storm's rain reaches the river much sooner, so the river rises higher and faster. Wetlands along the Mississippi once held at least sixty days of its floodwater; with most drained or filled, they hold about twelve.

Behind a dam the river slows into a still lake, a reservoir, where the sand and mud it carries, called sediment, sink to the lake bed. Big reservoirs trap most of what flows in: Lake Nasser, behind Egypt's Aswan High Dam, holds back over 95 percent of the Nile's. With little new sand to replace what waves carry off, beaches and deltas wear away; the Nile delta has retreated faster since the dam's completion in 1970.

Each summer, where the Mississippi meets the sea, a dead zone forms: bottom water so short of oxygen that most fish flee or die. Fertiliser washed off farms across the river's vast watershed feeds algae; when the algae die and sink, the bacteria rotting them use up the deep water's oxygen. A wet spring washes more fertiliser down the swollen river, so the dead zone grows larger. Extra water does not thin the fertiliser out: the rainy spring of 2019 brought a large dead zone, and the 2012 drought one of the smallest on record.

Winds and Earth's spin drive currents that slowly circle each great ocean in vast loops called gyres, and floating rubbish drifts into a loop's calm middle and stays. So the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, about halfway between Hawaii and California, gathers litter from Pacific shores and nets lost by fishing boats far out at sea. Tides cannot gather it, for they happen across the whole ocean and only slosh water back and forth.

A fish population is overfished when fishing takes fish faster than breeding replaces them. Sardines breed within about a year, so young fish soon fill the gaps. The deep-sea orange roughy breeds only after twenty years or more; one caught at fifteen never bred at all. So with the same share caught each year, the late-breeding orange roughy shrinks far faster; many of its stocks crashed within three to twenty years of fishing.

designing-a-controlled-experiment.title: Designing a Controlled Experiment
designing-a-controlled-experiment.context_blurb:
How can you tell whether one thing really causes another? Scientists run a controlled experiment: change one thing on purpose, keep everything else the same, and compare the results. Tests can break in a few classic ways, and spotting them lets you check claims yourself.

A variable is anything in a test that can change. The independent variable is the one the experimenter changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is the result she measures to see its effect. When fertiliser is tested on daisies, the amount given is the independent variable, their growth the dependent one, and water, sunlight and pot size, kept alike, are controlled variables. Setting something yourself does not make it controlled; controlled means held the same. The dependent variable must also measure what the question asks: if it asks about flowers or fruit, count them, for a plant's height shows something else.

Charles Darwin grew maize seedlings in pairs. One came from a seed made with another plant's pollen, the other with pollen from a second flower on the same plant, since each maize flower is male or female. Each pair shared one pot of evenly mixed soil, a plant on each side; a partition between them always faced the light so both were lit alike, and both were watered together. With soil, light and water held the same, these were controlled variables, so only the way each seed was made, the independent variable, could explain a difference in height, the dependent one. In thirteen of fifteen pairs, the plant from another plant's pollen grew taller.

A control group is something else: a whole group left without the thing being tested, but treated like the others in every other way. In the daisy test, the unfed daisies are the control group. From 1843, at Rothamsted in England, Lawes and Gilbert fed each strip of a wheat field its own fertiliser or manure, but one strip has had nothing at all ever since. Wheat is still sown on it every year, so it shows what the wheat gives with nothing added: about a tonne of grain a hectare, against ten or more on the best-fed strips.

Without a control group, a change cannot be pinned on the treatment. Marks often rise from practice alone, as people grow used to a kind of test. So if every pupil got a lucky pencil for each spelling test and the marks climbed all term, the pencil might have done nothing. Only a matching class taking the same tests with ordinary pencils could show whether it helped. Another round with every pupil holding one would not help, since nothing untreated is left to compare.

A test also breaks when two things change at once, because neither can take the credit. A cyclist who tries new tyres downhill and old ones on the flat learns nothing about tyres: the hill could explain it. Seedlings fed in brighter light than the unfed ones may have grown taller from the extra light alone, for light helps plants grow.

Around 1890 in Java, the Dutch doctor Christiaan Eijkman saw the chickens in his laboratory sicken with a nerve disease like beriberi while they ate polished white rice; unpolished rice cured them. To test the rice alone, feed one flock polished rice and a matching flock unpolished rice, with all else alike. Eijkman's trials in the early 1890s did just that: nearly all the birds on polished rice fell ill, and those on unpolished rice did not. Polished rice, it was later found, lacks thiamine, vitamin B1, and Eijkman shared a Nobel Prize in 1929.

Living things vary: even a good packet holds dead seeds and dormant ones, alive but resting, that will not sprout. So with just one seed in each group, a seed that fails may simply have been dead, and the result is left to chance. With many seeds in each group, chance failures fall on both sides and a real difference shows through. Darwin judged tests of only two to six pairs of plants nearly worthless.

Last, a result speaks only for what was tested. Francis Galton, checking Darwin's maize figures, warned that they held only within the conditions tested. If three brands of glue are tested on paper, the winner is the best of those three on paper; other brands, and wood or glass, stay untested and unknown. A fair test that finds no difference has not failed either, for no difference is a result too.

redis-jars-and-life-from-life.title: Redi's Jars and Life from Life
redis-jars-and-life-from-life.context_blurb:
A dead animal left out in summer soon crawls with maggots. For some two thousand years, most learned people thought the rotting flesh itself made them. In 1668 the Italian doctor Francesco Redi published experiments that tested it with nothing but flasks, paper, string and gauze.

The old belief was spontaneous generation, the idea that living things can spring from lifeless matter with no parents. In ancient Greece, Aristotle wrote that eels and certain insects come from mud and decaying matter. In the 1600s the Flemish chemist van Helmont even gave a recipe for mice: wheat grains and a dirty shirt, left in a pot for three weeks. The wheat and the shirt simply gave mice food and a place to hide. The opposite idea, that life comes only from life, is called biogenesis.

Redi, chief doctor to the Medici rulers of Tuscany, watched snakes, fish and meat rot one summer. Each time, before a single maggot showed, flies had landed on the flesh, always of the kinds that later hatched. He saw maggots turn into hard, egg-shaped cases, now called pupae, from which flies of those same kinds broke out. He also found eggs on meat and fish like the clusters flies leave there. So he began to suspect that maggots are young flies, hatched from eggs that flies leave behind.

In July he filled four wide-mouthed flasks with a piece of veal, a snake, some river fish and four little eels from the river Arno, one to a flask. He sealed each mouth tightly with paper and string. Four more flasks got the same things but stayed open. Soon the open flasks swarmed with maggots, as flies came and went freely. In the sealed ones he never saw a maggot, though months passed. Now and then a maggot was found outside, at a flask's lip, as if trying to get in.

The open flasks held the same meats in the same weeks, so the covering was the only difference, and their swarms were a check that this meat, that summer, could breed maggots. Without that check, a critic could say the sealed flasks would have stayed empty anyway.

Redi saw a second objection coming. Paper and string shut out the air as well as the flies, so a critic could say the meat had bred no maggots only because it lacked fresh air. Nor had the sealed meat simply stayed fresh: the fish broke down into a cloudy liquid and the veal slowly dried hard, yet no maggot appeared.

So Redi let the air in and kept the flies out. He put fish and meat in a much bigger vessel, where air could move freely, and stretched a very fine Naples gauze over the top. Drawn by the smell, flies buzzed round it and landed on the gauze, and some left maggots there, but on the meat and fish no maggot ever appeared. Air reached the meat but flies did not, so the maggots came from flies, not from meat or air.

The German Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher had written that dead flies, steeped in honeyed water and warmed over hot ashes, breed tiny worms that sprout wings. Redi replied that the sweet water had a single job: it drew living flies to the dead ones, and those flies left their young on the bodies. In his own trial, dead flies shut in a sealed vessel bred nothing, while maggots appeared among dead flies in an open one.

Still the argument did not end. Through the new microscopes, naturalists saw tiny living things crowding drops of water and broths, and some held that these sprang up on their own. Redi had watched only for maggots and flies, which anyone can see, so his flasks said nothing about life too small for the eye. His results stood; they simply never tested the tiny life.

In the 1740s John Needham, an English priest skilled with the microscope, briefly boiled mutton broth and sealed it. Days later it teemed with tiny life. Needham believed the boiling had killed every living thing in the broth, so to him the new life must have arisen there by a life force of its own. Later the Italian priest Lazzaro Spallanzani boiled broths an hour or more and melted the flask necks shut, and nothing grew. Needham's short boil had most likely left some tiny life alive. Louis Pasteur's flasks ended the old idea in the 1860s.

reading-deep-time.title: Reading Deep Time
reading-deep-time.context_blurb:
Many cliffs and quarries show rock in layers, piled like the pages of a book that Earth has been writing since its birth. Geologists, the scientists of Earth's rock, learned to read those pages: their order, how layers far apart match, and how long the whole story runs.

In 1669 the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno saw that layers of sand and mud settle one on another, so in an undisturbed stack each layer is younger than the one beneath it.

In the 1790s William Smith, an English canal surveyor, saw the same layers turn up again and again in mines and cuttings. Two sandy layers could look like twins, yet Smith could name each one. He went by its fossils, the remains of ancient living things kept in stone: each layer held fossils of its own, so it could be known by them wherever it showed, however much it thinned or thickened. His 1815 map of England and Wales was the first detailed geological map of a whole country; William Maclure's rougher map of the United States came out in 1809.

A fossil that links layers in distant lands, showing they formed at one time, is an index fossil. The best index fossil comes from a kind of creature that spread all over the world but lived for only a short span. Its spread links continents, and its short life pins the layers to a narrow slice of the past, while a long-lived kind turns up in rocks of many ages.

In 1788 the Scottish geologist James Hutton sailed to Siccar Point, where grey layers stand almost upright, their tops worn level, under red sandstone. Such a junction is an unconformity, a gap in the rock record. The grey layers had settled flat on an old sea floor, hardened, been tipped on end and worn down before any red sand arrived, and Hutton knew how slowly such work goes on today. So he concluded that Earth's history reaches back an immense time, far beyond the few thousand years many in his day allowed. In the rocks, he wrote, he found "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end."

Hutton's reasoning rested on an assumption later named uniformitarianism: reading the past through the present. A geologist who finds ancient ripples in sandstone, shaped like those a stream leaves in sand today, reads them as the work of flowing water, trusting that the same natural laws worked in the past as now. That does not mean Earth's face never changed: seas and mountains came and went, and rare great events struck, all under the same laws.

Through the 1800s geologists built the geologic time scale, a calendar of Earth's past whose longest spans, eons, split into eras and then periods. Layers and fossils gave each span a relative age: its place in the order, older or younger than the rest. They could not give an absolute age, an age in years, so no one could say how many years ago any period began. A wall of layers is like a pile of undated letters: the order shows, but not when each was written. Dates in years came only in the 1900s.

The last three eras are named for their life: Paleozoic means old life, Mesozoic middle life and Cenozoic new life. Geologists drew the lines between them where the fossils suddenly change, and both lines mark mass extinctions, times when many kinds of living things died out together. The Paleozoic ended about 252 million years ago in the Great Dying, which took some nine in ten kinds of sea life; the Mesozoic ended about 66 million years ago with the last big dinosaurs.

In the 1800s Lord Kelvin, reckoning from how fast Earth cools, gave it 20 to 400 million years, far too few. Today geologists know that Earth formed, with the rest of the solar system, about 4.6 billion years ago, a third of the universe's age of 13.8 billion years.

Squeeze all 4.6 billion years into one day, from Earth's birth at midnight to now at the next midnight, and each second stands for about 53,000 years. The last big dinosaurs vanish some twenty minutes short of midnight, and the human line splits from the chimpanzees' about two minutes before the end. The first modern humans, who appeared about 300,000 years ago, arrive just a few seconds before midnight. No person ever saw a big dinosaur alive.

wegener-and-the-drifting-continents.title: Wegener and the Drifting Continents
wegener-and-the-drifting-continents.context_blurb:
On a map, South America's east coast fits Africa's west coast like a jigsaw piece. In 1912 Alfred Wegener, a German scientist of weather and an outsider to geology, claimed that the fit was no accident: the continents move. The sea floor settled the argument fifty years later.

At the end of 1910 he wrote to Else Köppen, his future wife, wondering whether the two coasts had once been joined. A year on, he told her father that the whole idea had begun with the way the coastlines across the Atlantic fit together.

All of today's continents, he claimed, were once one land, a single supercontinent that broke up, its pieces drifting slowly apart to where they lie now. The name Pangaea, Greek for all the land, came in his book's 1920 edition. Most geologists held that continents and oceans had always kept their places, rising or sinking at most.

A continent's true edge lies offshore: its rock runs on under shallow sea as the continental shelf, and the shore is only where the sea happens to stand. In 1965 the British geophysicist Edward Bullard and two colleagues had a computer match South America and Africa along a line some 900 metres down, at the edge of the continental shelf, and they fit snugly.

The critics granted that Mesosaurus, a small lagoon reptile, left fossils of one age on both sides of the South Atlantic. Most explained them with a land bridge: a strip of land had once joined the two continents, then sunk beneath the sea. Wegener replied that a continent's light rock could not sink into the sea floor's denser rock, heavier for its size; it would bob back up like a cork.

Wegener pictured each continent ploughing through the sea floor like an ice floe, driven by Earth's spin, which he thought pushed continents away from the poles, and by the tides. In 1924 the British geophysicist Harold Jeffreys calculated those forces and found them far too weak to move a continent: a tide strong enough to shift one would stop Earth turning in less than a year. It was a fair objection; others added that the sea floor was too firm to plough through. In 1929 Wegener suggested currents in the hot rock below, but he could show no force strong enough; the Newton of drift theory, he wrote, had not yet appeared.

Women were then barred from research ships, so the American geologist Marie Tharp mapped the Atlantic floor from depths measured by ships. In 1952 she spotted a rift valley along the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an undersea mountain chain, where she believed the floor was being pulled apart. Her colleague Bruce Heezen groaned that it looked like drift and dismissed it as "girl talk". Then Howard Foster's map of undersea earthquakes was laid over hers, and the quakes lined up along her valley. The rift was active, and Heezen came round in 1953.

Meanwhile ships towing magnetometers, which measure magnetism, found the sea-floor rock striped in bands beside the ridges. In 1960 the American geologist Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading: melted rock wells up at the ridges as new sea floor, which spreads away both ways, carrying the continents along.

As lava at a ridge cools, grains of an iron mineral line up with Earth's magnetic field, which turns a compass needle, and lock its direction in. Every so often the field flips, so that a compass would point south instead of north, and each flip starts a new stripe. A magnetometer reads the bands as stronger and weaker, but they record the field's direction.

In 1963 Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews saw what spreading must do to that record. Each stripe is split as it forms, half carried off each way, so the two sides of a ridge should bear matching stripes in mirror image. In 1965 the ship Eltanin crossed a Pacific ridge, and Walter Pitman's "magic profile" of its readings matched its own mirror image almost perfectly.

Maps and magnetic readings of the sea floor gave geologists the evidence Wegener never had, and within a few years nearly all came round. Later in the 1960s Hess's spreading grew into plate tectonics: Earth's shell is cracked into plates of continent and sea floor together, which move as one. So Wegener was right that the continents move and wrong about how: a continent does not plough through the sea floor, because the sea floor moves with it.

inside-the-atom.title: Inside the Atom
inside-the-atom.context_blurb:
Everything around you is built of atoms, each about a ten-billionth of a metre across, far too small to see inside. Yet between 1897 and 1932 a few physicists worked out what an atom holds. The parts they found decide what each element is and how it reacts.

In 1897 at Cambridge, J. J. Thomson studied cathode rays, which stream from the negative plate of a glass tube pumped almost empty of air. Charged plates bent them toward the positive side, so they were negative. A magnet bent them too, and the two bends gave their mass for each unit of charge, the same whatever gas or metal he used. Thomson concluded that the rays were negatively charged pieces of atoms, found inside every atom. He called them corpuscles; we call them electrons, each some 1,800 times lighter than a hydrogen atom.

A whole atom, though, has no charge, so something positive must balance its electrons. In 1904 Thomson pictured that positive charge spread evenly all through the atom, with the electrons set inside it. Later it was nicknamed the plum pudding. Charge spread so thin could only nudge a passing particle by a few degrees at most.

At Manchester in 1909, Hans Geiger and an undergraduate, Ernest Marsden, working for Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at gold foil. An alpha particle is a helium atom that has lost both its electrons. A whole helium atom has no charge, so losing two negative electrons leaves an alpha particle with a charge of plus two. Counting the tiny sparks the particles made on a screen, in the dark, they saw most go straight through, but a very few bounce back. Rutherford later said it was as if a 15-inch artillery shell fired at tissue paper had come back and hit him.

In 1911 Rutherford worked out why. Only something very heavy and strongly charged, packed into a tiny space, could hurl an alpha particle back. So each atom has a tiny, heavy centre holding nearly all its mass: the nucleus. Most of each atom is empty space. The nucleus is less than a ten-thousandth of the atom's width, so nearly every alpha particle misses every nucleus, and the electrons it meets are far too light to turn it.

Rutherford's atom had a flaw: by the old physics, a circling electron would leak light and spiral into the nucleus in about a hundred-millionth of a second. Niels Bohr answered in 1913 with a new rule. An electron can only be at certain energy levels, like the steps of a staircase. It gives off light only when it drops to a lower level, and each drop makes one set colour, which is why glowing hydrogen shows just a few sharp colours. Physicists later swapped his neat orbits for a cloud, but kept the levels.

Until 1932 most physicists thought a nucleus held protons, its positive particles, with electrons tucked among them. In Paris, Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot saw a strange radiation from beryllium knock fast protons out of paraffin wax and took it for gamma rays, a powerful kind of light. At Cambridge, James Chadwick aimed it at paraffin and at several gases. Light, he showed, would need impossibly great energy to kick protons so hard, while a particle as heavy as a proton could do it easily, as one billiard ball knocks another. The radiation was a stream of neutral particles about as heavy as protons: neutrons. So a nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, and the electrons move in a cloud far outside it.

The number of protons, the atomic number, decides which element an atom is: 79 makes gold, and 82 makes lead. For centuries alchemists dreamed of making gold from lead, but to turn a lead atom into gold, three protons would have to leave its nucleus. Remove electrons and it is still lead, only charged; remove neutrons and it is lighter lead. Chemistry only shuffles electrons and never touches the nucleus, so no alchemist's furnace could ever make gold.

Electrons decide how an atom reacts. They sit in shells, and the outermost ones, the valence electrons, meet other atoms in a reaction. Sodium's eleven electrons fill shells of 2, 8 and 1; potassium's nineteen fill 2, 8, 8 and 1. Yet both have the same number of outer electrons, a single one that is easily given up, so both react fiercely with water.

chemical-reactions-conserve-mass.title: Chemical Reactions Conserve Mass
chemical-reactions-conserve-mass.context_blurb:
A log burns down to a pinch of ash, and an iron nail left in the rain rusts, as if matter could vanish or appear. It cannot. A chemical reaction, a change that makes new substances, only rearranges what was already there, and a balance, a scale for weighing, proves it.

Atoms come in kinds called elements and join into molecules, held together by bonds. In a reaction some bonds break and new ones form, so the atoms regroup into new molecules, but no atom is made, destroyed or turned into another element. So every element keeps exactly as many atoms when a reaction ends as it had at the start, which is why the mass never changes. This rule is the law of conservation of mass.

In 1673 Robert Boyle heated tin for hours in a sealed glass flask. Breaking the seal, he heard outside air rush in, which he put down to having sealed the flask while it was hot. Finding the tin heavier, he blamed particles of fire seeping in through the glass.

Through most of the 1700s, chemists explained burning with Georg Ernst Stahl's phlogiston, a fiery substance thought to pour out of whatever burns. Burned wood left ash, and a heated metal left a calx, the crumbly powder now called an oxide. A metal that had given something off should have come out lighter, yet a calx always weighs more than its metal, so some defenders gave phlogiston a weight below zero.

In 1774 Antoine Lavoisier sealed tin and air in a glass vessel and weighed the whole closed vessel before heating and again after, without opening it. The balance showed no change, the same weight as before, so nothing had come in from outside. The tin had gained 3.12 grains, and the air shut in with it had lost exactly as much. Boyle's tin really had grown heavier, but from air, not from fire. Lavoisier went on to show that burning is a joining with oxygen, and he called phlogiston imaginary.

Magnesium burns in a crucible, a small heat-proof pot, with a dazzling flare, and 0.24 grams of ribbon leaves 0.40 grams of white powder. The extra 0.16 grams is oxygen from the air: burning joins magnesium atoms to oxygen atoms, making magnesium oxide. Heat and light are energy, not matter, and add no mass.

Marble is calcium carbonate, which fizzes in acid. In an open flask of acid on a balance, marble chips make the reading sink while they bubble. The bubbles are carbon dioxide gas, and they escape from the open flask into the air, taking their mass along. A gas has mass like any other matter: sealed tight, the same reaction leaves the reading unchanged.

Wood is mostly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and as it burns, its carbon and hydrogen join oxygen and rise into the air as invisible gases, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Only its minerals, a few percent of it, stay behind as ash, and the smoke's dark soot is a small share.

Pour clear lead nitrate solution into clear potassium iodide solution on a balance, and lead iodide, a vivid yellow solid, appears instantly, yet the reading holds steady. Every atom of the yellow solid was there all along, dissolved, spread unseen through the clear liquids, and an atom weighs the same dissolved or in a solid.

In a chemical equation the reactants, the substances that react, stand left of the arrow and the products they become stand right; the arrow means yields, not equals. Since H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, H2O water and O2 oxygen, 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 says that hydrogen peroxide breaks into water and oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide is a compound, not a mixture. Two molecules become three, yet four hydrogen and four oxygen atoms stand on each side.

A number in front of a formula, its coefficient, counts whole molecules; a small number after a symbol, its subscript, counts that element's atoms in one molecule. Iron and oxygen join as iron oxide, the stuff of rust: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. Here 3O2 means three molecules of oxygen take part, two atoms each, so 6 oxygen atoms, as many as 2Fe2O3 holds. A Bunsen burner burns methane: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. On the right, carbon dioxide holds two oxygen atoms and each of the two water molecules holds one, so that side holds four, like the left: every atom that enters a flame leaves it.

waters-sticky-properties.title: Water's Sticky Properties
waters-sticky-properties.context_blurb:
Water is sticky. It beads into round drops, bears insects on a pond, climbs thin tubes and rises to the tops of the tallest trees, and its ice floats. All of it comes from one fact: the two ends of a water molecule carry slight, opposite electric charges.

A water molecule, H2O, is an oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, each bond a pair of shared electrons. Oxygen tugs harder on those electrons and keeps them closer. Electrons carry negative charge, so the oxygen end is left slightly negative and each hydrogen end slightly positive. No electron leaves or joins, so the molecule stays neutral overall; its electrons only shift toward one end, which makes it polar, slightly charged at each end.

Opposite charges attract, so when two water molecules meet, the oxygen end of one draws a hydrogen end of the other. That pull, a hydrogen bond, is far weaker than the bonds inside a molecule and is not a shared pair of electrons, but each molecule makes several at once. Together these bonds give water its cohesion, its cling to itself.

Cohesion draws water's surface in as tight as it will go, and a ball wraps its water in less surface than any other shape. Aboard the space station, where the station and everything in it fall around Earth together, a loose blob of water does not sag under its weight, so its molecules pull it into the shape with least surface: a nearly perfect ball. The drop's own gravity is far too weak to round it; even an icy moon 420 kilometres across can stay lumpy.

Cohesion also gives water a skin. Deep down, each molecule is tugged equally on every side, so the pulls cancel. A molecule at the top has water only beside and below it and almost nothing pulling from the air above, so the surface molecules are pulled inward by the water around and below them. The top layer draws tight: surface tension, which lets a water strider dimple a pond without sinking.

That skin can bear a steel paper clip set down gently, though steel is nearly eight times denser (heavier for its size) than water. A soap molecule has one end drawn to water and one end that is not, so soap crowds into the surface with those other ends poking into the air. There it weakens the pull of the surface molecules on each other, cutting their grip to less than half, and the clip sinks.

Water also clings to other things: adhesion. Water clings to glass more than to itself, so in a narrow glass tube it creeps up the wall, its surface curving up at the edges, and draws a column up above the level outside. Mercury, a liquid metal, clings to itself far more than to glass, so in a tube dipped in mercury the surface bulges and is held down below the level outside.

In 1718 the English doctor James Jurin showed the Royal Society how water rises in glass tubes of different widths. The narrower the tube, the higher the water climbed: half as wide, twice as high, and a tube 0.4 millimetres across lifts water about 7 centimetres. The glass pulls the water up all round the edge of its surface, and a narrow tube has less water to hold up for each bit of edge. Francis Hauksbee had already shown that the glass's thickness makes no difference.

In 1894 John Joly and Henry Dixon explained how cohesion and adhesion lift water up a coast redwood, over 100 metres, and their explanation is still the leading one. As water evaporates from the leaves, it tugs on the water behind it in the wood's thin tubes. Since water clings to itself and to the tube walls, the tug passes down an unbroken thread to the roots: evaporation at the leaves pulls up a clinging chain of water. Eduard Strasburger found water still rising in plants whose living cells had been poisoned, so no living pump is needed.

Hydrogen bonds even explain floating ice. As water freezes, each molecule's charged ends lock onto exactly four neighbours, building an open, six-sided pattern with empty gaps. In the liquid the molecules tumble closer together, but in ice they lock into an open pattern, held farther apart, so water swells by about nine percent as it freezes, and the ice, less dense than the water, floats. The molecules themselves stay the same size.

acids-bases-and-ph.title: Acids, Bases and pH
acids-bases-and-ph.context_blurb:
Acids and bases are all around: acid in a car battery, in polluted rain and in your own stomach, bases in soap and drain cleaner. Chemists rank them all on the pH scale, from 0 to 14, with pure water at 7 in the middle.

In 1884 the chemist Svante Arrhenius argued that an acid gives water extra hydrogen ions, which are hydrogen atoms carrying an electric charge. A base is the other kind: it gives water hydroxide ions and uses acid up. Pure water is neutral, holding equal numbers of the two ions.

An indicator is a dye that changes colour with acid or base. Litmus, a dye from lichens, was already in use around 1300. Red litmus turns blue in a base and blue litmus reddens in an acid, and that is all it says, never a number. Soapy water near pH 9 or 10 and household ammonia near 11.5, far more basic, turn red litmus the very same blue, so litmus shows that both are bases but not which is stronger.

The purple juice of red cabbage is an indicator too. Its colour comes from a pigment, a coloured substance, called anthocyanin. In an acid the pigment gains hydrogen ions, and in a base it loses them; each change reshapes its molecule and gives it a new colour: red in acid, purple near neutral, then blue, green and, in the strongest bases, yellow.

Litmus could tell acid from base, but chemists had no simple, agreed way to write how acidic a liquid was: the amount of hydrogen ions in pure water is written 0.0000001. In 1909 the Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, head of chemistry at Copenhagen's Carlsberg Laboratory, a brewery's research lab, was studying proteins and enzymes, which acidity changes. He turned each of those tiny amounts into one short number for how acidic a sample is, and called it pH. Pure water became 7; acids, with more hydrogen ions, sit lower, and bases higher.

Each step down the scale means ten times as many hydrogen ions, and the farther a liquid sits from 7, on either side, the stronger it is. Sulfuric acid, the battery acid in a car, sits below pH 1; sodium hydroxide, or lye, used to clear drains, sits at 14. Both burn skin badly, since strong bases burn as acids do. Many people think only acids are dangerous, but lye eats deep into skin, and some strong bases do more harm than acids.

The body watches its own pH closely. Healthy blood is held between 7.35 and 7.45, just above 7, so it is slightly basic. Below 7.35 doctors call it acidosis, and below about 7.2 the danger to life climbs steeply.

Stomach juice is the opposite: hydrochloric acid near pH 2. Yet the stomach wall survives, because living cells in its lining cover it with thick mucus, a slimy layer, and give off bicarbonate, a base, into that layer: a coat of mucus with a base mixed into it. The base neutralises, or uses up, the acid that reaches it, so the pH climbs from about 2 in the middle of the stomach to nearly 7 against the wall. The cells themselves are not acid-proof.

The gullet, the tube from mouth to stomach, has no thick coat of mucus and base, only a little base from small glands and swallowed spit, so acid splashing up into it burns: heartburn. An antacid tablet is a base that uses up some of the stomach's acid, leaving fewer hydrogen ions, so the pH rises toward 7, from between 1.5 and 3.5 to about 4 or 5, never all the way to neutral.

Rain turned acid by smoke from coal-burning power stations can drag a lake from neutral pH 7 down to pH 5, where most fish eggs cannot hatch. Those two steps mean ten times ten as many hydrogen ions, so the lake is 100 times as acidic: count the steps, not the numbers.

The rock beneath matters too. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate, which acts as a base, and many antacid tablets are made of it. As acid water soaks through limestone, the rock dissolves a little and uses the acid up, so the limestone lake, whose rock neutralises acid, stays near neutral. Granite resists acid, which is why it lasts in buildings, but a rock that resists acid uses up very little of it, so lakes on granite grow more acidic.

newtons-laws-force-mass-and-acceleration.title: Newton's Laws: Force, Mass and Acceleration
newtons-laws-force-mass-and-acceleration.context_blurb:
A force is a push or a pull, and whenever something speeds up, slows down or turns, a force is at work. Isaac Newton set out the rules in 1687 in his Principia, near the book's start, just after eight definitions: three laws of motion that still steer rockets and footballs.

The second law links three things. Acceleration is any change in speed or direction, measured as how much the speed changes each second. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, and net force is the total of all the forces on it, once opposite pushes cancel. One newton of force speeds up 1 kilogram by 1 metre per second every second.

In a classic test, a spring scale pulls a cart along an almost frictionless track, where hardly any rubbing holds it back, with a steady 1 newton, then 2, 3 and 4. Twice the pull gives twice the acceleration, so the graph is a straight line rising from zero: with the mass fixed, acceleration grows in step with the net force. A steady pull gives a steady speeding up, not a steady speed.

Mass works the other way, since acceleration is the net force divided by the mass. Give a truck loaded to twice its empty mass the same net force, and its acceleration is half as great. Turned around, force equals mass times acceleration: if two friends as heavy as a girl on a light sled climb on with her, the mass triples, so the puller must pull three times as hard for the same acceleration. Smooth ice removes friction, not mass. A rocket burning its fuel shows the rule too: with a steady push on less and less mass, its acceleration grows as the craft gets lighter.

Weight, the pull of gravity on an object, grows in step with mass. In 1971 on the Moon, the Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather together before a television camera. The Moon pulled far harder on the hammer, but the hammer had far more mass to speed up, so its acceleration was the same as the feather's, and both hit the dust at once, as Galileo had concluded. On Earth only the air holds a feather back: in a vast Ohio vacuum chamber, pumped empty of air, feathers and a bowling ball fall together.

Mass is not weight. On the International Space Station, Earth still pulls on an astronaut about 90 percent as hard as on the ground, but he and the station fall around Earth together, so he presses on nothing and a scale reads zero. To find his mass, a device gives him a known push from springs and tracks his acceleration, and a laptop divides force by acceleration, to within about 0.2 kilograms.

Acceleration always points the way the net force does. A striker's kick speeds the ball up for as long as his boot pushes it, so the ball moves fastest at the instant it leaves his boot. Then the grass and the air push against its motion, and it slows. In a catch, the mitt pushes a fastball back toward the pitcher, so the net force and the ball's acceleration both point back toward the pitcher while it still moves forward: a slowing object accelerates backward.

The ball pushes forward on the mitt just as hard, but that push acts on the mitt, not on the ball. This is Newton's third law: two objects always push on each other equally hard, in opposite directions. Many people expect a heavy tackler to push harder than the ball carrier he hits, but the pushes match. Having twice the mass, the tackler gets half the acceleration, so the ball carrier's acceleration is twice the tackler's.

The Saturn V Moon rocket's five engines drove gas down, and the gas pushed back up with a force of about 34 million newtons, against a full weight of about 28 million. Only the engines' push less the rocket's weight could speed it up: some 6 million newtons for nearly 3 million kilograms, a gain of about 2 metres per second each second. Drag from the air needs motion to build up, so at liftoff it hardly counted. As the fuel burned off, the acceleration climbed until the crew felt about four times their usual weight.

describing-waves.title: Amplitude, Wavelength and Frequency
describing-waves.context_blurb:
A wave, such as sound or light, carries energy from place to place, while the material it passes through stays put. Three measurements describe any wave, and bold experiments with cannon, an underwater bell and lanterns on hills found how fast sound and light travel.

Sound is a wave of squeezes and stretches in air, water or any other material. A loudspeaker's cone shoves the air forward and back. How far it swings sets the wave's amplitude: a bigger amplitude carries more energy and sounds louder. How many times it swings each second sets the frequency, counted in hertz and heard as pitch. Turn up a steady note and the cone swings farther, just as often, so the pitch stays the same.

Musicians have known since the ancient Greeks that a shorter string sounds higher, and in 1636 the French friar Marin Mersenne found the law linking a string's frequency to its length, how tightly it is stretched and its weight. A shorter string vibrates more times each second: one half as long vibrates twice as often, an octave higher.

Wavelength is the distance from one crest, or peak, to the next, and a wave's speed equals its frequency times its wavelength. So if a girl shaking a rope moves her hand twice as often while the waves keep their speed, the crests lie half as far apart.

Ernst Chladni made such waves visible by bowing the edge of a sand-strewn metal plate until it sang; the sand leapt off the shaking parts and settled on nodal lines, where the plate held still. At a much higher note, with shorter waves across the plate, the sand broke into more lines, set closer together. He published his figures in 1787 and years later showed them in Paris to Napoleon himself.

In 1635 Pierre Gassendi timed distant cannon from flash to bang and showed that low and high sounds keep the same speed, though Aristotle had taught that high sounds are faster. In 1738 the Paris Academy of Sciences sent a team to time cannon over some 28 kilometres, and it found loud and faint bangs equally fast, at about 337 metres a second. Neither pitch nor loudness changes the speed of sound, which in room-temperature air is about 343 metres a second.

Lightning's flash arrives almost at once, but its thunder covers only about a kilometre every three seconds, so a wait of nine seconds puts the lightning about 3 kilometres away.

On Lake Geneva in the 1820s, Charles Sturm and Jean-Daniel Colladon rang an underwater bell as gunpowder flashed above it, and timed the sound from a boat over ten kilometres off: 1,435 metres a second, about four times as fast as in air. Stiffness, how hard a material is to squeeze, speeds sound up, while density, how much mass fills each bit of space, slows it. Water is far denser than air but far stiffer, and stiffness wins.

Steel carries sound at nearly 6,000 metres a second, so an ear on a long railing hears a tap through the metal first. A solid's particles are tightly bound to one another, so a push on one reaches its neighbours almost at once. Steel's particles, mostly iron, are heavier than air's, but stiffness wins again, and each particle only shakes about its own place.

Light is far faster. In 1638 Galileo described a test with lanterns on two distant hills: one man uncovers his, a partner answers as soon as he spots it, and the first times the reply. Galileo could not settle whether light is instantaneous, and judged that if not, it is extraordinarily rapid. It travels about 300,000 kilometres in a second, so a trip to a hill a few kilometres away and back takes a few hundred-thousandths of a second, far too quick to catch.

At the Paris Observatory, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer timed Io, one of Jupiter's moons, as it slipped into the planet's shadow or out of it. As Earth pulled away from Jupiter, each eclipse ran later than predicted, and as Earth drew closer, earlier. In 1676 he explained why: from farther away, Io's light has farther to go, so light takes time to cross the space to Earth, about 22 minutes across the width of Earth's orbit. Christiaan Huygens turned that into about 220,000 kilometres a second.

the-electromagnetic-spectrum.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
the-electromagnetic-spectrum.context_blurb:
Phone calls, thermal cameras, sunburn and X-ray pictures all come from one family of waves, and visible light is only a thin slice of it. These electromagnetic waves, ripples of electricity and magnetism, need no air and cross empty space at the speed of light. Their wavelengths decide what each can do.

Frequency is how many waves pass each second, and wavelength is the distance from crest to crest; since all share one speed, the higher the frequency, the shorter the wave. In order of rising frequency come radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light from red to violet, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

Within visible light, wavelength is colour. In nanometres, billionths of a metre, visible light runs from violet at about 400 to red at about 700, so a laser shining at 650 nanometres glows red, the colour of lowest frequency.

In 1800 William Herschel split sunlight with a prism and set a black-bulbed thermometer in each colour. The readings rose toward the red and peaked just past it, in the dark. Two more blackened thermometers kept out of the light read cooler than every colour, so the warmth came from rays in sunlight that eyes cannot see. Herschel came to think heat rays differed from light; they are now known to be a kind of light, infrared.

In 1801 Johann Ritter, spurred by Herschel's find, laid paper wet with silver chloride, which blackens in light, across a prism's colours and beyond. It darkened faster in violet than in red, and fastest of all just beyond the violet end, where nothing showed. His chemical rays are now called ultraviolet, meaning beyond the violet.

At Karlsruhe in 1887, Heinrich Hertz made sparks jump between two metal rods, and a wire loop a few metres off, joined to nothing, sparked in reply. Reflecting the waves from zinc, he measured their length and found that they travel as fast as light, and reflect and bend as light does. They were the waves James Clerk Maxwell had predicted, now called radio waves.

In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen found that a discharge tube shut in black cardboard still made a coated screen across the room glow, and he named the unknown rays X-rays. They pass easily through flesh, wood and paper, but denser things stop more of them. When he photographed the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, the bones and her ring cast shadows and the flesh barely showed: bone stops more of the rays than flesh does.

A mobile phone talks to its tower with radio waves, too long for eyes to see: a millimetre to many kilometres long, while visible light's waves are under a thousandth of a millimetre. Sound is something else, a shaking of air, made by the phone's speaker only at the very end.

In a microwave oven, a device called a magnetron makes microwaves some 12 centimetres long. A water molecule has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, so the changing electric field makes the molecules twist to and fro billions of times a second, and that jostling heats the water. Glass hardly absorbs microwaves, so an empty beaker stays cool.

Everything warm gives off infrared. A body at 37 degrees Celsius gives off about one and a half times as much as the cool ground, and a thermal camera shows small differences in warmth. So in total darkness it sees a lost hiker glow: it picks up infrared light given off by his warm body.

Light comes in tiny packets of energy called photons, and the higher the frequency, the more energy each one carries. Each packet of ultraviolet carries more energy than one of red light, from its higher frequency, enough to damage a germ's DNA, its genetic material, so that it cannot multiply. A bright red lamp may pour out more energy in all, but each of its packets is too weak, however many arrive.

Gamma rays, whose packets carry the most energy of all, pass deep through flesh and bone and damage the DNA of the cells along their path, healthy or not. The Gamma Knife aims some 200 thin beams from cobalt sources around the head to meet at a brain tumour. Each beam alone does little harm, but where they cross the tumour gets a dose that destroys it, while one strong beam would harm all the healthy brain along its path.

fields-pushes-and-pulls-without-touching.title: Fields: Pushes and Pulls Without Touching
fields-pushes-and-pulls-without-touching.context_blurb:
Hold a magnet over a paper clip and the clip leaps up before anything touches it. Physicists explain such forces at a distance with fields: a field is the space around a charged object or a magnet where it pushes or pulls on other things. Fields steer every compass and hold some doors shut.

Every atom holds positive protons, locked in its centre, the nucleus, and light negative electrons, which move far more easily. Hair gives up electrons more easily than rubber, so rubbing a balloon on dry hair carries electrons off the hair and onto the balloon. The balloon turns negative and the hair, short of electrons, positive; no charge is made, and no proton moves.

Like charges, both positive or both negative, repel, and unlike charges attract, so balloon and hair cling. Rub two balloons on the same hair and hang them on threads, and they swing apart: both carry the same kind of charge, and like charges push each other away across the gap. More charge gives a harder push, and the push weakens as they spread apart.

A rubbed balloon even clings to a wall with no charge. The balloon's negative charge pushes the wall's like charges a little way back and draws the wall's opposite charges a little nearer, so the patch under the balloon turns slightly positive. Electric forces weaken with distance, so the nearer pull beats the farther push. On a metal door its extra electrons drain away, and it drops.

Magnets have their own rule: each has a north and a south pole, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract. William Gilbert, an English doctor, studied them by experiment. He carved a lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, into a sphere, his terrella or little Earth. In 1581 the mariner Robert Norman had found that a compass needle free to tilt dips below level. Over Gilbert's ball such a needle lay level above the middle and dipped ever more steeply nearer a pole, until over the pole it pointed straight down. Since compasses dip that way across Earth, Gilbert argued in De Magnete, in 1600, that Earth itself is a giant magnet.

A compass needle's N end is its north-seeking pole, drawn toward the North Magnetic Pole in the Arctic. Since unlike poles attract, that pole must, by its kind, be a south pole: it is named for where it lies, not for what it is.

Earth is by far the stronger magnet, but its field at the surface is weak, and a magnet's field fades very fast with distance. So a few centimetres from a small bar magnet its field is many times Earth's, and a compass needle turns to face it; across the room its field falls far below Earth's, and the needle swings back to north.

Until 1820 no one had shown a link between electricity and magnetism. That April, lecturing in Copenhagen, Hans Christian Oersted sent a current through a wire over a compass needle that sat under glass. The needle turned aside from north, and when he broke the circuit it settled back. No current could reach the needle through the glass, so the current in the wire must have made a magnetic field, and that field turned the needle. Later tests showed the field runs in circles around the wire.

A coil of wire carrying a current is an electromagnet, a magnet made by electric current. Its strength grows with the current and with the number of turns, so winding more turns of the same wire onto a nail lets it lift more paper clips. From 1830 Joseph Henry wrapped his wire in silk so he could wind it layer on layer. An iron core matters most: it can make a coil thousands of times stronger than the coil alone.

An electromagnet is a magnet only while current flows. A magnetic lock grips a steel plate on a door with a force of some twelve hundred pounds, yet if the lock loses its power, the grip vanishes at once and the door comes free. Such a lock is called fail-safe: with no power, it traps no one in a fire. Many keep a standby battery for blackouts, but once the lock's own current stops, the door is free. A scrapyard crane drops its steel the same way.
