genes-chromosomes-and-mutations.title: Genes, Chromosomes and Mutations
genes-chromosomes-and-mutations.context_blurb:
Coiled inside nearly every cell of your body is a set of instructions for building you, written in DNA, and half of it came from each parent. Small changes in it, called mutations, can cause a deadly blood disease that also guards against malaria, or give the world a new fruit.

DNA is packed into chromosomes, thread-like bundles in the cell's nucleus, its control centre. A gene is a section of that DNA holding the instructions for one working part of the body, often a protein. Virtually every cell holds a complete copy of a person's genes in its nucleus, so cells scraped from inside a girl's cheek hold her eye-colour genes, though only her irises use them.

In 1902 at Columbia University, the graduate student Walter Sutton watched a grasshopper's chromosomes. Nearly all were matched pairs whose partners split up, one into each sex cell, a cell that passes to the young, just as Mendel's paired factors for a trait do. So the factors, later named genes, must ride on chromosomes, and since an animal has far more traits than chromosomes, Sutton proposed in 1903 that each chromosome carries many genes. A human chromosome holds hundreds to thousands.

Theophilus Painter's count of 48, made in the early 1920s from clumped, overlapping chromosomes, stood for some thirty years. In December 1955, at Lund in Albert Levan's laboratory, Joe Hin Tjio studied human cells grown in culture, supplied by Rune Grubb. He halted them mid-division with the drug colchicine, swelled them in weakly salted water and pressed them flat, so each chromosome lay apart. Almost every whole cell held 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 matched pairs plus one pair of sex chromosomes.

Photograph one cell's chromosomes and sort them into look-alike pairs, and you have a karyotype. Each pair holds one chromosome from the mother and one from the father, so a person carries two copies of nearly every gene. Partners carry the same genes, in versions that can differ. Each parent passes on one copy of each gene, chosen by chance, so each child gets a different half of each parent's genes. That is why sisters can look unlike: full sisters share only about half their DNA, and only identical twins share all of it.

In 1905 Nettie Stevens counted a mealworm's chromosomes: a female's cells held 20 large ones, a male's 19 large and one small. Many biologists thought surroundings settled sex, but Stevens showed that it follows the chromosomes. Human females are XX and males XY. A mother gives every child an X; a father carries an X and a Y and passes on one or the other, his X to every daughter and his Y to every son, so the father's chromosome decides.

A mutation is a lasting change in a gene, from copying mistakes, radiation or some chemicals; most harm or do nothing, and a few help. In Austin, Texas, in 1926, Hermann Muller blasted fruit flies with X-rays and bred them beside untreated flies. The X-rayed flies' young showed new inherited changes far more often: about 150 times as many deadly mutations. The rays had reached the cells that make the next generation, and in 1946 Muller won a Nobel Prize for showing that radiation can change genes.

In 1910 James Herrick of Chicago described the sickle-shaped red cells that his intern Ernest Irons had seen in a Grenadian dental student's blood. The cause is one small change in a single gene, a gene for haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. A child with two changed copies has the disease; where care is poor, half or more such children die before turning five.

Yet in the early 1950s Anthony Allison found that over one in five people on malaria-ridden coasts of East Africa carried the gene. A child with one copy has the sickle-cell trait, usually with no illness, and survives malaria far better, with fewer malaria parasites in the blood. Where malaria kills many children, carriers live to pass the gene on, so it stays common. Malaria never makes the gene; it only decides who lives to pass it on.

Not every mutation harms. A nectarine is a smooth-skinned peach, of the same species. Its smooth skin comes from a change in one gene that peach fuzz needs, and every nectarine traces back to a single mutation long ago. The belief that a nectarine is a peach crossed with a plum is a myth.

three-kinds-of-adaptation.title: Three Kinds of Adaptation
three-kinds-of-adaptation.context_blurb:
A rattlesnake in ambush, a lizard on a sunny rock, a fish in seawater below freezing: each survives by adaptations, inherited traits that help a living thing survive and raise young where it lives. Natural selection spreads them, for animals whose traits suit their home leave more young.

Adaptations come in three kinds: structural, part of the body's build, such as its shape, fur or colouring; behavioural, something the animal does; and physiological, an inner working of the body, such as its chemistry or the way an organ does its job.

A desert rattlesnake shows all three. Its blotchy scales hide it against the ground, part of its build; its venom is a chemical made in its venom glands; and lying motionless in ambush is something it does. So its colouring, venom and ambush are structural, physiological and behavioural, in that order.

Kangaroo rats, desert rodents, waste little water, for their kidneys make urine some five times more concentrated than human kidneys can. The kidneys are body parts, but the adaptation is the way the organ works, so it is physiological.

Lizards were long called cold-blooded, as if they were simply as warm as the air. But in 1944, after four years in the California desert, Raymond Cowles and Charles Bogert showed that active lizards hold their bodies near a favourite temperature by behaviour, basking when cool and slipping into shade when hot. A mouse makes its warmth inside, a physiological way, by burning food day and night. The lizard burns little food to keep warm, so it lives on ten to twenty times less food than a mammal its size.

In 1961 Arthur DeVries, a graduate student, went to Antarctica to study fish in seawater nearly two degrees Celsius below zero, a cold that would freeze an ordinary fish's blood. He and Donald Wohlschlag found that dissolved salts did only about half the job; a protein studded with sugars, an antifreeze, did much of the rest. Ice crystals get in with food and through the gills, and the antifreeze binds to tiny crystals so they cannot grow, keeping the blood liquid below its normal freezing point. This inner chemistry is a physiological adaptation.

Such traits begin as chance mutations, changes in genes that some animals inherit. Rock pocket mice of the Southwest are mostly sandy like the desert rock, but on dark lava nearly all are black, since owls that hunt by sight pick off pale mice there. Hopi Hoekstra and Michael Nachman found that black mice on one flow owe their coats to changes in a single coat-colour gene, while black mice on a flow hundreds of miles off inherit theirs through other genes. Two genetic routes to one coat mean that black coats arose separately on the two flows. Mutations happen by chance, but selection does not: the same dark rock favoured black coats twice.

For nearly eleven years Henry Walter Bates collected insects in the Amazon, where birds left alone some boldly marked, foul-tasting butterflies. He found rare look-alikes from an unrelated family that were good to eat: mimics, harmless copies of a harmful kind. Birds learn to shun the pattern by tasting foul ones. Were the mimics far commoner than the foul kind, birds would mostly find a meal behind the pattern and learn to hunt it, so this mimicry works only while the mimics stay rare.

Harmless scarlet kingsnakes copy the red, yellow and black rings of the venomous coral snake. David Pfennig's team laid hundreds of soft plasticine snakes, ringed, striped or plain brown, across the Carolinas, inside the coral snake's range and north of it. Bite marks in the clay showed that inside the range only about 6 percent of attacks fell on ringed models, but farther north, with no coral snakes, about half did. So the rings protect only where coral snakes live, because only there have hunters learned to fear the real thing.

John Endler tested guppies, small fish of Trinidad's mountain streams. He moved some from a stream where the fierce pike cichlid eats showy males to a stretch whose only other fish was a small killifish, a feeble hunter. Within about two years, some fifteen generations, the males there had bigger, brighter spots. Choosy female guppies prefer colourful males as mates, so once no pike cichlid picked off the showiest, the brightest males won the most mates and fathered the most young.

when-a-food-web-breaks.title: When a Food Web Breaks
when-a-food-web-breaks.context_blurb:
A food web is the map of who eats whom in a place: plants and algae catch the Sun's energy, plant-eaters eat them, and predators eat the plant-eaters. Pull out one thread, a predator, a newcomer or a poison, and the change can ripple several links away.

From 1963 Robert Paine tore every ochre sea star off one stretch of rock at Mukkaw Bay, Washington, and hurled it out to sea, leaving the next stretch untouched. Barnacles spread over the cleared rock, then mussels, the strongest competitors for space, crowded out the rest: its fifteen species fell to eight within a year. Paine called the sea star a keystone species, one whose loss changes its community far more than its numbers suggest.

Thirty-one wolves from Canada were released in Yellowstone in the mid-1990s, and within a decade the northern range's elk had halved. By thinning the elk, the wolves left fewer to browse young willow and aspen shoots, so beside certain streams the young trees grew taller. Ecologists call this a trophic cascade, a change at the top tumbling down a food chain. Yet they still debate how big the wolves' share was, since bears, hunters and drought also cut the elk.

In the 1990s, as seals and sea lions grew scarce, Aleutian killer whales turned to hunting sea otters; the whales did not multiply; they changed their prey. With the otters gone, the sea urchins they eat, freed from their main predator, multiplied about eightfold and grazed the kelp down. James Estes was sure the whales were to blame, partly because otters in a lagoon beyond their reach held on.

Cane toads, shipped into Queensland in 1935, have spread across the north, and poison in its skin makes each toad an invader that few native animals can safely eat. In the Kimberley, monitor lizards died from eating them, and water monitors fell by nearly half. Those lizards had raided crimson finches' nests, so with fewer of them more finch chicks lived, the share leaving the nest alive rising from 55 to 81 percent.

Rabbits, released in Australia in 1859, fed feral cats and foxes, wild-living hunters that also prey on native hopping mice. From 1995 a virus that infects only European rabbits cut them sharply in South Australia's deserts. Four kinds of small native mammals, two hopping mice among them, then spread widely, most to several times their old range, as the cats and foxes grew fewer.

Harm can climb from a web's base, too. Zebra mussels reached the Hudson River in 1991, and soon billions of them had strained out four-fifths of its floating algae. Those algae feed zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, and zooplankton feed young open-water fish such as shad and herring. So the fish went short, though the mussels never touched them.

In northern Australia's savannas, ecologists burned patches hot or cool and tracked native rodents, which dwindled, most of all after hot burns. The flames had not killed, starved or driven them off. Instead, more of them were caught by predators, above all where hot fires had stripped away the grass that hid them. Filmed feral cats killed in 70 percent of hunts in the open, against 17 percent in dense grass.

Once rinderpest, a cattle virus that also strikes wildebeest, was stamped out in the 1960s, the Serengeti's wildebeest multiplied to about 1.4 million. Their grazing left too little grass to fuel the fires that kill small trees. With fewer fires sweeping the grazed grass, more young trees lived, and the number of trees rose. Ricardo Holdo's team found fewer fires, not elephants or rainfall, explained it best.

In the 1960s George Woodwell's team traced the insecticide DDT through a Long Island estuary, where a river meets the sea. DDT dissolves in fat, not water, and breaks down slowly, so an animal stores most of what it swallows. A fish eats many plankton and an osprey many fish, so each eater stores the DDT of countless meals. Counted per kilogram of body, the level rose over six hundred times from plankton to fish-eating birds: biomagnification.

In the 1950s Derek Ratcliffe found British peregrine nests with far too many broken eggs, and weighed old museum shells against fresh ones. Shell thickness had held steady for over 125 years, then dropped suddenly, by about a sixth, from 1947, just after farmers began spraying DDT widely. David Peakall later found enough DDE, a breakdown product of DDT, in British eggs of 1946 to thin them.

ecological-succession.title: Ecological Succession
ecological-succession.context_blurb:
Bare ground does not stay bare. Fresh lava, rock left by a glacier, a burned forest or an abandoned field fills, stage by stage, with one community after another; a community is all the living things that share a place. Ecologists call this slow change ecological succession.

Primary succession begins where there is no soil at all: on new lava, bare rock or a new island. Secondary succession starts where a fire, logging or farming cleared the plants but left the soil, with its seeds, roots and nutrients, the chemical foods plants draw from the ground, so regrowth is much faster. So what decides the kind is whether any soil is left for plants to root in. Cold rock bared by a melting glacier starts primary succession too, so heat does not decide.

The first living things on bare rock, the pioneer species, are often lichens. A lichen has no roots and drinks rain, dew and damp air. Part of every lichen is a fungus, and the fungus gives off acids that eat away at the minerals of the rock's surface. Rain weathers granite too, but far more slowly. Loosened grains mix with dead lichens into a thin first soil, where mosses take hold.

Each stage of plants leaves deeper soil behind as it dies and rots, and that is what lets the next, bigger kind move in. Deeper soil holds the water and nutrients that the bigger roots of grasses, then shrubs, then trees need. Each stage casts more shade, not less.

No one lives long enough to watch a dune become a forest, so how do we know? In the 1890s Henry Chandler Cowles studied the dunes along Lake Michigan: beach grass by the water, then cottonwoods, then pines, then oaks farthest inland. The lake had built its dunes one after another, so the farthest were the oldest. Cowles read the bands as stages that every young dune passes through as it ages: a line in space was a line in time.

On abandoned farmland in North Carolina, horseweed, asters and broomsedge grass come first, and within a few decades pines stand over them, because in bright sun pines grow faster than oaks and hickories. But the pines' shade keeps young pines from growing beneath them, while hardwood seedlings can grow in that shade, ready to fill each gap as the old pines die at 80 to 120 years. Shade does the work, not poison.

A forest has layers, from tall trees through shrubs to plants on its floor, and each layer gives its own food and hiding places, so far more kinds of animals can find a living there than among mosses. The newcomers move in from the land around; they do not evolve on the spot. Mosses make food from sunlight just as trees do.

In May 1980 the eruption of Mount St. Helens laid waste to two kinds of ground. Where the blast only knocked the forest flat, plants were green again within months. On that quicker ground, plants and roots had lived through the blast, sheltered by late snow or living on as roots in the soil, so it grew back as in secondary succession. Nearby, flows of hot rock left metres of pumice that stayed hot for weeks and killed everything, so that ground began almost from nothing, as in primary succession. Even so, a lupine took root there within about a year.

Surtsey, a volcanic island that rose off Iceland from 1963, has been closed since 1965 to all but a few scientists, so that life must arrive unaided. Its lava cooled fast: lichens grew on it three years after the eruption ended. Still, two decades on, just ten or so plant species had settled. Then gulls arrived to breed. Gulls feed at sea, so their droppings carried nutrients from the sea, nitrogen and phosphorus, onto the bare lava, and plants crowded into their colony while the ground outside stayed bare.

In his 1916 book Plant Succession, Frederic Clements held that each climate's succession ends in one climax community, which then stays; to him a plant community was like a living body. Henry Gleason challenged him from 1917, and in 1926 called a plant community a coincidence rather than an organism. Most ecologists today see the climax as far less fixed than Clements thought, because fires, storms and floods keep knocking patches back to earlier stages. Yet succession is not random either: its stages follow real patterns.

biodiversity-and-stability.title: Biodiversity and Stability
biodiversity-and-stability.context_blurb:
Biodiversity is the variety of life in a place. Ecologists have long asked whether it matters: does a richer meadow, forest or farm field ride out drought and disease better, and keep giving people clean water, fertile soil and fruit? Long experiments have begun to answer.

Biodiversity counts at three levels: the variety of species, of ecosystems such as forests and grasslands, and of genes within each species. Many people count species alone, but genes matter too. A plant grown from a cutting is a clone, with exactly its parent's genes, while seeds from many parents carry many mixes of genes. So a meadow grown from the seed of many wild parents holds more biodiversity than one grown from cuttings, for the variety in its genes, even with the same species.

At Cedar Creek, a Minnesota field station, David Tilman's grassland plots met the worst drought in half a century in 1987 and 1988, and plots with many species kept more of their growth, in proportion, than plots with few. With John Downing he found that each species lost cost more drought resistance than the one before. Critics noted that fertilizer had cut the species of many plots; the two found the pattern held anyway, though a 2017 reanalysis disputes this. Later sown experiments found that richer plots did resist drought better.

Tilman also found a puzzle. In plots rich in species, the total weight of plants changed little from year to year. Yet each species in those rich plots swung up and down more than in plots with few species. When weather harms some species, the spared competitors grow into the room they leave, so each species swings more but the total holds steady. The more species, the likelier some thrive in any weather: the insurance effect.

Studies lasting about two years had found no gain beyond six or eight species. Peter Reich's team followed Cedar Creek plots sown with up to sixteen species for over a decade. Each added species, all the way to sixteen, slowly raised both the soil's fertility, its store of nutrients, and plant growth, because species gather water and nutrients in different ways.

In 1845 Phytophthora infestans, a water mould, arrived in Ireland and rotted the potatoes with late blight. A large share of the crop was the Lumper, a single variety planted from pieces of tuber, so its plants were clones sharing one weakness. Breeders later found genes that resist late blight in wild relatives of the potato, such as Solanum demissum, a wild potato of Mexico. Spraying protects a plant but never changes the genes it passes on.

In 1970 American corn came in many named hybrids, each from crossing inbred parent lines. Yet to make hybrid seed without pulling off the tassels by hand, seed companies had bred one trait, Texas male-sterile cytoplasm, into some 85 to 90 percent of them. A new fungus strain, race T, made a poison that struck corn with that inherited trait, so most hybrids shared one weakness and the harvest fell by about 15 percent.

In Yunnan, China, a prized sticky rice suffers from blast, a fungus disease. In 1998 and 1999 Zhu Youyong's team had farmers plant lone rows of it among rows of a blast-resistant hybrid, and the disease dropped by 94 percent. Most spores from a sick sticky-rice plant now landed on rice the fungus could not infect, which ecologists call the dilution effect. The taller sticky rice also had drier leaves, which helped, and the farmers stopped spraying fungicide.

Living things also do work for people, called ecosystem services, such as pollination. Across forty-one crop systems worldwide, Lucas Garibaldi's team tallied how often hive honeybees and wild insects visited crop flowers, and how many flowers set fruit. More wild-insect visits meant more fruit everywhere, and an equal rise in wild-insect visits raised fruit set about twice as much as one in honeybee visits. Wild insects helped whether honeybees were many or few: hives add to their work and cannot replace it.

A living forest also keeps streams clean. In 1965 Herbert Bormann and Gene Likens had a small valley in New Hampshire's Hubbard Brook forest cleared and kept bare with weedkiller. With no leaves to give water back to the air, and no roots to take up the nitrate that soil microbes keep making, the nitrate washed out of the soil. So more water flowed, and it carried far more nitrate, 41 times that of undisturbed streams.

photosynthesis-atoms-in-and-out.title: Photosynthesis: Atoms In and Out
photosynthesis-atoms-in-and-out.context_blurb:
You know that a green plant builds its food from carbon dioxide and water, powered by light. Now follow the atoms. No atom is made or lost in a chemical reaction, so the atoms going in always match the atoms coming out. Tracing which atom goes where took 170 years, from a candle in a jar to algae fed heavy oxygen.

In symbols, photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2: six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules become one molecule of glucose, a sugar, and six oxygen molecules. Each formula counts one molecule's atoms, so CO2 holds one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, H2O two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen, and C6H12O6 holds six carbon, twelve hydrogen and six oxygen. Carbon dioxide is the only thing going in that carries carbon, so each glucose takes six carbon dioxide molecules, and two glucose molecules take twelve, two times six.

Light has no formula in the equation, because it brings energy but no atoms: every atom of the glucose comes from the carbon dioxide and the water. A leaf cell does this work in its chloroplasts, tiny green bodies filled with chlorophyll, a pigment, or colouring substance, which catches the light and passes its energy straight on. That energy ends up stored in the glucose as chemical energy, energy held in the way its atoms are joined, and the plant can draw on it long after the light is gone.

An early clue came from a candle. Joseph Priestley burned one in a sealed jar until its flame died, and on 17 August 1771 he set a sprig of mint inside that spoiled air and kept the jar shut. On the 27th, ten days on, a new candle, lit in the same air, burned perfectly well: the mint had mended the air the first flame had spoiled. He also split spoiled air in two and gave a plant to one part only, and a candle burned only in that part. Plants, he concluded, restore air that burning spoils; the mint, we now know, was giving off the oxygen a flame needs.

In the early 1880s the German biologist Theodor Engelmann found where the oxygen is made, and by which light. Under his microscope he laid a thread of green alga, whose cells hold chloroplasts as a leaf's do, among bacteria that gather wherever oxygen is richest, then used a prism to fan sunlight into a rainbow along it. The bacteria crowded thickest around the alga's chloroplasts, most of all where red and blue light fell, for there the oxygen poured out fastest. Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light most strongly and takes in little green, which is why leaves look green and why the bacteria were fewest in the green and yellow.

Chemists had long believed that a plant's oxygen came from its carbon dioxide, which holds more oxygen than water does. Cornelis van Niel doubted it in 1931. The purple bacteria he studied use light to build their food from carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide (H2S), which is built like water (H2O) but with sulfur in place of oxygen, and they give off sulfur where plants give off oxygen. That sulfur can only come from the hydrogen sulfide, so, he reasoned, a plant's oxygen must come from its water.

In 1941 at the University of California, Martin Kamen, Samuel Ruben and two co-workers tested his idea with oxygen-18, or heavy oxygen. It is an isotope, a form of an element whose atoms hold a different number of neutrons: ten instead of the usual eight, so its atoms weigh a little more and can be told apart. One batch of algae got water rich in heavy oxygen; a second got carbon dioxide loaded with it. Only the algae with the heavy-oxygen water gave off oxygen rich in heavy atoms, in the same share as their water held, so a plant's oxygen comes from the water it splits. The textbook equation is only a net count, what is left once the ins and outs cancel: to free six oxygen molecules, which hold twelve oxygen atoms, a plant splits twelve water molecules and makes six new ones.

clues-to-common-ancestry.title: Clues to Common Ancestry
clues-to-common-ancestry.context_blurb:
Every living thing on Earth is related: a bat, a whale, a horse and you all descend, with changes, from shared ancestors. This common descent is settled science, and fossils, the bones of limbs, embryos and leftover body parts all show it.

Fossils fall in the order descent predicts: fish appear more than 500 million years ago, the first mammals about 225 million and rabbits, which are mammals, about 55 million. So a rabbit in rock older than the first fish would break that order outright, for mammals descend from fish-like ancestors. The biologist J. B. S. Haldane is said to have named Precambrian rabbits, in rock over about 539 million years old, as a find that would shake his belief in evolution; none has turned up.

Fish with fleshy, lobed fins are known from rock about 380 million years old, and the first four-legged animals from rock about 365 million. So Neil Shubin's team searched the Canadian Arctic in stream-laid rock from about 375 million years ago, laid down as fish were moving onto land. In 2004 it found Tiktaalik, a transitional fossil: a fish with scales and gills, yet also a neck, and arm and wrist bones in its fins. Reptiles come only tens of millions of years later.

Archaeopteryx turned up in 1861, two years after Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species. It had a bird's feathers and wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long tail of bone, like small theropods, the mostly meat-eating dinosaurs. In 1868 Thomas Huxley compared it with fossil reptiles and argued that birds descend from small, meat-eating dinosaurs. Birds are now counted as the last living theropods.

Whales once walked. In 1981 Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell named Pakicetus, a wolf-sized mammal from northern Pakistan that ran on four slender legs about 50 million years ago. Its ear bones, unusually thick and dense, mark it as a whale, a feature all later whales inherited from a shared ancestor. Ambulocetus then paddled with webbed hind feet, and Basilosaurus lived wholly at sea on tiny hind legs.

A cat's foreleg, a whale's flipper, a bat's wing and your arm run, swim, fly and grasp, yet each has one upper-arm bone, a pair of forearm bones, then wrist bones and fingers. Parts matched bone for bone, whatever their job, are homologous. Richard Owen, who gave homology its meaning in biology in 1843, read the shared build as an ideal plan in the Creator's mind. Charles Darwin argued instead that all four were inherited from one shared ancestor, each line reshaping the old limb for its own way of life. Indeed all four-legged animals' forelegs, a lizard's as much as a horse's, are homologous, inherited from an ancestor of them all. Parts that share a job but not a build, like a bat's wing and an insect's boneless one, are analogous: they arose separately.

Every backboned embryo, an animal at its earliest stage, from a shark's to yours, grows a row of ridges at its throat called pharyngeal arches; a fish turns most into the frames of its gills. In a human the same arches build parts of the jaw, the middle ear and the throat. A human embryo never has working gills. The arches are a homology, inherited from an ancestor fish and people share.

Ernst Haeckel's drawings of 1874 showed five early embryos, from a fish to a human, almost alike. He had exaggerated, adding or leaving out features and fudging sizes. In 1997 Michael Richardson and his colleagues photographed real embryos of many backboned animals: the embryos differ more than Haeckel's drawings show. Yet real embryos do share pharyngeal arches and a tail, and in 1998 Richardson wrote that on a fundamental level Haeckel was correct. Haeckel's belief that embryos replay their ancestors' adult forms is long abandoned.

A vestigial part has lost the main job it did for the animal's ancestors. A grown whale keeps a pair of small hip bones, not joined to the spine, and its embryo starts hind limb buds that then stop: leftovers of the legs its ancestors walked on. Its hip bones still anchor mating muscles, so they are vestigial yet not useless. Your coccyx, or tailbone, is all that remains of the tail a human embryo grows and loses between its fourth and eighth weeks. Pelvic-floor muscles anchor to it, but it does no tail's work, so it is still vestigial: vestigial means it lost its old job, not every job.

the-life-cycles-of-stars.title: The Life Cycles of Stars
the-life-cycles-of-stars.context_blurb:
Stars are born, shine and die, and one thing decides how: a star's mass, the amount of matter it holds. A star like the Sun shines for billions of years and ends as a small, fading ember; a giant blazes briefly, then explodes.

Stars are born in nebulae, huge clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls each clump inward while the heat in its gas pushes outward, and warmer gas pushes harder. Only in the coldest, densest clumps does cold gas push back too weakly to resist gravity, so the clump collapses into a protostar, a young star that heats up as it shrinks.

A star of 16 Suns has 16 times the Sun's fuel, yet lasts some 10 million years to the Sun's 10 billion. Holding up its weight takes more pressure in its core, so the core is hotter, and a hotter core burns its fuel far faster, thousands of times faster than the Sun's.

Colour shows a star's surface temperature: the hotter the surface, the bluer the light. In Orion, blue-white Rigel's surface is about 11,800 degrees Celsius and orange-red Betelgeuse's about 3,300. So Rigel's surface is far hotter than Betelgeuse's. Many people, thinking of fire, take red for hottest; it means cooler.

Ejnar Hertzsprung in 1911 and Henry Norris Russell in 1913 each charted stars by surface temperature and luminosity, the light a star truly gives off. Nine stars in ten, the Sun included, fall in one band of this Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, the main sequence. When the Sun's core fuel runs low, its outer layers will balloon and cool, so it will glow red yet shine far more, being so vast: brighter, with a cooler surface, a red giant.

A red giant then puffs its outer layers into space. William Herschel named such glowing shells planetary nebulae because they looked like planets' discs, but they have nothing to do with planets. The Ring Nebula is one: gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star around its hot leftover core, a white dwarf. The Sun will end this way.

Sirius B, the white dwarf beside bright Sirius, has a surface over four times the Sun's temperature yet gives under a tenth of the Sun's light, for light depends on both heat and size. Sirius B packs about the Sun's mass into a ball about the size of Earth: white-hot all over, but tiny.

Electrons hold a white dwarf up: squeezed close, they resist being packed tighter. In 1930 the 19-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar asked how heavy a white dwarf could be, using Einstein's special relativity: in a heavier one the electrons near the speed of light, and their push falls behind gravity. The older sums, without relativity, set no ceiling. His own first figure was about 0.91 Suns, for stars' make-up was then misjudged; today's sums give at most about 1.4 times the Sun's mass. Above that, a dead core collapses into a neutron star or a black hole.

When Chandrasekhar presented his limit in London in 1935, Arthur Eddington, Britain's leading astrophysicist, attacked it at once. Eddington, who had shown how a star's brightness follows from its mass, accepted white dwarfs, but a dead star collapsing with nothing to halt it struck him as absurd: Nature, he declared, should have a law against it. Niels Bohr and Wolfgang Pauli agreed with Chandrasekhar but stayed out of the public quarrel; Eddington never recanted. The evidence sided with the younger man: weighed white dwarfs fall below the limit, and in 1983 Chandrasekhar shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Stars above about eight Suns swell into brilliant supergiants, and when the spent core can no longer bear its weight, it collapses and the star explodes as a supernova. The guest star that Song dynasty astronomers logged in 1054 was a massive star exploding as a supernova. Its wreckage is the Crab Nebula, still rushing outward.

At its heart spins the core the blast left, a neutron star heavier than the Sun yet about 20 kilometres across. In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a graduate student, spotted what she called a bit of scruff on a new radio telescope's charts: pulses every 1.337 seconds, steady as a clock. The source was a neutron star spinning very fast, sweeping a radio beam past Earth like a lighthouse: a pulsar. In 1968 the Crab's own pulsar, flashing about 30 times a second, proved too fast for anything else. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics; Bell was left out.

galaxies-and-the-expanding-universe.title: Galaxies and the Expanding Universe
galaxies-and-the-expanding-universe.context_blurb:
A pale band of light arches across the night sky: the Milky Way, our home galaxy, seen edge-on from inside. A galaxy is a vast system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Measuring the sky showed a universe vaster than anyone had dreamed, and still growing.

A light-year is a distance, not a time: how far light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, lies about 4.2 light-years from Earth.

Henrietta Leavitt, one of the women "computers" Edward Pickering hired at Harvard to measure photographic plates, followed 25 Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud. A Cepheid swells and shrinks, brightening and dimming in a regular beat. The cloud's stars lie at nearly one distance from us, so the brighter-looking ones really were brighter. In 1912 Leavitt reported her law: the longer its cycle, the brighter the star.

So two Cepheids with the same cycle give off about the same light, and if one looks far fainter, it must lie much farther away. A lamp ten times farther off looks a hundred times fainter, so Cepheids became a yardstick for the sky.

Harlow Shapley turned that yardstick on 69 globular clusters, round swarms of many thousands of stars; he timed pulsing stars in a few and scaled the rest from their brightest stars and sizes. Seen from Earth, the clusters bunch toward Sagittarius, but they swarm around the galaxy's centre, so the centre must lie far off that way. In 1918 Shapley concluded that the Sun lies far from the galaxy's centre, not near it, as counts of nearby stars had suggested.

In 1920 Shapley argued that spirals such as Andromeda lay inside the Milky Way, and Heber Curtis that they were galaxies of their own. In 1923 Edwin Hubble photographed Andromeda at Mount Wilson and marked one speck N, for a new star. It was a Cepheid; the plate still shows the N crossed out and "VAR!" beside it. Its cycle and faintness put it some 900,000 light-years away, far outside even Shapley's oversized Milky Way. So Andromeda is a separate galaxy beyond the Milky Way, now measured at about 2.5 million light-years.

In 1926 Hubble sorted galaxies by shape: spirals, whose arms are lit by young stars; smooth, round or oval ellipticals; and shapeless irregulars. Stars are born only where clouds of cold gas and dust collapse. An elliptical has little gas and dust left to make stars, most of it used up or blown away when the galaxies that built it merged.

From 1912, Vesto Slipher measured the spirals' light. Light travels in waves, and red waves are longer than blue. Light from a source moving away arrives stretched toward red, a red shift; from one approaching, it is squeezed toward blue. Andromeda's was shifted blue: it is coming our way. Nearly every other spiral showed a red shift, so those galaxies were moving away from Earth. A red shift shows motion, not a cooler temperature.

Hubble set his galaxies' distances beside speeds measured by Slipher and Milton Humason. In 1929 Hubble reported that the farther the galaxy, the faster it moves away: one twice as far off flees about twice as fast. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest, had derived it from Einstein's theory of gravity in 1927; it is now often called the Hubble-Lemaître law.

Run the expansion backward and everything crowds into the Big Bang, the universe's hot, dense start some 13.8 billion years ago. It was no explosion at one spot. Space itself stretches everywhere, like a rising raisin loaf spreading every raisin from the rest. So the expansion has no centre: from any galaxy, the others would seem to move away.

In 1948 Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle offered a rival with no beginning. In their steady state, the galaxies fly apart, but new matter forms in the widening gaps, an atom at a time, so the universe never thins out.

In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson of Bell Labs heard a faint microwave hiss in a giant horn antenna, coming from every direction, day and night. They evicted nesting pigeons and scrubbed out the droppings, but the hiss stayed. The hiss was the glow left over from the Big Bang, stretched by the expansion into microwaves and cooled to 2.7 degrees above absolute zero, the coldest possible. Most astronomers then gave up the steady state, though Hoyle, who had coined the name Big Bang, never accepted it.

winds-air-masses-and-fronts.title: Winds, Air Masses and Fronts
winds-air-masses-and-fronts.context_blurb:
Wind is air on the move, carrying the weather. It has one cause and one twist: the Sun warms Earth unevenly, and Earth's spin bends the moving air. A lawyer, an engineer, a balloon-watcher and a Norwegian father and son pieced it together.

Over a year the tropics soak up more solar energy than they lose to space, while the polar regions lose more than they gain. Winds and ocean currents carry heat toward the poles to keep the balance; a warm current gives its heat to the air, which is why a coast it washes has milder winters.

Air pressure is the push of the air's weight, and air flows from high pressure toward low. Air warmed at the equator rises, leaving low pressure below, while cold air sinks over the poles, piling up high pressure. So if Earth did not spin, the ground wind would blow straight from the poles toward the equator. The Sun's heating drives the wind, not Earth's spin, which only bends it.

The trade winds flow toward the equator to replace its rising air, yet north of it they blow from the northeast. Galileo had tied them to Earth's spin; in 1735 George Hadley, an English lawyer who preferred physics, showed how the spin turns air moving across it. Air arriving from the north lags behind the ground near the equator, which moves east fastest because it has the widest circle to cover each day, so Earth spinning beneath the moving air turns it into a northeast wind.

In 1835 the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis worked out the maths of spinning machines such as water wheels; others later applied it to Earth. Looking along a wind's path, the Coriolis effect turns it to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. The bend fades to nothing at the equator, and it is far too weak to steer a draining sink.

Air rising at the equator spreads poleward high up and sinks near 30 degrees, building belts of high pressure. From there, air heading for the equator becomes the trade winds. Air heading toward the pole is bent to its right, toward the east, so it blows from the southwest: the westerlies, filling the belt from 30 to 60 degrees north.

High above blow the jet streams, narrow rivers of fast wind 9 to 16 kilometres up. In the mid-1920s Wasaburo Ooishi tracked over 1,200 balloons through a surveyor's telescope called a theodolite and found fierce westerlies over Japan, strongest in winter: the first known evidence of a jet stream. Jets blow hardest where cold and warm air meet, and fastest when the difference is greatest. In winter the poles grow far colder while the tropics stay warm, so the poles and tropics differ most in temperature then.

B-29 bomber crews met the same winds over Japan in 1944, at some 320 kilometres an hour. Forecasters follow a jet stream because storms below tend to travel along its path: it is the main steering current for storms between the tropics and the poles.

During the First World War, with Europe's weather reports cut off, Vilhelm Bjerknes had weather stations built all over Norway. In Bergen he mapped the reports with his son Jacob. Sharp weather changes lay along boundaries between air masses, huge bodies of air each with its own temperature and dampness, and father and son named such a boundary a front, after the war's battle lines. The Bergen maps showed Norway's storms forming along the polar front, where cold polar air meets warm tropical air.

Cold air is denser than warm air, so the two do not easily mix, and the cold air stays low. At a cold front, cold air pushes under the warm air and forces it up steeply, so it cools fast into towering thunderclouds. At a warm front, the lighter warm air rides slowly up a gentle slope of cold air, spreading wide layers of cloud that give steady rain. Warm fronts also move about half as fast as cold ones, so the rain lasts for hours.

A barometer measures air pressure. In a low, an area of low pressure, air flows inward and rises, building clouds. So a falling barometer means a low is moving in, with rising air and storms; a fast fall often warns of rain or a gale. A rising barometer usually means a high, with sinking air and clear skies.

how-hurricanes-form.title: How Hurricanes Form
how-hurricanes-form.context_blurb:
A hurricane is a giant spinning storm born over a warm tropical sea: a wheel of thunderstorms around a calm eye. Its winds are fierce, and the sea it drives ashore can drown a coast. Pilots, buoys and satellites have shown how it works.

A hurricane needs a sea of about 26 degrees Celsius or warmer. When sea water evaporates into water vapour, an invisible gas, it takes in heat, and the vapour carries that heat aloft. High in the storm the vapour condenses, turning back into cloud droplets. Condensing warms the air around it, setting free the heat the vapour held, about 2.5 million joules for every kilogram of water. The warmed air rises faster and draws in more moist sea air, so a hurricane is a heat engine, turning the sea's heat into wind. It runs on the sea's heat, not on sunlight falling on its clouds.

The storm also needs a twist to start it turning. Earth's spin bends moving air to one side, an effect that is zero at the equator and grows toward the poles. Within 5 degrees or so of the equator, Earth's spin barely twists the air, so a hurricane almost never forms there, however warm the sea. The same bend sets which way the storm turns. Northern hurricanes always spin counter-clockwise, and the storms of the south spin clockwise, their mirror image. A draining sink is far too small for Earth's spin to steer, so its swirl can go either way.

In 1943 an Army pilot, Joseph Duckworth, flew a small training plane into a hurricane coming ashore in Texas; no one is known to have flown into one on purpose before. Whether he meant to reach the eye is disputed. Through hammering rain he broke into calm, sunlit air with the ground in sight. The eye is clear because its air sinks, warming and drying as it falls, and sinking air makes no clouds. Around it stands the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms where air rises and the strongest winds blow. On a second flight that day, the weather officer William Jones-Burdick recorded temperatures inside the storm.

Those winds circle the centre. So once the eye has passed a place, the far side of the eyewall strikes with fierce winds again, from the opposite way. Sailors of old took the eye's calm for the end of the storm; forecasters still warn that the worst winds soon return.

Hurricane and typhoon are regional names for one kind of storm, the tropical cyclone: a hurricane in the Atlantic and the eastern and central Pacific, a typhoon in the western Pacific. The name says nothing of strength. When Hurricane John, born off Mexico in 1994, crossed the International Date Line, it became Typhoon John only because it had moved into another part of the ocean. Back east in September, it was a hurricane again.

A slow hurricane's winds churn the sea, mixing its warm surface water with colder water from below, so the storm cools the sea beneath it by a few degrees and leaves a trail of cooler water, a cold wake. Buoys at sea have measured the drop, and forecasters check how deep the warm water goes, not just how warm its surface is. Over cool water or over land, a hurricane weakens for the same reason: it has lost its supply of warm, moist air. On land, rough ground slows its winds too. Dropsondes, instrument packs dropped by parachute from hurricane-hunter planes, radio back the weakening winds.

Forecasters rank hurricanes on a five-step scale drawn up in the early 1970s by the engineer Herbert Saffir and the meteorologist Robert Simpson. Since 2010 it has rated storms by their strongest steady winds alone. So the scale says nothing of the storm surge, the rise of the sea that a hurricane's winds push ashore, which is often the deadliest part of the storm. Surge caused about half the deaths in US Atlantic storms from 1963 to 2012, though in recent US counts freshwater flooding from rain has killed more. Hurricane Ike, only a Category 2 near Texas in 2008, drove in a surge typical of a Category 4 or 5.

the-greenhouse-effect.title: The Greenhouse Effect
the-greenhouse-effect.context_blurb:
In a desert, a baking afternoon can turn into a chilly night, while a muggy night in the American Southeast stays warm until dawn. The difference is water vapour, a gas that holds in the ground's heat. That warming is called the greenhouse effect.

Much sunlight crosses the air and heats the ground, and the warm ground sends out infrared rays, invisible light that carries heat. A greenhouse gas, such as water vapour or carbon dioxide, absorbs those rays and soon gives the energy off again in any direction, so part of it heads back down to the ground and part goes on toward space. Earth still sends out to space about as much energy as it takes in from sunlight; the gases only slow its escape.

In 1856 Eunice Foote set two identical glass cylinders with thermometers in the sun, one holding carbon dioxide and one plain air. The carbon dioxide grew hotter, reaching 125 degrees Fahrenheit against the air's 106, and once both were back in the shade it stayed hot many times as long. An atmosphere of that gas, she wrote, would give Earth a high temperature. Her cylinders took in all of sunlight, though, not just the heat rays the ground gives off.

In London three years later, John Tyndall tested gases with invisible heat rays alone. He sent heat from a copper cube of hot water down a brass tube to a detector whose needle swung as the heat arrived. Dry air, nitrogen and oxygen barely moved it; their molecules, each a pair of matching atoms, hardly respond to infrared. Air straight from his laboratory stopped far more heat, and most of that was the work of its water vapour, which absorbed at least thirteen times as much as the dry air itself. Carbon dioxide absorbed heat too, but the air holds far less of it.

The Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius was after an old riddle, what had brought on the ice ages, for no one could explain how Earth had grown cold enough for one. With Samuel Langley's readings of the Moon's invisible heat, he worked out by hand, in thousands of calculations he called tedious, published in 1896, how each band of latitude would warm or cool as the air's carbon dioxide rose or fell. A deep enough cut in the gas, he calculated, would cool the middle latitudes enough, he thought, for an ice age.

Many 1950s scientists expected the sea to swallow nearly all the carbon dioxide from burning coal and oil. In 1958, on the bare lava of Mauna Loa, a Hawaiian volcano far out at sea, Charles David Keeling started measuring the gas. His first reading was 313 parts per million: 313 molecules in every million molecules of air. By 1960 his readings showed the gas building up from one year to the next. It has risen every year since.

Keeling's line also zigzags, dipping each year between May and October and rising again until the next May. Most of Earth's land, and so most of its plants, lies in the northern half of the world. Through the northern spring and summer, forests and fields take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow, and in autumn and winter their dead leaves and plants decay and give it back. The southern half has far less land, and at the South Pole the swing almost vanishes.

Plants take carbon from the air, breathing and decay return it, the sea dissolves it, and burning coal, oil and gas, the fossil fuels made from long-buried life, returns their ancient carbon to the air. Leave aside the carbon locked away in rock, and the greatest store is the oceans, with about 38,000 billion tonnes dissolved in sea water, some forty to fifty times as much as the air holds.

Volcanoes can cool the world instead. In April 1815 Mount Tambora, in Indonesia, blew apart in the most powerful eruption ever recorded, and its cloud reached the stratosphere, the layer of air above the weather. There Tambora's sulfur gas, some sixty million tonnes of sulfur dioxide, turned into a haze of tiny droplets of sulfuric acid, which reflected sunlight back into space for a year or more. Ash cannot do that, since it falls out of the sky within days or weeks. So 1816 was the year without a summer, with June snow in New England and failed harvests across Europe.

correlation-causation-and-error.title: Correlation, Causation and Error
correlation-causation-and-error.context_blurb:
The faster a windmill's sails spin, the harder the wind is blowing: the two are correlated, rising and falling together. Yet the sails do not make the wind. A correlation is a clue, not proof, and measurements can mislead too.

One trap is a confounder, a hidden third thing that drives both. A seaside town sells the most ice cream on its hottest days, when the most swimmers drown. Hot weather drives both, filling the ice-cream shops and the sea, so a ban on ice cream would hardly change the drownings.

In 1999 Graham Quinn and Richard Stone linked sleeping with a light on before age two to later nearsightedness, in which faraway things look blurred. In 2000 Karla Zadnik's team checked some 1,220 children and found nearsightedness about as common after a dark room as after a lit one. Nearsightedness runs in families, and nearsighted parents more often used night lights, so the parents' own eyes, a confounder, tied the lights to the children's.

Yet a link can be strong evidence. From 1951 Austin Bradford Hill and Richard Doll followed some 40,000 British doctors who had told them how much they smoked. Lung-cancer deaths rose step by step with the dose, the amount smoked, and such a dose-response pattern, more of a suspect bringing more harm, is hard to explain any other way.

The great statistician Ronald Fisher doubted that smoking was to blame. In 1958 he suggested that lung cancer begins years before it shows, with a slight inflammation that might lead a person to seek comfort in cigarettes. Fisher's idea turns the arrow round, the illness causing the smoking, and a link explained that way is called reverse causation. Fisher, a lifelong pipe smoker, was also a paid tobacco-industry consultant, and the evidence proved him wrong: doctors who gave up smoking went on to have far less lung cancer than those who kept on.

Chance makes links too. Setting thousands of yearly counts from public records side by side, the law student Tyler Vigen found American pool drownings rising and falling with Nicolas Cage's films from 1999 to 2009. Nothing ties films to drownings: compare enough pairs and a few will match by luck alone, so out of thousands, some rise and fall together by chance.

Precision is how closely repeated readings agree; accuracy is how close they come to the true value. Darts bunched tightly far from the bullseye are precise but not accurate, like a scale that shows the same wrong weight every time. Averaging cannot remove an error that repeats; only calibrating, checking and correcting the instrument against a known mass, can.

The Hubble Space Telescope's mirror, among the smoothest ever made, gave blurred pictures in 1990. The tool that tested the mirror's shape had been built wrong, one lens 1.3 millimetres out of place, so the polishers carefully ground it into the wrong shape. Every reading from that tool erred the same way: precise, but not accurate.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky asked which of two hospitals, one with about 45 births a day and one with about 15, logs more days when over 60 percent of the babies are boys. The small hospital does, because each day the share of boys wanders from one half by chance, and the fewer the babies, the farther it can wander. Four tossed coins come up three-quarters heads or more nearly a third of the time; a hundred coins almost never do, so bigger samples swing less.

In the usual telling, returning bombers had many holes in the wings and body but few in the engines, and the statistician Abraham Wald said to armour the engines. Wald assumed hits were spread over the whole plane, so the few engine holes meant that planes hit in the engines had mostly been lost: an engine hit often brought a bomber down. Studying only the survivors hides the losses, a trap called survivorship bias. That telling, with its red-dotted plane first drawn around 2005, simplifies Wald's real work, mathematical memos of 1943.

Bacteria multiply by splitting in two, each about every 20 minutes, so 100 become 200, then 400. The more there are, the more new ones each step adds, so on a graph marked in equal steps the points curve upward ever more steeply: exponential growth. Equal additions would make a straight line instead. When food runs low and wastes build up, growth slows and levels off.

testing-a-claim.title: Testing a Claim: Blindfolds and Fair Trials
testing-a-claim.context_blurb:
How do you test a claim that sincere people believe? Honest people can fool themselves, and others, without meaning to. Three famous tests show two guards that keep a test fair: hiding what could sway the result from the people involved, and fixing a pass mark before testing.

In Paris the German physician Franz Mesmer taught that an invisible fluid flows through all living things, that illness comes when its flow is blocked, and that a healer can set it flowing again: animal magnetism. His patients often fell into fits, which he held were healing. In 1784 a commission headed by Benjamin Franklin tested the claim on patients of Mesmer's follower Charles d'Eslon, since Mesmer refused to take part.

The chemist Antoine Lavoisier designed trials to pull apart the two possible causes of the fits, the fluid and the patients' belief. Some patients were magnetised in secret; others only thought they were. If the fluid were real, the secret treatment would bring on fits; if belief were the cause, the pretend one would. Blindfolds and screens kept the patients from knowing, so their expectations could not sway the result, which makes these among the first blind tests on record.

One woman sat blindfolded, assured that d'Eslon was at work on her though he was nowhere near, and fell into a fit within about three minutes. Another, truly magnetised through a paper screen for thirty minutes without knowing it, showed nothing. Only the woman who believed she was being treated had a fit. The fit was real; its cause was expecting a treatment, not the treatment itself, an effect now called a placebo effect.

In Berlin, a retired mathematics teacher, Wilhelm von Osten, sincerely believed his horse Hans could do arithmetic, spell and read a clock, tapping out answers with a hoof, and charged nothing to watch. In 1904 a panel of thirteen, led by the psychologist Carl Stumpf, found no tricks. The panel was right that nobody cheated, for Hans did as well for strangers as for his owner, yet the horse was not counting: ruling out cheating had left the real question open.

Stumpf's assistant Oskar Pfungst kept testing, changing one thing at a time. Hans failed only when the person asking did not know the answer himself, or stood where the horse could not see him. Hans was right 98 times in 100 for a questioner who knew the number, and 8 for one who did not. Pfungst watched the questioners grow tense as Hans tapped. At the right count the questioner relaxed and his head jerked upward a tiny bit, about a millimetre by one account, and Hans stopped on that signal.

Taking the questioner's place himself, Pfungst gave Hans the cue without meaning to, though he knew exactly what it was. No one can simply decide not to give a cue, so a fair test keeps the answer from the questioner, or the questioner out of sight. The trap is now called the Clever Hans effect.

Therapeutic touch is a nursing practice from the 1970s: practitioners hold their hands near a patient to sense and adjust what they call the human energy field. In 1996 nine-year-old Emily Rosa tested it for her school science fair. Each practitioner slid both arms under a tall screen, out of sight; a coin toss picked one hand, Emily hovered her own hand over it, and the practitioner named the hand. Each had described feeling the field, as tingling, heat or cold.

In 280 tries the 21 practitioners found the right hand 123 times, or 44 percent. Pure guessing would be right about half the time, some 140 times, so the authors called the score close to what chance would give: no sign of any sense at all. A true ability, they noted, should have found her hand every time.

The pass mark, fixed before any trial, was at least 8 right in 10, far above the 5 that guessing gives on average, because guessing alone often reaches 6 or 7: it gets 6 or more over a third of the time. Luck reaches 8 only about once in 18 tries. Fixed in advance, the mark could not be moved to fit the scores once they were in.

Practice made no clear difference either: the practitioners had from one to twenty-seven years of it, and the authors found no clear link between their years and their scores.

when-the-experts-were-wrong.title: When the Experts Were Wrong
when-the-experts-were-wrong.context_blurb:
Four times in the last century, researchers defied what most experts believed, and the evidence proved them right; once it proved a bold claim wrong. Each time the doubters had real reasons. And each time a test that other scientists could check settled it.

In Western Australia the pathologist Robin Warren kept finding spiral bacteria in inflamed stomach lining, and the young doctor Barry Marshall joined him. Ulcers were blamed on worry and acid, and with reason: stomach acid kills nearly every germ swallowed, and a 1954 study had found none of these bacteria in stomach samples. In 1984, with piglets failing to catch the germ, Marshall swallowed a broth of the bacteria himself. Ten days on, a camera on a tube and a snip of tissue showed gastritis: an inflamed lining, with the bacteria in it. It was no ulcer, but his paper argued that a lasting infection prepares the way for one. In a trial of a hundred infected patients with ulcers just past the stomach, far fewer ulcers came back within a year where the bacteria were cleared: 21 in every 100, against 84 where they stayed. Marshall and Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize. Marshall said everyone had been against him; others say his doubters showed proper scepticism until such evidence arrived.

In 1982 Dan Shechtman aimed electrons at an aluminium-manganese alloy and counted a ring of ten bright spots. Textbooks defined a crystal as a solid whose atoms repeat one small pattern over and over, and geometry forbids any repeating pattern to have tenfold symmetry, just as regular pentagons cannot tile a floor. Shape was never the test: a metal's tiny grains are crystals without flat faces. Linus Pauling, a double Nobel winner, blamed twinning, the crystallographers' standard answer: several normal crystals joined at angles, their spots adding into a pattern that none makes alone. But Shechtman had squeezed his beam onto one tiny grain, and that single grain gave the whole tenfold pattern. Other labs confirmed the patterns, Pauling held out until his death in 1994, and in 1992 crystallographers redefined a crystal as any solid giving a clear-cut pattern of spots; Shechtman's Nobel Prize came in 2011.

In 1967 Lynn Margulis argued that mitochondria and chloroplasts, small parts inside animal and plant cells, began as swallowed bacteria; over a dozen journals had rejected her paper. Critics wanted firmer evidence, and a cell might have built these parts from within. A cell gets more mitochondria only when old ones grow and split in two, as bacteria do; if it loses them all, it can never make more. By 1982 Michael Gray, Ford Doolittle and others had found chloroplast DNA closest to that of cyanobacteria, bacteria that make food from sunlight. Mitochondrial DNA soon matched oxygen-using bacteria, and most biologists were won over. Her third claim, that flagella, the whip-like tails some cells swim with, came from spiral bacteria, failed the same kind of test: flagella have no DNA of their own at all.

In 1923 J Harlen Bretz proposed that one sudden, giant flood had cut eastern Washington's Channeled Scablands. For a century geology had explained the land by slow, everyday change instead of Noah's Flood, so a sudden catastrophe seemed a step back. Critics also asked where so much water could have come from, and for years he could not say. In 1940 Joseph Pardee showed that huge gravel ridges on the floor of Montana's vanished, ice-dammed Glacial Lake Missoula are giant current ripples. Only a deep, fast torrent builds ripples that size: the ice dam had failed, and the lake had emptied in a sudden rush. Geologists now count forty or more such floods, so Bretz was right about the kind of event, not the number. He won the Geological Society of America's Penrose Medal in 1979.

Not every bold claim wins. In 1989 the noted electrochemist Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced that a palladium rod in heavy water, whose hydrogen is a heavier kind, gave off more heat under an electric current than chemistry could explain. They credited it to nuclear fusion, though fusion in the Sun needs some 15 million degrees. Labs around the world found no extra heat and no sign of fusion, and fusion making that much heat would have given off neutrons deadly to the experimenters. Energy Department reviews in 1989 and 2004 found no convincing evidence. Other scientists could repeat the earlier tests; no one else could get this result.

sciences-dark-chapters.title: Science's Dark Chapters
sciences-dark-chapters.context_blurb:
Science and medicine have done harm as well as good, and some of today's safeguards answer that harm: a glowing paint sold as safe, a sleeping pill tested too little, and a government study that left sick men untreated. In one case, a reviewer's demand for evidence held firm.

From about 1917, young women painted luminous numbers onto watch faces at the United States Radium Corporation's New Jersey plant. Supervisors taught them to point their brushes between their lips, and the company called the paint harmless. Radium sits in calcium's column of the periodic table, so the body treated the two alike and built the swallowed radium into bone, as it does calcium. There, decaying by half only every 1,600 years, it kept firing alpha particles into nearby cells, and many painters fell ill. The company's president, Arthur Roeder, invited a Harvard expert, Cecil Drinker, who found the plant thick with radium dust and blamed radium; Roeder blamed an infection caught elsewhere. The state's labour department then received from the company Drinker's report, changed to say all were well. Alice Hamilton, another Harvard expert, suspected forgery, and the Drinkers published their true findings.

In 1957 the West German firm Chemie Grünenthal put the sleeping pill thalidomide on sale over the counter and advertised it as non-toxic. The claim rested on rodents: rats and mice had survived huge doses. Rodent-only tests were usual then. No pregnant animal was tested, though doctors gave the pill for morning sickness, and rodents later proved far less sensitive than rabbits to its harm to unborn young. Late in 1961 Widukind Lenz and William McBride tied it to babies, over ten thousand worldwide, born with shortened or missing limbs.

In America, Richardson-Merrell's request to sell it went to Frances Kelsey, newly hired by the Food and Drug Administration. The file leaned on doctors' praise instead of clinical data. In November 1960 she sent it back because the drug had not been shown to be safe. She knew of no harm to babies yet. A request nobody refused took effect after sixty days, so she sent it back again and again. The burden of proof, she wrote, lay with the applicant. Early in 1961 a Scottish doctor reported nerve damage in four people who had taken the pill nightly for more than a year. Her own wartime research on malaria drugs had shown her that some drugs cross the placenta to the unborn, so she demanded proof that thalidomide was harmless to a baby in the womb. Merrell, claiming without evidence that the drug stayed out of the womb, withdrew in March 1962. That October the Kefauver-Harris Amendments added a second demand to safety: controlled studies showing the drug works as claimed. The economist Sam Peltzman argued that the rules also cut the flow of new drugs, a cost their defenders weigh against the harm they prevent.

In 1932 doctors of the United States Public Health Service began following six hundred Black men in Macon County, Alabama: 399 with syphilis, 201 without. Calling it treatment for "bad blood", a local phrase for many ills, the doctors gave free check-ups and hot meals. They meant to record what syphilis does when left untreated, at first for months, then for the rest of the men's lives. They argued that the knowledge would help fight a disease whose arsenic and mercury treatments were toxic and weak, and they infected no one: the 399 already had syphilis. But the men were never told they had it, nor asked for their informed consent. Penicillin was the standard cure by the late 1940s, but the doctors did not offer it to the men. Some of the men's wives caught the disease, and some of their children were born with it.

Peter Buxtun, a Service interviewer in San Francisco, protested in 1966 and 1968, but a 1969 Service panel, seeing a rare chance to study late syphilis, let it go on. Buxtun then took his papers to the Associated Press, and on 25 July 1972 its reporter Jean Heller broke a news story carried across the nation. The study ended that November, with 74 of the men still alive. Under the National Research Act of 1974 and its rules, most federally funded research on people needs approval first from a review board that includes a non-scientist and an outsider. Such a board weighs the risks and checks that each person gives informed consent: told the truth, understanding it, and free to refuse.

momentum-and-collisions.title: Momentum and Collisions
momentum-and-collisions.context_blurb:
A loaded truck at walking pace and a bullet in flight are both hard to stop: one is heavy, the other fast. One quantity, momentum, covers both. It explains why rifles kick and why car fronts are built to fold in a crash.

Momentum is mass times velocity, an object's speed in a given direction. A truck twenty times a cyclist's mass, at a twentieth of his speed, carries just his momentum. A force acting over a time changes momentum by the force times the time. So steady brakes drain momentum at a steady rate, and the truck and the cyclist, holding equal momentum under equal brakes, stop at the same moment. His twenty times the energy of motion means a longer braking distance, not a longer time.

Momentum is also conserved, or kept: with no outside force, bodies pushing only on each other keep their total, since each push comes back equally hard. Two skaters who push apart from standing still began at zero and must still total zero, so her momentum is just as big as his, pointing the opposite way. With half his mass, she glides at twice his speed.

A rifle and its bullet also start at zero. Pulled tight into the shoulder, the rifle and the hunter's body move back as one great mass, and so much mass recoils only slowly. Held loosely, the light rifle alone speeds backward and slams into him.

A cue ball striking an equal ball squarely stops dead, passing on all its momentum. When the struck ball then slows and stops, no law is broken, because the total is kept only while no outside force acts, and the cloth's friction is one. It hands the momentum to the table and Earth; only the energy of motion becomes heat.

In 1644 René Descartes held that every body's size multiplied by its speed always adds up to the same total. Yet two matching clay balls flying at each other at equal speeds smack, cling and halt, and by his count their motion is lost. Christiaan Huygens, working out rules for hard bodies, took account of the direction each body moves in, scoring one way as plus and the other as minus. The clay then totals nothing before and after. That directed count, mass times velocity, is momentum. Huygens's other rule, that mass times speed squared adds up the same, holds only for hard bodies: soft clay, as was learned much later, turns energy of motion into heat.

In 1668 and 1669 Christopher Wren and Huygens brought the Royal Society rules for hard, bouncing bodies, and John Wallis for soft ones. Isaac Newton tested such rules by swinging pairs of glass, steel, cork or wound-wool balls on ten-foot threads, reading each speed from its arc. Steel rebounded almost at its meeting speed, wool at little more than half. Yet for every kind of ball, the momentum one gained in one direction matched what the other gained the opposite way, so each pair's total stayed the same.

For a given change in momentum, a longer stop means a smaller force. A girl jumping off a low wall lands just as fast each time and ends at rest, so her momentum changes by the same amount whether she lands stiff-legged or on bending knees. Bent knees stretch the stop and soften the force, like air bags and a catcher's padded glove.

The Air Force doctor John Paul Stapp tested this on his own body. In 1954 his rocket sled took him from rest to 632 miles an hour in five seconds, then braked to a halt in 1.4 seconds. Stapp gained and lost the same momentum, but the stop took little over a quarter of the time, so its force was far greater, reaching 46.2 g, over forty-six times his weight. The windblast at top speed pressed far less; a steady speed alone presses on no one. Textbooks then put the human limit at 18 g, and he lived through more than twice that.

At Daimler-Benz the engineer Béla Barényi questioned the old belief that safety meant a rigid car. His 1952 patent put a stiff passenger cell between a front and back made to fold, first built into a 1959 Mercedes. A car hitting a wall must lose all its momentum, whatever its front, and no front lowers the speed it hits at. A folding front stretches that loss over more time, so the push on the people inside is gentler.

fission-fusion-and-mass-energy.title: Fission, Fusion and Mass-Energy
fission-fusion-and-mass-energy.context_blurb:
A uranium fuel pellet about a centimetre across holds about as much energy as a ton of coal. That energy lies in the nucleus, an atom's tiny core: fission frees it by splitting a heavy nucleus, fusion by joining light ones.

Gravity is the feeblest of the four fundamental forces: between two protons, the electric push outdoes it a trillion trillion trillion times. Gravity still rules the Moon's path, because mass only attracts: the pull of every atom in Earth and the Moon adds up, while each body's plus and minus charges almost exactly cancel.

The strong force, felt by protons and neutrons alike, holds a nucleus together, pulling about a hundred times harder than its protons push each other apart. But it fades to almost nothing beyond two and a half trillionths of a millimetre, so each particle grips only the particles right next to it. Electrons do not feel it at all.

Albert Einstein's E = mc² says mass can turn into energy, a tiny mass into an enormous amount: one gram into about 90 trillion joules. A helium nucleus holds a little less mass than its two protons and two neutrons weighed apart: the mass defect. When the particles join, energy leaves them and carries a sliver of their mass away, so pulling the nucleus apart means putting that energy back.

Late in 1938, testing neutron-struck uranium in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann kept turning up barium. Hahn wrote to Lise Meitner, his partner in research for some thirty years, who had escaped Nazi Germany that July, and over Christmas in Sweden she worked it out with her nephew Otto Frisch. Barium's nucleus holds 56 protons, little more than half of uranium's 92, so the uranium nucleus had not been chipped or built up: it had split into two middle-sized nuclei. Frisch named it fission, after a cell dividing.

In Copenhagen the next January, Frisch tried to sink the idea. He coated a counting chamber inside with uranium, placed a neutron source nearby, and set the counter to ignore pulses as small as those from uranium's own alpha particles. Big pulses came. Splitting needs neutrons, so big pulses still arriving with the source taken away would have meant something else was making them, but in hours of check runs he saw none. Hahn alone won the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Meitner was left out.

Each split of a uranium-235 nucleus, set off when it captures a neutron, throws out two or three new neutrons for other uranium-235 nuclei to capture in turn: a chain reaction. The two flying pieces split nothing; their speed becomes heat. Water round the fuel carries the heat away to make steam for a turbine, in the most common designs by heating a separate loop. Control rods of boron or cadmium soak up neutrons before those can split more nuclei, so rods pushed in slow the reaction and rods lowered fully stop it. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, and it makes splits likelier, not rarer.

Fusion joins light nuclei, such as deuterium and tritium, hydrogen's two heavy forms, into helium. Every nucleus is positively charged, so two nuclei push each other away, and only nuclei moving very fast, which means very hot, come close enough for the short-reaching strong force to take hold. So the fuel is heated past 100 million degrees Celsius into plasma, bare nuclei and free electrons; nothing burns.

In California in December 2022, the National Ignition Facility fired lasers into a tiny gold can holding a frozen fuel pellet. The fusion gave out 3.15 megajoules (millions of joules) against 2.05 of laser light, the first time a pellet had given out more energy than the lasers put in: ignition. But its lasers drew about 300 megajoules from the grid, and no fusion machine yet makes more electricity than it uses.

A nuclear plant runs in any weather and, over its life, releases about as little carbon dioxide per unit of electricity as wind. Its used fuel, solid pellets in metal rods, cools for years in water pools, then goes into steel-and-concrete casks, which give off a little radiation, within limits, and have been shipped thousands of times without any radioactive material escaping. The hard part is time: used fuel stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years and must be kept away from people all that while. Finland has built the world's first deep underground store; the United States still has no permanent one.
