circuits-motors-and-generators.title: Circuits, Motors and Generators
circuits-motors-and-generators.context_blurb:
Flip a switch and a lamp lights. Behind it lie a few rules of charge flowing round a circuit, and two discoveries by Michael Faraday: a current and a magnet can make motion, and motion and a magnet can make a current.

Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes with an ammeter; voltage is the push that drives it, in volts; resistance is how hard a material holds back the flow, in ohms. Every bit of charge that flows into a bulb flows out again, so an ammeter reads the same current on both sides of it. The bulb takes energy, given off as light and heat, not charge.

In Cologne the schoolteacher Georg Ohm read the current in test wires from a magnetic needle's turn, with a steady push from a thermocouple of copper and bismuth, one end in ice and one in boiling water. His 1827 book gave Ohm's law: current rises in step with the voltage and falls as resistance rises, and a wire of one metal resists more the longer and less the thicker it is. So at the same push a shorter or thicker wire carries more current and a longer one less, and only a longer wire carrying more current would have broken the law. One Berlin journal's review dismissed the book as "a web of naked fancies"; the doubters mostly objected to treating electricity by mathematics. Gustav Fechner's careful tests of 1831 bore Ohm out.

Parts in series sit end to end on one path and share the battery's voltage; take one out and the path breaks, as on old strings of holiday lights. In parallel, every part has a branch of its own across the source. So when three bulbs share one battery, only if all three are in parallel can any one come out and leave the other two lit.

A house is wired in parallel because each lamp and socket, joined straight across the supply, then gets its full voltage whatever else is on. Old filament bulbs of 60 and 25 watts, the energy each uses each second, get the same voltage from house sockets. With the same push, more current flows only where there is less resistance, so the brighter 60-watt bulb has the filament with less resistance, not more.

In September 1821, at London's Royal Institution, Faraday made the first electromagnetic motor. He fixed a magnet on end in a bowl of mercury, a liquid metal, and let a hanging wire dip into it. When he sent a current down the wire, it swept round and round the magnet for as long as the current ran. The magnet's push on a current is at right angles to both the current and the field, so it shoves the wire sideways, never in; most motors since use that push.

Faraday then sought a current from magnetism; steady currents and still magnets gave nothing. On 29 August 1831 he wrapped two unjoined coils on an iron ring, one on a battery and one on a galvanometer, a needle meter for current. The needle flicked one way as the battery was connected and the other way as it was disconnected, but sat still while the current flowed steadily. Only a changing current in one coil makes a current in the other.

Later that year Faraday thrust a bar magnet into a wire coil joined to a galvanometer; the needle jumped as it entered, but a magnet resting in the coil gave nothing. Pushed in faster, the magnet changes the field through the coil faster, and the faster that field changes, the bigger the current and the flick. Power-station generators work by just such a changing field in coils.

That October Faraday built the first electromagnetic generator, a copper disc spinning between the arms of a horseshoe magnet, its axle and rim wired to a galvanometer. Each part of the turning copper sweeps across the magnet's field, and a conductor moving through a field has a current driven along it, so a current flows for as long as the disc spins. The magnet need not move.

Motor and generator are one machine run two ways: at Vienna in 1873 Hippolyte Fontaine wired an idle Gramme generator to a working one by mistake, and its shaft spun. Coasting downhill, an electric car's turning wheels spin its motor, which now works as a generator, charging the battery and holding the car back. This is regenerative braking.

energys-two-great-laws.title: Energy's Two Great Laws
energys-two-great-laws.context_blurb:
Every engine, power station and fridge obeys two laws of heat found in the 1800s. The first: energy is never made or destroyed, only changed in form. The second: energy left alone spreads out, and spread-out energy can do less work. So no machine runs forever.

Most chemists around 1800 took heat to be caloric, a weightless fluid. In Count Rumford's 1798 test at Munich, horses turned a cannon under water against a fixed blunt borer, and caloric's believers said the grinding squeezed heat from the brass. A squeezed fluid would run dry, yet the heat kept coming for as long as the cannon turned. What a body gives without limit, Rumford argued, cannot be a substance: heat must be motion.

In the 1840s James Joule, a Salford brewer, measured the warming as falling weights churned water with paddles, then mercury, and as iron ground on iron. Every method came close to the rate he found in water: 772 foot-pounds, or 772 pounds dropped a foot, for each degree Fahrenheit a pound of water warmed. So steady a rate, whatever the material and however the work was spent, showed that work and heat are two forms of one thing. Energy changes form but is never lost: the first law of thermodynamics, the science of heat and work.

Perpetual motion, a machine running forever on nothing, breaks that law. Overbalanced wheels swing their weights wide on the falling side, where a weight far from the axle turns the wheel harder, as on a seesaw. But the far-out side carries fewer of the weights, so the wheel swings to rest where the two sides' turning pulls balance. Over a full turn every weight rises as far as it falls.

In 1824 the French engineer Sadi Carnot showed that the share of its heat an ideal engine, free of friction and leaks, can turn into work is fixed only by the temperatures of its hot and cold sides: the wider the gap, the larger the share. Steam near 540 degrees Celsius, cooled by a river, wins easily; on the sea's 20-degree gap a perfect engine turns only 6 to 8 percent of its heat into work.

Carnot pictured heat passing through an engine undiminished; Joule showed that work uses heat up. In 1850 Rudolf Clausius joined the two. An engine turns some of its heat into work and must hand the rest on to something colder, in a coal plant the cooling water of a river or a tower.

A gasoline engine is a heat engine too, working from the heat of burning fuel, so Carnot's limit binds it. An electric motor makes motion without first making heat, turning electrical energy straight into motion, so that limit does not apply and good motors pass on 90 percent or more.

Clausius's second law says heat never passes from a colder body to a warmer one without some other change. A fridge moves heat out of its cold box only by its motor's work, so its coils shed more heat than it takes in. With a fridge's door propped open in a sealed room, the pumped heat flows straight back in, and the motor's work ends up as heat too, so the room slowly warms.

Picture a ship that turns heat drawn from the sea wholly into work. Such a ship would create no energy, since it spends the sea's real heat, but it would break the second law: no engine working round and round can take heat from one place and turn all of it into work.

In 1865 Clausius named entropy, a measure of how spread out energy is; as it rises, energy becomes permanently unable to do work. Drive a long way on a full tank, park where you began, and the trip has used up none of the energy, but nearly all of its ability to do work. The energy still warms the air, too thinly spread for any engine to gather back; the fuel's atoms leave as carbon dioxide and water.

Entropy also gives time its direction. Run a film of a breaking egg backwards and the pieces leap up into a whole egg, yet nothing in it breaks a law: every bump between molecules works just as well backwards. But the pieces have far more ways to lie scattered than joined, so the reverse, though not forbidden, is overwhelmingly unlikely. Arthur Eddington called this one-way direction time's arrow in 1927.

waves-at-work.title: Waves at Work
waves-at-work.context_blurb:
Sound, light, radio and the microwaves in an oven are all waves: travelling ripples that carry energy without carrying along the stuff they pass through. Waves add, cancel, echo, bend and bunch up, and people have put each habit to work.

A wave's speed is its frequency, the waves passing each second, times its wavelength, the distance from crest to crest. With the turntable out, a microwave oven melts spots in a chocolate bar half a wavelength apart, about 6 centimetres, so the waves are about 12 long. Multiply 12 centimetres by 2,450 million waves per second, the oven's frequency, and the result, about 294 million metres a second, is the speed of the microwaves. That is near light's speed: both are electromagnetic waves.

Overlapping waves add: crest on crest builds a bigger wave (constructive interference), and crest on trough, high point on low, cancels (destructive interference). In 1803 Thomas Young described splitting a narrow sunbeam with the edge of a card a thirtieth of an inch across. In its shadow, light from both sides overlapped in bright and dark bands. In each dark band, light from one side arrived half a wave behind light from the other, so the two met crest on trough and cancelled; blocking one side left nothing to cancel. Light plus light making darkness is what waves do, which told against Isaac Newton's particle theory.

Noise-cancelling headphones play a jet engine's drone back flipped upside down, so crest meets trough. Were the flipped wave to fall exactly half a wave behind, crest would meet crest, and the drone would sound louder than with the speaker off.

Waves also echo. After the Titanic sank in 1912, Paul Langevin in France built sonar, sending pulses of ultrasound, sound too high to hear, from quartz crystals that also caught the echoes; in 1918 trials it found a submarine over a kilometre away. Sound crosses sea water at roughly 1,500 metres each second, so an echo from an iceberg that returns in 4 seconds has gone six thousand metres there and back, and the iceberg lies half as far, about 3,000 metres away.

In 1955 the Glasgow doctor Ian Donald tested growths cut from his patients with a boilerworks' ultrasound flaw detector at Renfrew, beside a large steak. A cyst is a thin bag of fluid, and fluid has no boundaries inside it to send sound back. So the cyst echoed from its near wall, then fell silent until the pulse reached its far wall: echoes from those two walls only. A solid tumour's echoes weakened steadily with depth.

Radio waves echo too. In 1935 Arnold Wilkins and Robert Watson-Watt showed that a bomber miles away sends back a radio echo strong enough to catch, the start of radar. But sea water carries electric current, so it soaks up a radio wave's energy within a short way, a quarter of a metre or less, while sound crosses kilometres of sea.

Light bends, or refracts, on entering a material where it travels at a different speed. In 1966 the engineer Charles Kao argued that glass pure enough could guide light for kilometres. A fibre's core is wrapped in glass in which light travels a little faster. Light running down the core meets that boundary at too glancing an angle to cross, so all of it is reflected back in: total internal reflection, with no mirror needed. Purity did another job: Kao blamed the fibres' heavy losses on traces of iron and water soaking up the light.

In 1845, testing Christian Doppler's idea that motion changes the pitch heard, Christoph Buys Ballot had trumpeters hold one note on an open railway car, and people by the line heard it rise about a half-tone as the train neared. The trumpets never changed their note, and the air, not the train, set the sound's speed. But each crest set out from a little nearer the listener than the last, so the waves arrived bunched, more of them each second, and the note sounded higher.

Telephone cables need repeaters, stations that strengthen the fading signal and send it on. An analog call's smooth wave copies the voice, so each repeater amplifies the noise with it, and the hiss piles up. A digital call is a code of pulses, each either on or off. A digital repeater only has to decide which each pulse is, so it sends out fresh, clean pulses and drops any noise too small to change that answer.

the-periodic-tables-patterns.title: The Periodic Table's Patterns
the-periodic-tables-patterns.context_blurb:
The periodic table lines up the elements by the protons in each atom's nucleus, in rows called periods, so that elements that behave alike share a column, or group. It explains why one metal fizzes in water and another explodes, and it let chemists foretell unseen elements.

An atom's electrons sit in shells around the nucleus, and the outer shell decides how it reacts. Neon's ten electrons fill shells of two and eight, so its outer shell is full, with nothing to gain or lose. Fluorine (two and seven) is one electron short and sodium (two, eight, one) has one to spare, so both react fiercely.

A column's elements share their number of outer electrons, so they act alike. The first column's alkali metals each have one outer electron and react by giving it up. Each step down the column adds a shell, so the outer electron sits farther out, screened from the nucleus by more inner electrons, and comes away more easily. So lithium only fizzes in water; caesium explodes.

The halogens, fluorine down to iodine, run the other way, growing less reactive down the column: each has seven outer electrons and takes in one more. Fluorine's outer shell lies closest to its nucleus, with the fewest inner electrons in the way, so its small atom pulls hardest on an electron it takes in. Iodine has more protons, 53 to fluorine's 9, but its outer shell lies much farther out.

Across a row, from sodium to chlorine, every new electron goes into the same third shell while the inner shells stay put. So more protons pull harder on the same outer shell, and the atoms shrink, chlorine's to about half sodium's width, even as they grow heavier.

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev ordered the known elements by atomic weight, how heavy their atoms are, leaving gaps where nothing fitted. Below aluminium he forecast a low-melting metal weighing about 68, and in 1875 Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium, weighing 69.7 and melting below 30 degrees Celsius. Lecoq de Boisbaudran's first density, 4.7, was off; Mendeleev had written that it would be 5.9, and purer metal gave 5.9. A table built to fit the known elements was bound to fit them; a forecast made before the metal was found could fail, and did not.

Eka means one place below. Mendeleev's eka-silicon had to fall between silicon above it and tin below it in the same column, so with no sample to weigh he read its weight, about 72, off the trend down that column. Silicon itself weighs only about 28. In 1886 Clemens Winkler found it, germanium, at 72.6, the best confirmation of the table up to then.

Mendeleev trusted chemistry over weight. Tellurium is slightly heavier than iodine, yet iodine acts like chlorine and bromine, so Mendeleev put it with them, after tellurium, and claimed tellurium had been weighed wrongly. Brauner's 1883 weighing gave about 125, and Mendeleev cited it, but later careful weighings showed tellurium (127.6) really is heavier than iodine (126.9).

In 1913 Henry Moseley struck metals with electrons and found that each metal's X-rays rose in frequency by one even step per element. Each step is one more proton in the nucleus. Cobalt, though a little heavier, sits one step before nickel because it has one proton fewer, 27 against nickel's 28. The table is a count of protons, the atomic number, not an order of weights. Though Moseley never measured tellurium or iodine, the same count, 52 protons against 53, puts tellurium first.

The rare-earth metals, lanthanum to lutetium, are so alike that chemists of the early 1900s sometimes mistook a blend of two for one pure metal. Because each element's X-rays rise one even step above the last's, every element takes one whole number, none skipped and none spare, so there was room for exactly fifteen, lanthanum and lutetium included. A sniper killed Moseley at Gallipoli in 1915, aged 27.

Lord Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen drawn from air was heavier, litre for litre, by about half a percent, than nitrogen made from chemicals. William Ramsay soaked up air's nitrogen with hot magnesium until a trace of gas remained that would react with nothing. They named it argon in 1894, from a Greek word meaning lazy, and its weight, about 40, matched no empty square. Argon proved the first of a whole family the table lacked: neon, krypton and xenon followed in 1898, and in 1902 Mendeleev gave them a column.

light-from-atoms.title: Light from Atoms
light-from-atoms.context_blurb:
Pass the glow of a thin, hot gas through a prism and it splits into sharp coloured lines, like a barcode, and every element prints its own. Those lines colour neon signs and let astronomers read what stars are made of.

A hot solid, like an old bulb's white-hot filament, glows in every colour at once. A thin gas cannot, because an atom's electrons may sit only at set energy levels. In a neon sign a current knocks electrons up a level; dropping back, each gives off a photon, a packet of light holding exactly the energy it lost. So a neon atom gives off energy only in set amounts, each one colour: its many sharp lines include a bright red one at 640 nanometres. Nothing in the tube burns.

A hydrogen electron on the third level may fall straight to the first, releasing one ultraviolet photon of 12.1 electronvolts, a unit sized for atoms, or stop at the second, releasing a red photon of about 1.9 and then an ultraviolet one of 10.2: again 12.1. Each photon carries off exactly what its electron lost, so one drop or two gives the same total: both routes start and end on the same levels.

Each element's electrons have energy levels spaced in its own way, so the drops between them, and their colours, belong to that element alone. In a burner flame strontium glows crimson, copper blue-green and sodium yellow, and a prism splits each glow into thin lines. The flame's heat only lifts the electrons; it does not choose the colour.

In 1814 Joseph von Fraunhofer, a Munich lens maker, found sunlight's colours crossed by dark lines, the same through different glass, so they were no flaw of the prism. With a prism on a telescope he saw the Sun's lines in the Moon, Venus and Mars, which shine by reflected sunlight, but other lines in Sirius and Castor, though their light passed the same air, prism and lens. So those extra lines were made in the stars themselves, before their light set out.

In 1859 at Heidelberg, Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen built a spectroscope, a prism set up for reading the lines of coloured flames. They burned each metal as half a dozen compounds, from chloride to carbonate, in flames of many fuels, cool and fierce. Whatever the compound or the flame, the lines of every metal stayed in the same places.

In 1835 the philosopher Auguste Comte held that the stars' chemistry could never be known. Yet a sodium flame shines a yellow pair exactly where sunlight has two dark lines, called D. In 1859 Kirchhoff sent bright sunlight through a sodium flame, and the D lines, instead of filling in, grew darker. Sodium gas soaks up light of exactly the energies its electrons can jump by, the very colours it gives off. So, Kirchhoff concluded, sodium lies in the cooler gas above the Sun's glowing surface; Comte had died two years before.

At an eclipse in India in August 1868, Pierre Janssen recorded a yellow line from the Sun's rim, and Norman Lockyer saw it in England that autumn. It sat near sodium's pair but on neither, so Lockyer named its maker helium, from helios, Greek for the Sun. Doubt and mockery followed. Proof came in March 1895, when William Ramsay treated cleveite, a uranium mineral, with acid and collected a gas that glowed with the Sun's yellow line. Helium turned up in natural gas only in 1905.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne read stellar lines with Meghnad Saha's theory of ionization, atoms losing electrons in heat. Astronomers had read a strong line as plenty of an element. But in the hottest stars nearly all hydrogen has lost its electron, and in cooler ones like the Sun nearly all sits on its lowest level, out of visible light's reach; only near 10,000 kelvins, as on Sirius, are many atoms ready to make lines. A line's strength, she found, is set mostly by how hot the star's surface is. Read so, stars are mostly hydrogen and helium.

Henry Norris Russell of Princeton, one of her examiners, held, like most astronomers, that the Sun was made of Earth's elements in much the same proportions. He wrote to her that a millionfold excess of hydrogen over the metals was plainly impossible, and her thesis called its figures almost certainly unreal. He reached her answer by another method in 1929, yet for years got most of the credit.

balancing-equations-and-reaction-rates.title: Balancing Equations and Reaction Rates
balancing-equations-and-reaction-rates.context_blurb:
A chemical equation writes a reaction as a sum: reactants, the substances going in, left of the arrow; products on the right. Since a reaction never makes or destroys atoms, both sides must hold the same ones. Then a second puzzle: why does rust creep while a dust cloud explodes?

Balancing changes only the coefficients, the big numbers in front; a formula's small numbers, its subscripts, fix what substance it is. The Space Shuttle's main engines joined liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen into water, but H2 + O2 → H2O loses an oxygen atom. Balanced, it reads 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, with four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms on each side. H2O2 would even the count too, but it is hydrogen peroxide.

For Fritz Haber's ammonia, 2NH3 on the right holds six hydrogen atoms. Each H2 molecule brings two hydrogen atoms, so a 3 goes in front of H2, giving N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. A 6 would count atoms, not molecules. Made over hot iron, his ammonia now fertilises the crops that feed about half the world's people and won him the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The same Haber oversaw Germany's first large chlorine gas attack, at Ypres in April 1915, and is called the father of chemical warfare.

A metal such as zinc, magnesium or iron fizzes in an acid, giving off hydrogen and leaving a salt dissolved, such as zinc chloride. Hydrogen burns, so a lit splint at the mouth of its tube goes off with a squeaky pop, the classic test. Acid on marble makes a gas that puts a splint out; oxygen, which does not burn, only makes a glowing splint flare.

A base, such as sodium hydroxide, is an acid's chemical opposite, and neutralising one with the other makes new substances rather than merely diluting both. The acid's hydrogen ions, charged particles, join the base's hydroxide ions as water. With hydrochloric acid and just enough sodium hydroxide, the leftover sodium and chloride form sodium chloride, so the flask holds only a salt and water.

Rust is iron joined with oxygen and water; three nails show that both are needed. One lies in water boiled free of air, under oil that keeps air out. That nail has water but no oxygen and stays bright, so water with no oxygen cannot rust iron. A second, in air kept dry by calcium chloride, stays bright too, ruling out oxygen alone. Only the nail in open water, with air above, rusts.

Particles react only when they collide with at least a minimum energy, the activation energy. Ten degrees of warming roughly doubles many reactions' rates, yet in a gas going from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius the particles meet under two percent more often. Warming greatly raises the number of fast, energetic particles, so many more of the collisions carry enough energy to react. The minimum itself stays put.

Crowding particles closer also speeds a reaction: fire needs oxygen molecules to strike its fuel, and only a fifth of air is oxygen. On 27 January 1967, in a launch-pad test, Roger Chaffee, Ed White and Gus Grissom were sealed in their Apollo 1 capsule in pure oxygen. A spark, most likely electrical, lit nylon and foam, fire filled the cabin within half a minute, and the three astronauts died. Pure oxygen packs about five times as many oxygen molecules into each litre as air, so far more strike the fuel every second. NASA afterwards launched crews in 60 percent oxygen, 40 percent nitrogen.

Surface matters too, because burning happens only where a fuel's surface meets oxygen. In a heap of sawdust, air reaches only the specks on top, so the heap just smoulders. Blown into a cloud, each flying speck meets the air all round, so the whole surface of every speck burns at once. In 1878 a spark lit flour dust in the air of the Washburn A Mill in Minneapolis, and the blast and fire killed 18 people.

A catalyst speeds a reaction without being used up, by offering a route with a lower activation energy. Hydrogen peroxide slowly splits into water and oxygen by itself; a pinch of manganese dioxide makes it froth in seconds. A reactant is used up as it turns into products, so if the powder were one, less of it would be left after the frothing. Filtered, washed and dried, the manganese dioxide weighs just what it did and sets fresh peroxide frothing: a catalyst.

the-molecules-of-life.title: The Molecules of Life
the-molecules-of-life.context_blurb:
A living cell is a drop of water crowded with polymers, large molecules each built as a chain of small units. Four kinds do most of life's work: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Around them lies the cell membrane, a thin, oily skin that decides what gets in and out.

Leaves make the sugar glucose, and a plant joins much of it into starch, a glucose chain stored as grains in tubers, roots and seeds. Loose glucose would dissolve in a cell's water, and water would follow it in by osmosis, flowing through the membrane toward where more is dissolved, until the cell swelled. Starch does not dissolve, so its packed grains draw no extra water into the cells.

Lipids, the fats and oils, do not dissolve in water either. An animal keeps a quick store, glycogen, a branched glucose chain in muscle and liver, but the bulk of its reserve as fat. Gram for gram, fat packs in more than twice the energy of glycogen, and it is stored dry, while each gram of glycogen holds three or four grams of water.

Ernest Overton gave the first clue to the membrane in the 1890s. He bathed living cells in some five hundred substances and timed how fast each got in. Those that mix with oil slipped in far faster than water-loving ones, whatever their size, for a fatty barrier lets through what mixes with fat. So the cell's outer boundary, Overton concluded, is a thin layer made largely of fat.

In 1925 Evert Gorter and François Grendel measured that layer. A mature mammal red blood cell has neither a nucleus nor inner membranes, so all its fat lies in its outer skin. They dissolved out that fat and spread it across water in a film one molecule deep, and it covered about double the cells' surface. So the membrane must be a double layer of fat molecules, stacked two deep. Its fat molecules, phospholipids, turn their oily tails inward and their water-loving heads out. Two errors in the pair's work roughly cancelled, and the double layer has stood.

Proteins, chains of about twenty kinds of amino acid, include antibodies, the keratin in hair and enzymes, which speed reactions. Many chemists thought proteins shapeless mixtures, varying from molecule to molecule. From 1943 to 1955 Frederick Sanger broke cattle insulin into short overlapping pieces, identified each, and fitted the overlaps together. Insulin proved to be two chains, of 21 and 30 amino acids, each in one exact order, and by extension every protein has its own sequence. That order sets each chain's folded shape.

In the 1860s Friedrich Miescher found the nucleic acid DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, in white blood cells; Phoebus Levene later showed it to be a chain of units called nucleotides, in just four kinds. Into the 1940s most biologists took genes, the units of heredity, to be protein. Genes must hold a vast store of varied instructions, and twenty kinds of unit seemed to promise far more different chains than four. Experiments in 1944 and 1952 proved genes are DNA: four kinds of unit, in any order along a long chain, spell endless messages.

Small molecules cross the membrane by diffusion, spreading from crowded to less crowded with no energy spent. A human cell holds some thirty times more potassium than the fluid outside; potassium leaks out all the time, yet the gap lasts, because the cell pumps it back in by active transport, spending energy against the crowd. The proof is a poison such as cyanide that cuts off the cell's energy supply: the leak then wins, and the difference fades.

Water crosses membranes too. In 1748 Jean-Antoine Nollet sealed a jar of alcohol with pig's bladder tied across its mouth and sank it in water. The bladder let water in far more readily than it let alcohol out, so the jar overfilled and pushed the bladder out tight, sometimes until it burst. In the 1820s the French doctor Henri Dutrochet coined endosmose and exosmose, the roots of the word osmosis.

Osmosis is why salt kills a slug. The salt dissolves in its slime into a brine saltier than its body, and water flows out through its skin toward the salt until the slug dies of drying out; Gordon Port of Newcastle University says the salt simply draws the water out. A slug's skin lets water out very easily, while a person's lets far less through, so salt on a hand does no harm.

viruses-bacteria-and-antibiotics.title: Viruses, Bacteria and Antibiotics
viruses-bacteria-and-antibiotics.context_blurb:
Two kinds of germ make people ill. A bacterium is one whole living cell, with its own wall and its own ribosomes, the tiny machines that build proteins. A virus is far smaller and is not a cell at all. That difference decides which medicines can help.

In 1892 the Russian botanist Dmitri Ivanovsky forced sap from diseased tobacco plants, their leaves mottled by mosaic disease, through a fine porcelain filter that stopped every known bacterium, and the clear sap still infected healthy plants. On its own, that showed only that the cause was smaller than the bacteria then known. Ivanovsky himself suspected a tiny bacterium, or a poison made by bacteria, and dissolved poisons do pass such filters.

In 1898 the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck passed filtered sap from plant to plant along a chain. Each plant got only a little sap from the one before, so a poison would have been watered down at every step until the disease faded. It never faded: the agent was multiplying inside each living plant. It grew in no broth, only in living leaves, and Beijerinck named it a virus.

In 1935 Wendell Stanley purified it into needle-like crystals that, once dissolved, still caused the disease. He took them for pure protein, but they were soon found to hold RNA. A virus is genetic material, DNA or RNA, in a coat of protein, with no ribosomes or energy-making chemistry of its own. That is why most biologists say a virus is not alive: it can copy itself only inside a living cell, using that cell's machinery. Whether viruses are alive is still argued.

Bacteria, being cells, have parts a drug can strike. In September 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to find a blue-green mould on a dish of staphylococcus, with dead bacteria all around it. Did the killing need the living mould? To find out, Fleming grew the mould in broth, filtered the mould out, and tested the clear broth alone. It still killed several kinds of bacteria, so the killer was a substance the mould gives off. In 1929 he named it penicillin.

Yet for a decade it went almost unused, because penicillin falls apart quickly and no one, from Fleming's assistants to Harold Raistrick's team in 1932, could purify it before it broke down. From 1939 Ernst Chain, Howard Florey and Norman Heatley at Oxford found how to extract and keep it.

On 25 May 1940 the Oxford team gave eight mice a killing dose of streptococci and treated four with penicillin. By a quarter to four next morning every untreated mouse was dead and the treated four lived; the untreated ones, the control, proved the dose deadly. Fleming had tested penicillin only in dishes and on healthy animals, so this showed for the first time that it could save an animal from an infection. The first human patients came early in 1941.

An antibiotic is a drug that kills bacteria or stops them multiplying, by striking parts that bacteria have and human cells lack: penicillin wrecks the wall a growing bacterium builds, and others jam bacterial ribosomes. A cold virus has none of the parts such drugs attack: it has no wall and no ribosomes, and it copies itself using the machinery of the patient's own cells. Taking an antibiotic for a cold only adds to the overuse that breeds resistant bacteria.

Besides passing genes on when it divides, a bacterium can pass copies directly to other living bacteria, even of another kind, often on plasmids, small extra loops of DNA. Animals, as a rule, pass genes only to their young. This sideways sharing is the main way resistance spreads, and its mark is one gene, identical to the last base, in distantly related kinds. A gene handed down from so distant an ancestor would no longer match.

Such genes are older than our drugs. Vanessa D'Costa, Gerard Wright and colleagues read DNA from permafrost in the far north, frozen for some thirty thousand years; mammoth DNA, with no trace of moose or spruce, proved it ancient. It held genes that defeat today's antibiotics, vancomycin included. The reason is that most antibiotics are natural weapons, which soil microbes such as Streptomyces have long made against their rivals, so resistance was favoured in the soil long before the first antibiotic drug. Heavy use in hospitals and on farms favours these old defences all the more.

the-cell-cycle.title: The Cell Cycle
the-cell-cycle.context_blurb:
Your body makes billions of new cells every day: red blood cells in the bone marrow, a fresh gut lining every few days, new cells to close a cut. Each comes from an older cell dividing in two, in a fixed order called the cell cycle. When that order fails, the result can be cancer.

Walther Flemming named mitosis, the division of a cell's nucleus, in 1882 for the threads that appear as a nucleus divides: chromosomes, strands of DNA carrying the genes. He took interphase, the time between divisions, for a rest. It is not: Alma Howard and Stephen Pelc fed bean root tips radioactive phosphorus, which goes into new DNA. The label entered the nuclei in one part of interphase, before any threads showed, so a cell copies its DNA in interphase, before mitosis begins. They named that part the S phase, for synthesis.

In prophase the chromosomes coil up thick; in metaphase they line up across the cell's middle. Each is now two identical copies, and spindle fibres from the cell's two ends, or poles, grip one copy each. The cell waits until every chromosome is gripped from both sides, which guards against a new cell getting both copies of a chromosome when, in anaphase, the copies are pulled to opposite poles. Moving on too soon can leave one cell with an extra chromosome, an error common in tumour cells.

Then cytokinesis splits the cell itself. An animal cell is squeezed in two by a tightening ring of protein fibres, but a plant cell's wall is too stiff, and its water pressure pushes back. So a plant cell builds a new wall from the centre outward: sacs from the Golgi apparatus fuse into a cell plate that spreads until it meets the old wall.

Mitosis grows the body, mends wounds and replaces worn cells. The hair roots, the gut lining and the bone marrow, which replaces red cells that last about four months, never stop dividing. Many chemotherapy drugs fight cancer by stopping cell division, so they also strike these healthy tissues, whose cells divide again and again.

A body's trillions of cells all descend from one first cell, yet nerve cells carry signals and muscle cells pull on bone. Nearly every cell keeps the full set of genes, but each kind puts a different set of its genes to work, steered by signals around it. August Weismann proposed that specialising cells lose hereditary material; John Gurdon's frogs showed they keep it.

In 1962 Gurdon wrecked a frog egg's nucleus with ultraviolet light and gave it a nucleus from a gut cell of a feeding tadpole; a few eggs became tadpoles. The donor nuclei had a mutation leaving one nucleolus, a small dark body in the nucleus, instead of the normal two. The new tadpoles' single nucleolus settled the doubt that the egg's own nucleus, surviving the light, had built the tadpole. A Basel team later did it with a white blood cell's nucleus.

In 2006 Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka put two dozen genes, all active in stem cells that can become any cell type, into fibroblasts, mouse connective-tissue cells, resetting a very few. Leaving out one gene at a time showed that four were each needed. To show they were enough, the two put in the four alone, with none of the other twenty, and those four reset cells by themselves.

Leland Hartwell and Ted Weinert broke the DNA of baker's yeast with X-rays. Normal cells paused before dividing; yeast cells whose RAD9 gene was broken kept dividing and soon died. Held still by a drug that blocks division, those cells mended their DNA. So RAD9 does not mend DNA; its job is making the cell wait until the damage is mended. Hartwell called such controls checkpoints. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize with Paul Nurse, who found the enzyme, a protein that speeds a chemical change, that drives a cell through its cycle, and Tim Hunt, who found cyclins, proteins that build up through each cycle and are destroyed at every division.

Cancer is cell division that no longer stops when it should. In a dish, healthy cells divide until they cover it one cell deep, then stop with food to spare. Cancer cells usually lose that check: they go on dividing, and pile up over one another. Many also divide fast, but their mark is that they do not stop. In the body the pile becomes a tumour.

from-dna-to-protein.title: From DNA to Protein
from-dna-to-protein.context_blurb:
Nearly every cell holds DNA, a long molecule that spells out genes in four chemical letters. To use a gene, a cell copies it into a working message, then turns the message into a protein, a molecule that builds and runs the body.

Many biologists thought genes were protein. In 1952 Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase checked with a phage, a virus of bacteria made of DNA inside a protein coat. Sulfur is in protein but not DNA, and phosphorus the reverse, so radioactive sulfur marked the coats and radioactive phosphorus the DNA. They let the phages infect bacteria, then blended off the empty coats. Had protein been the genes, the sulfur would have turned up inside the bacteria and the phosphorus outside. Instead most phosphorus went in and most sulfur stayed out: genes are DNA.

DNA's four letters are bases: A, T, G and C. Around 1950 Erwin Chargaff found human DNA held A and T near three tenths each and G and C near a fifth. Only one pairing of bases across the two strands fits such figures: A with T, and G with C. Facing bases must come in equal amounts.

Watson and Crick built that pairing into their 1953 double helix, two strands wound round each other, helped by Photo 51, an X-ray picture of DNA taken by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, her student; its dark cross showed a helix. As she prepared to leave King's College London, Gosling passed it to Maurice Wilkins. When James Watson visited King's in January 1953, Wilkins showed it to him without telling her. Nothing was taken from her desk, but she was not asked. Franklin died in 1958, four years before Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared a Nobel Prize, which is never given to the dead.

Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl then tested how DNA copies. They made bacterial DNA heavy with heavy nitrogen, let it copy once on ordinary nitrogen, and spun it in a tube that sorts by density. If old helices stayed whole beside all-new copies, the tube would show two bands, heavy and light, in equal amounts. Instead one band sat midway. So the strands part, each a template, or pattern, for a new partner.

The message is messenger RNA, read by ribosomes, the cell's protein builders. It is built along one DNA strand, each RNA base pairing with the base opposite: A with T, G with C, C with G, and U with A, as RNA uses uracil, U, in place of thymine. So a strand reading TAC-GGA yields the messenger A-U-G-C-C-U.

Two-letter words from four bases give only 16, too few for the twenty amino acids of proteins; three-letter words give 64. In 1961 Francis Crick, Sydney Brenner and colleagues added bases to a phage gene with the chemical proflavin. One or two extra bases shifted how every later base was grouped, garbling the gene. With three, the bases between the additions were misread, then reading fell back into step and the protein worked. So a gene is read in words of three bases, from a fixed start, without overlap.

That year Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei gave a protein-building juice from bacteria an artificial messenger of pure U, with all twenty amino acids. It built only phenylalanine. Since genes are read in threes, the messenger said U-U-U over and over, so U-U-U is the code word for phenylalanine.

Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells. In 1956 Vernon Ingram cut normal and sickle-cell haemoglobin into pieces with trypsin, an enzyme that cuts proteins, and sorted them into spots; one spot differed. That piece held one amino acid in place of another: valine where glutamic acid belongs. He was the first to show that one changed amino acid can cause a disease.

In 1983 Kary Mullis invented PCR, a way to copy a chosen stretch of DNA over and over. Each round begins with heat, which parts the two strands of each helix. As the tube cools, an enzyme builds a partner along each strand, so one helix becomes two, then four.

In 1984 Alec Jeffreys found DNA fingerprints, band patterns unique to each person. A current pulls cut DNA, which is negatively charged, through a gel toward the positive end. Charge grows with length, so in plain liquid all sizes move alike. But a gel is a tangle of fibres, a sieve, and the gel's mesh holds long pieces back more, so short ones run farther.

meiosis-and-patterns-of-inheritance.title: Meiosis and Patterns of Inheritance
meiosis-and-patterns-of-inheritance.context_blurb:
Every person begins as one cell, made when a sperm and an egg fuse. Meiosis, the division that makes those sex cells, explains how traits reshuffle, why blood must be matched for a transfusion, and why some illnesses strike mostly men.

A chromosome is a strand of DNA carrying genes; a gene's versions are its alleles. Human body cells hold 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent. Meiosis divides twice, leaving each sex cell one set of 23, and August Weismann saw why. Halving keeps the count from doubling every generation: if eggs and sperm kept all 46, a child's first cell would hold 92.

In the first division the partners of each pair line up side by side and part, each pair facing either way at random. So each of a woman's eggs gets a chance mix of chromosomes from her mother and her father, every pair sorting on its own: over eight million possible mixes. This is independent assortment.

In 1911 Thomas Hunt Morgan found two genes on a fruit fly's X chromosome, for white eyes and miniature wings, linked: inherited together far more often than chance predicts. Yet some young broke the pair. Morgan proposed crossing over: paired chromosomes, lying side by side, break and swap matching pieces, so a white-eye gene can land beside a normal-wing gene.

Morgan's student Alfred Sturtevant skipped his homework one night to draw the first gene map. Crossing over splits genes far apart more often, since more swap points lie between them, so he read that percentage as distance. For three genes, the outer pair's figure nearly equalled the inner two added. Distances add like that only along a line, so the genes lie in a line, each in a fixed place, like beads on a string.

Gregor Mendel had seen independent sorting in peas, crossing round yellow with wrinkled green, round and yellow being dominant, and letting the offspring self-pollinate. Round is three chances in four and green one in four, so round with green is a quarter of three quarters, about three in sixteen; Mendel counted 108 of 556. Genes close together on one chromosome seldom part, so they give only a few new mixes.

Some alleles do not mask their partners. A pure-breeding red snapdragon crossed with a white one gives pink offspring: incomplete dominance. Cross two pinks, and since each parent hands on red or white by chance, the seedlings come out about one red to two pink to one white. Red and white return because the alleles never blended.

Around 1900 Karl Landsteiner mixed his colleagues' serum, the liquid part of blood, with one another's red cells. Some mixes clumped, as serum's antibodies attack foreign markers: group A serum attacks the B marker, group B serum the A. His students Adriano Sturli and Alfred von Decastello found rare cells clumped by both. Those cells carried both the A marker and the B marker, so the group was named AB; group O cells carry neither. In an AB person each allele makes its marker in full: codominance.

Emil von Dungern and Ludwik Hirszfeld, having shown the groups are inherited, proposed two genes: A or no A, and B or no B. In 1924 Felix Bernstein proposed one gene with three alleles, O, A and B. Most families fit both. The telling case is an AB parent: under two genes, such a parent could pass on a no-A and a no-B copy together, making a group O child possible; Bernstein's AB parent has only A and B to give. Families bore Bernstein out.

The genes for the eye's red-sensing and green-sensing pigments lie on the X chromosome, of which a man has one and a woman two. One faulty copy on a man's single X makes him colour-blind, but a woman is colour-blind only when both her X chromosomes carry the fault, because one working copy is usually enough. John Dalton's preserved eye, studied in the 1990s, lacked the green-pigment gene.

Queen Victoria never had haemophilia, in which blood fails to clot, and no case is known before her; yet her son Leopold did, and two daughters without signs, Alice and Beatrice, had sons who did. Victoria carried the faulty gene on one of her X chromosomes, so each child had an even chance of getting it: a son who did was ill, a daughter a carrier. Prince Albert could not have given it to Leopold: a father gives his sons his Y.

how-evolution-works.title: How Evolution Works
how-evolution-works.context_blurb:
Evolution is change in living things over generations, driven chiefly by natural selection, one of the best-tested ideas in science. It can be watched in a flask of bacteria and read in DNA. Its parts are simple: inherited differences, more young than can survive, and chance.

Charles Darwin worked natural selection out by 1838 but left it unpublished until 1858, when Alfred Russel Wallace wrote from the Malay islands with the same idea. Both took their key from Thomas Malthus. Malthus argued that people multiply faster than their food supply, so famine, disease and war must hold their numbers back. In such a struggle, helpful variations tend to survive.

Jean-Baptiste Lamarck held that a body's gains in life pass to its young, an idea genetics later retired. August Weismann docked the tails of white mice for five generations, and all 901 young had full tails. Weismann saw support for his germ plasm idea: traits are carried by egg and sperm, set apart from the body and beyond reach of its wounds.

Wilhelm Johannsen raised beans in pure lines, each from one self-pollinating plant, so all the beans in a line shared their genes. Weights still varied, yet a line's heaviest and lightest beans, sown apart for generations, bred offspring alike in weight. The extra weight came from growing conditions, not genes, such as how well each mother plant was fed. Selection acts only on inherited differences.

To a biologist, evolution is a change across generations in a population's genes: in how common each gene version is. So in a wild herd of sheep, a gene for dark wool growing more common in each crop of lambs is evolution. Selection acts on single animals, but only a population evolves.

Genetic drift is such change by pure chance, strongest in small populations. Hunted for blubber oil to perhaps twenty by the 1890s, northern elephant seals now top 200,000, protected since the 1920s, yet at one DNA stretch they show only two types. Only seals that died before numbers crashed can show what the species once carried, and their DNA, from museum skins and old bones, is more varied. That crash was a bottleneck.

Chance can even spread a harmful gene. A typhoon in 1775 left about twenty people alive on the Pacific atoll of Pingelap. One of the few survivors, the island's ruler, is believed to have carried one copy of a gene for total colour blindness, harmless alone; among so few, chance let it spread until about three islanders in ten carry it. This is the founder effect.

Gene flow is genes moving between populations of a species, with wandering animals or drifting pollen. Migrants carry gene versions both ways, mixing whatever builds up in one population into the other: gene flow keeps them alike and works against their splitting. So species usually split only once a barrier, a sea or a river, cuts it off.

Biologists count two populations as one species while they can interbreed and have fertile young; horses and donkeys mate, but mules are sterile. So when populations long cut apart meet again and their hybrid young cannot have young of their own, they have become separate species. A species is not defined by looks, though people often tell species apart by looks.

DNA gathers small changes every generation, so lines that parted long ago differ more. The chimpanzee's genome, read in 2005, matches ours at close to 98.8 percent of the letters that line up; the human-mouse gap is sixty times wider. Humans and chimpanzees had a recent common ancestor, their lines parting six to seven million years ago, the mouse line about 75 million. Chimpanzees are cousins, not ancestors.

Since 1988 Richard Lenski's lab has kept twelve populations of the bacterium E. coli, from one ancestor, in fresh broth daily, freezing samples that stay alive. Fitness means success at leaving offspring against rivals. To measure it, the lab grows a thawed ancestor and a later population in one flask, marked to tell them apart, to see which multiplies faster. Grown alone, each would stop when the broth's little sugar ran out.

Around generation 31,500, cells in one flask began feeding on citrate, present in the broth from the start. Zachary Blount replayed the flask's history from its frozen samples: only cells from generation 20,000 on ever evolved the trick again. So an earlier genetic change had paved the way: the population's history mattered, not one rare mutation equally likely at any time.

respiration-and-enzymes.title: Respiration and Enzymes
respiration-and-enzymes.context_blurb:
Every cell in your body runs on a slow, controlled burning: sugar and the oxygen you breathe become water and carbon dioxide, freeing the energy behind every heartbeat. Enzymes, the cell's protein tools, run each reaction along the way.

Antoine Lavoisier thought breathing burns carbon slowly, as a fire does. Around 1783 he and Pierre-Simon Laplace weighed the ice a guinea pig's heat melted. Fast or slow, burning carbon gives the same heat, so the fair test is heat for each ounce of fixed air, our carbon dioxide. The animal melted 13 ounces where charcoal making as much fixed air melts about 10: near enough as much ice for each ounce of fixed air as burning charcoal melts.

That slow burning is cellular respiration, which stores its energy in ATP (adenosine triphosphate), a small molecule cells spend like coins, made mostly in the mitochondria. At the end of a reaction chain on their inner membrane, oxygen takes up electrons and hydrogen ions, ending up in the water made in the mitochondria. The carbon dioxide you breathe out comes from the sugar's own carbon.

In the mid-1930s Albert Szent-Györgyi found that traces of succinate or fumarate, acids cells make, sped minced pigeon muscle's oxygen use far beyond what so little acid could fuel. In 1937 Hans Krebs and William Johnson saw citrate do the same. Krebs reasoned that each is used up by one reaction and remade by a later one, at the end of a loop of reactions. This Krebs cycle frees carbon dioxide at each turn.

Without oxygen, cells fall back on fermentation, running only the first steps of breaking down sugar for 2 ATP per glucose, against many times more with oxygen. Around 1860 Louis Pasteur spread yeast thin in a dish open to the air, and it multiplied faster and fermented less. Sealed away from air, it fermented hard, spending far more sugar on each gram of new yeast. Each sugar yields far less ATP without oxygen, so sealed yeast needs far more sugar to grow as much.

Muscle short of oxygen in a hard run ferments too, making lactic acid, or lactate, once wrongly blamed for next-day soreness. But blood lactate is back to normal within about an hour, long before the ache peaks one to three days later. Tiny tears in muscle fibres, mostly where muscles lengthen as they pull, are thought to cause it: in a 1983 test, an easier downhill run left legs sore, a harder level run did not.

An enzyme is a molecule, nearly always a protein, that speeds a reaction and comes out unchanged. Dry glucose sits unchanged on a shelf, though it burns fiercely, because every reaction needs a push to start: its activation energy. An enzyme lowers the energy needed to start its step, offering an easier path, so the step runs millions of times faster at body heat.

Pasteur's followers held that only a living cell ferments. In 1897 Eduard Buchner pressed juice from yeast crushed with sand; given cane sugar, it bubbled out carbon dioxide for days. Yet stray living cells might explain that. The deciding test was a filter that holds back every cell: had the juice, filtered of all its yeast cells, not fermented, Buchner would have been wrong. It fermented: a dissolved substance, zymase, did the work.

In 1926 James Sumner crystallised urease, from jack beans, and found it was protein. Richard Willstätter said the protein was only a carrier for the real enzyme, a far smaller molecule. John Northrop recrystallised pepsin, a stomach enzyme, over and over. A clinging molecule should have been shed bit by bit, yet each gram kept the same activity through seven crystallisations, so pepsin itself is a protein.

Each enzyme acts on its own substrate, the molecule it works on. Methyl glucoside comes in two forms of the same atoms, differing only in which way one group points. In 1894 Emil Fischer found that a yeast enzyme split one form and emulsin, an almond enzyme, only the other. Fischer explained that only the matching form fitted each enzyme's own shape, as a key fits its lock.

Heat can ruin that shape. A moderate fever is a rise the brain sets on purpose, thought to help fight infection; heat stroke is the body's heat control failing. Above about 40 degrees Celsius proteins begin to unfold, and in a body held at 42 or more, enzymes lose the shape their work depends on, so cells and organs fail.

how-the-sun-shines.title: How the Sun Shines
how-the-sun-shines.context_blurb:
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, but its energy was made deep inside the Sun, in a core some fifteen million degrees Celsius hot. By weighing atoms, catching ghostly particles and counting dark spots, astronomers have learned how the Sun shines and how old it is.

For ages the Sun looked like a great fire. In 1862 Lord Kelvin worked out that even the best chemical fuel could give only about three thousand years of the Sun's heat, so a burning Sun would have burned out in a few thousand years, too soon for Earth's long history. Its stored heat and slow shrinking could keep it shining only some tens of millions of years.

In Cambridge, Francis Aston found that a helium atom is a little lighter than four hydrogen atoms put together, by about one part in 120. In 1920, at Cardiff, Arthur Eddington argued that shrinking could never power the stars for so long, so they must shine by building helium out of hydrogen. The lost mass comes out as energy, while breaking helium apart would cost energy instead.

That fusion happens only in the core, and slowly: at the very centre, models give under three hundred watts for each cubic metre, roughly the heat a compost heap makes. The Sun blazes anyway because its core holds a vast amount of gas, all of it fusing, and those small outputs add up.

The energy escapes slowly, because the gas around the core is so dense that light travels only a tiny way before an atom soaks it up and sends it off again in a random direction, so it zigzags outward like a lost walker. Rising and sinking gas then carries the heat through the outer third far faster.

Fusion also makes neutrinos, tiny particles that cross the whole Sun in about two seconds. From the late 1960s Ray Davis caught them in a huge tank of chlorine-rich cleaning fluid deep in a South Dakota gold mine, but found only a third of the number that solar models predicted. Chlorine reacts with just one of the three kinds of neutrino. In 2001 and 2002, Canada's Sudbury Neutrino Observatory counted all three kinds at once: the total matched the models, but only a third were of Davis's kind. Nothing had gone missing, because neutrinos change kind on their way from the core, which they can do only if they have mass.

The Sun's age, about 4.6 billion years, comes from dating the Solar System's first solids, grains rich in calcium and aluminium kept in some meteorites, by the radioactive elements inside them. Earth's oldest rocks are younger, about four billion years, because most of its first crust has been melted and remade.

Behind a solar filter, sunspots look black, though they are thousands of degrees hot. In 1908 George Ellery Hale found strong magnetism in them from the way it split the lines in their light. That magnetism chokes off the rising and sinking gas that carries heat up from below, so a spot is 1,500 degrees or more cooler than the surface around it and glows dimmer.

From 1826 the Dessau pharmacist Heinrich Schwabe spent every clear day for seventeen years searching the Sun for an unknown planet inside Mercury's orbit, logging each sunspot. He never found his planet, but his log showed the number of spots rising and falling over about ten years. The cycle averages about eleven years, and it is magnetic: each cycle, the Sun's magnetic poles swap places.

Magnetic energy stored near sunspots can burst out as a flare. On 1 September 1859 Richard Carrington saw two dazzling patches of white light blaze up among the spots and vanish within minutes. Some seventeen hours later a cloud of magnetised gas from the Sun struck Earth, and telegraph systems on both sides of the Atlantic threw sparks. Earth's changing magnetic field drove the current, because a swinging magnetic field drives electric current along a long wire, even with the batteries unhooked.

In 1957 Fred Hoyle, William Fowler and the Burbidges, Margaret and Geoffrey, set out how stars forge heavier atoms as they shine and explode, making most of what is in your body. The great exception is the hydrogen in your water: it was made in the Big Bang, before any star shone, and it is the very fuel that stars fuse into everything heavier. The oxygen bonded to it, like your carbon, was forged in stars.

reading-the-big-bang-in-light.title: Reading the Big Bang in Light
reading-the-big-bang-in-light.context_blurb:
Light from a distant galaxy is old light, and it carries a record. Its stretched waves show how the universe has grown, a faint glow from every direction shows how hot it once was, and the speeds of stars and galaxies reveal ingredients that no one has yet identified.

Each dark line in a galaxy's spectrum marks one exact colour, so astronomers can see every line slide toward red. Light's waves stretch as space expands, so waves that arrive twice as long as they set out mean the distances between galaxies have doubled since the light left. The universe was then half its present size. Dust can redden a galaxy's colour, but only a true red shift moves the lines.

In 1948 Robert Herman and Ralph Alpher reasoned that the hot young universe George Gamow pictured must have left a faint afterglow. It set out some 380,000 years after the beginning, from gas near 3,000 degrees above absolute zero. They expected it to arrive at only about five degrees above absolute zero, because the universe's expansion has stretched its light. In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the glow by chance, as faint microwaves.

Fred Hoyle, who rejected the Big Bang to the end, called the glow starlight that dust had absorbed and given out again. In 1989 the COBE satellite put that to the test: John Mather's team measured the glow's brightness wavelength by wavelength. A blackbody, an object that soaks up all light falling on it, glows in one smooth curve set by its temperature alone, and the glow matched one such curve almost perfectly. Dust lies near and far, some warmer and some cooler, and dust at many temperatures would blend many curves into a mix no single curve fits.

A second COBE instrument, led by George Smoot, compared the glow's temperature across the sky. In 1992 his team found spots warmer or cooler than average by only some thirty millionths of a degree. Theorists had expected such ripples because galaxies had to grow from slightly denser patches, which gravity drew together over billions of years.

By calculation, the first minutes made matter about one part in four helium by mass, the rest hydrogen. Stars turn hydrogen into helium too. So astronomers test the forecast in glowing gas clouds in small galaxies with hardly any heavy elements, because stars have added the least helium to them. There helium is about 24.5 percent of the mass, close to the forecast.

In 1933 Fritz Zwicky used red shifts measured by Milton Humason and Edwin Hubble to time the galaxies darting about inside the Coma Cluster. At about a thousand kilometres a second, they moved far too fast for the gravity of its visible stars to hold them. Zwicky concluded that far more matter is there than can be seen, and he called it dark matter. Modern studies agree.

In 1970 Vera Rubin and Kent Ford reported how fast gas clouds circle the Andromeda Galaxy. Around the Sun, Mercury races far faster than distant Neptune, but in Andromeda the outer clouds kept pace with the inner ones. The mass inside each orbit must keep growing outward, so much of the galaxy's mass lies far out, where little light shines, in a vast unseen halo. Rubin and others found the same in galaxy after galaxy, yet no detector has confirmed a particle of dark matter.

Two rival teams, one led by Saul Perlmutter and one including Adam Riess and Brian Schmidt, measured distant Type Ia supernovae, exploding stars that all peak at almost the same brightness, so their dimness gives their distance. Both expected gravity to be slowing the expansion, but in 1998 both found the distant blasts fainter, and so farther, than expected. Their light had travelled longer than a slowing expansion allows, so the expansion has been speeding up, for the last five or six billion years. Dust, which reddens light as it dims it, was corrected for. The unknown cause was named dark energy.

NASA's WMAP probe and Europe's Planck satellite later mapped the glow's ripples more finely, and the ripples' strength at each size depends on the universe's ingredients. By Planck's count in 2013, ordinary matter, the stuff of every atom, star and planet, is only about a twentieth of the universe. Dark matter is about 27 percent and dark energy about 68, so some 95 percent of the universe is stuff whose nature no one yet knows.

keplers-laws-and-newtons-gravity.title: Kepler's Laws and Newton's Gravity
keplers-laws-and-newtons-gravity.context_blurb:
Why do the planets circle the Sun instead of flying off into space? Johannes Kepler found the rules they follow, and Isaac Newton explained those rules with one law of gravity, a law later used to time a comet, find a planet and weigh the Earth.

Tycho Brahe, the last great astronomer to work without a telescope, logged Mars for nearly twenty years, and Kepler inherited his records. Kepler's best model of Mars still missed some sightings by eight arcminutes, roughly a quarter of the Moon's width. Tycho's own errors were only one or two arcminutes, far smaller than the gap, so the fault had to lie in the model, and Kepler threw it out. Those eight minutes, he wrote, would lead the way to the reform of all astronomy.

The shape that worked, published in 1609 in Astronomia Nova, was an ellipse, with the Sun off its centre at a focus, one of two points along the long axis. Kepler found it the hard way: an egg-shaped path missed by eight arcminutes in the other direction, and the truth lay between. The planets' ellipses are nearly round; drawn to scale, Mars's path looks almost like a circle.

Kepler's second law says the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so it crosses the northern winter stretch of its orbit a few days quicker than the summer stretch. The tilt makes the seasons but not this difference: in the south, winter is the longest season.

Newton asked whether the pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon, which lies about sixty Earth radii from Earth's centre; sixty times sixty is 3,600. The Moon's fall each second, bending it off a straight course, is about 3,600 times smaller than an apple's in its first second, so Earth's pull weakens with the square of the distance. Twice as far, a pull is a quarter as strong.

Kepler's third law says the farther out a planet lies, the longer its year. Saturn lies about nine and a half times as far out as Earth, yet takes nearly thirty years to go round. Saturn moves more slowly, because the Sun's pull out there is weaker, at about 9.7 kilometres a second, a third of Earth's speed. Newton showed why: so weak a pull can hold a planet on its curved path only at a slower speed.

Newton weighed Jupiter by how fast its moons circle it at their distances, since the stronger a planet's pull, the faster a moon must go round to stay in orbit. The four large moons Galileo found in 1610 gave Jupiter about a thousandth of the Sun's mass. A planet's own trip round the Sun reveals almost nothing of its mass: small asteroids sharing Jupiter's path take the same 12 years.

Newton's law says every mass pulls on every other, so Halley's comet feels the pull of Jupiter and Saturn as it passes them, which Halley had blamed for its uneven laps. Before its return, Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute worked out that those two planets would delay it by 618 days. It rounded the Sun in March 1759, within about a month of their forecast, one of the first great tests of Newton's law.

In 1797 and 1798 Henry Cavendish hung a long rod from a thin wire, with little lead balls on its ends, and set a big lead ball beside each, so the wire's twist measured the big balls' sideways tug. A small ball's weight is Earth's pull on it, and a body's pull depends on its mass alone, whatever it is made of. So comparing the two pulls told Cavendish how many big balls' worth of mass Earth holds. He gave it as Earth's average density, about 5.5 times that of water and far above the crust's, evidence for a dense metal core.

Uranus, too, wandered from its predicted path, first running ahead and then lagging. Working from the drift alone, the Paris mathematician Urbain Le Verrier calculated that an unseen planet farther out was pulling on Uranus, and where it must be. On 23 September 1846 Johann Galle and Heinrich d'Arrest in Berlin found Neptune less than a degree from his spot. Some had doubted Newton's law so far from the Sun; instead it led Le Verrier to a new planet.

earths-interior-and-age.title: Earth's Interior and Age
earths-interior-and-age.context_blurb:
Earth hides what lies inside it and how old it is. No one can visit its centre or watch it form, yet we know its layers and its age, some four and a half billion years. Earthquake waves and radioactive atoms told us.

Earthquakes give off two main kinds of wave. A P-wave, the fastest, pushes and pulls rock along its path; an S-wave shears it, shaking it crosswise. Solid rock springs back when sheared, but a liquid does not spring back when pushed sideways: it flows aside, so an S-wave dies in it. Squeezed, a liquid does push back, so P-waves cross it.

In 1909 Andrija Mohorovičić gathered a Croatian quake's records from forty-one stations. Near ones caught one P-wave; beyond some 240 kilometres, many caught two, the earlier one new. It was the same kind of wave by a second route: below a certain depth, rock carries the waves faster. Dipping into that rock, a wave outran the shallow one despite its longer road. That boundary is the Moho, the base of the crust.

Opposite a great quake, a wide band of stations gets P-waves but no S-waves straight through: the outer core is liquid. The solid mantle above it is hot and dense, yet carries S-waves.

The core was long thought liquid throughout, bending P-waves away from a broad shadow zone. Yet after a 1929 quake in New Zealand, two Russian stations deep in that shadow caught strong ones. In 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann proposed a smaller core inside the core, where waves travel faster; the jump in speed at its edge bends some waves into the shadow. By 1971 the planet's ringing after great quakes had shown the inner core solid.

In 1962 Harry Hess proposed that fresh ocean floor forms at the mid-ocean ridges and drifts outward on both sides. Mud settles on new rock soon after it forms, so bottom mud should be older farther from a ridge. Had the lowest mud been about the same age at every site, the floor would have been made all at once, the worst blow to Hess. In 1968-69 the ship Glomar Challenger drilled across the South Atlantic ridge: bottom fossils were some 11 million years old 200 kilometres out, 76 million beyond 1,600.

In 1862 Lord Kelvin timed Earth's cooling from a hot young planet, a sum that assumed Earth makes no new heat of its own inside. In 1903 Pierre Curie and Albert Laborde measured radium's own heat: enough to melt an equal weight of ice in less than an hour. Rock's radioactive uranium, thorium and potassium make about half the heat leaving Earth, so it cools far more slowly than Kelvin allowed.

Radioactivity also gave a better clock. In each half-life, half the unstable atoms left decay. A growing zircon takes in uranium but shuts out lead, so all its lead was made inside, by decay. Uranium-235 has a half-life of roughly 700 million years and turns into lead-207. Three lead-207 atoms for each uranium-235 atom left means a quarter of the uranium remains: two half-lives, about 1.4 billion years. Three half-lives would leave an eighth.

Physicists have heated and squeezed decaying atoms, and the rate barely moves. Heat, pressure and chemistry act on an atom's outer electrons, but decay happens in the nucleus, which heat and pressure barely touch. The crystal's job is to keep uranium and lead from being added or lost.

Earth's oldest rocks, remade by moving plates and weathering, are only about 4 billion years old, so the date came from space. In 1956 Clair Patterson plotted lead from five meteorites, one form of lead against another: all five lined up, and the line's slope gave about 4.55 billion years. Deep-sea mud, taken to stand for all of Earth's lead, lay on that same line. Earth's lead had built up from the same start for the same time: Earth formed at the same time as the meteorites.

Patterson, forced to build a sealed clean room against stray lead, grew sure most lead in people and air was not natural. Robert Kehoe, medical adviser to the maker of the petrol additive tetraethyl lead, held that lead in the body is normal and low doses harmless. Lead found anywhere shows only that it is there, not when it came. Snow piles up in yearly layers, so Greenland's ice keeps a dated record, and recent snow held far more lead than ancient snow: some 200 times as much.

what-drives-earths-climate.title: What Drives Earth's Climate
what-drives-earths-climate.context_blurb:
Earth's climate runs on an energy budget: sunlight pours in, heat radiates back to space, and while the two match the average temperature holds steady. When they drift apart, the planet warms or cools. That has happened many times, from ice ages to a forested Arctic, and it is happening now.

Carbon dioxide absorbs the infrared heat Earth gives off and slows its escape; that physics is settled, and so is the warming. In 2021 Norman Loeb's NASA team found Earth gaining more energy than it loses. Most of that heat has gone into the oceans, about 89 percent since 1971, while only about 1 percent has warmed the air.

Working by hand for almost thirty years, the Serbian engineer Milutin Milankovic calculated how the axis's tilt and wobble and the orbit's stretch move sunshine between seasons. An ice sheet grows, he reasoned, when summers are too cool to melt the winter's snow, so the snow piles up year after year. In 1976 Nicholas Shackleton, John Imbrie and James Hays tested him on 450,000 years of seabed mud, whose tiny shells record the ice on land. Its record of ice swung in time with all three cycles, at beats of about 23,000, 42,000 and 100,000 years. The 100,000-year beat was strongest, though the orbit's stretch barely changes yearly sunlight; why is still argued.

After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, James Hansen's NASA team fed its haze into a climate model and forecast, early in 1992, about half a degree Celsius of cooling for a year or two. The thermometers showed a cooling of about the size the model forecast, and the journal Science called it on target, though the model ran a little too cold. A forecast made first is a fair test, since no one can fit it to the result.

Snowy sea ice reflects about 80 to 90 percent of sunlight, open sea under a tenth. So when a warm summer melts Arctic ice back, the dark water absorbs sunlight the ice would have reflected, and that heat melts more ice. Such a feedback, like the extra water vapour warmer air holds, strengthens a change something else began.

On Ellesmere Island, in Canada's Arctic tundra, fifty-million-year-old rock holds alligators, giant tortoises and dawn redwoods. They lived there because Earth as a whole was far warmer than it is now: the early Eocene ran roughly 12 degrees Celsius hotter than before industry. In the Little Ice Age, which ended around 1850, the Thames sometimes froze hard enough for frost fairs. In 2019 Raphael Neukom's team compared ice cores, corals, lake mud and tree rings worldwide. Different regions were coldest in different centuries: the central and eastern Pacific in the 1400s, northwestern Europe and southeastern North America in the 1600s, most other places in the mid-1800s.

The IPCC, whose summaries government delegates approve line by line, drew its 2021 assessment from over fourteen thousand studies. It found about 1.1 degrees Celsius of warming since the late 1800s, judged the human influence unequivocal, and put the likely warming from doubled carbon dioxide at 2.5 to 4 degrees. The physicist Steven Koonin, once President Obama's Energy Department Under Secretary for Science, accepts the warming and a human part in it. In his 2021 book Unsettled he argued that the summary and the press overstate the certainty, building his case from the report's own technical chapters. The economist Gary Yohe and the climate scientist Benjamin Santer answered that scientists discuss those uncertainties openly.

Beside the 2009 UN climate talks in Copenhagen, Al Gore cited models he credited to the sea-ice scientist Wieslaw Maslowski: a 75 percent chance of a wholly ice-free Arctic summer in five to seven years. Maslowski said he had meant nearly ice-free; Gore's office called the figure a ballpark one from an old conversation. Satellites found ice in every one of the next seven summers, though each fell below the 1979 to 2000 average. Both halves hold: the summer ice shrinks about 12 percent a decade, and the dated forecast failed.

In 2016 Zaichun Zhu's team found a quarter to half of the planet's plant-covered land growing markedly greener, and models credited most of that to carbon dioxide feeding plants. In 2019 Chi Chen's team found that China and India, with nine percent of that land, supplied a third of the added leaf after 2000. Chen's team traced that share mainly to China's tree-planting programmes and to intensive farming in both countries.
