how-germs-were-proven.title: How Germs Were Proven
how-germs-were-proven.context_blurb:
Washing your hands before a meal rests on one idea: microbes, living things too small to see, cause many diseases. Between the 1840s and the 1880s, four doctors and a chemist proved it, one fair test at a time, against doubters with real reasons.

Most doctors then blamed disease on miasma, bad air from rot, and not foolishly: filth and sickness did go together. Many believed in spontaneous generation, life arising from lifeless matter. A fair test uses a control group, kept like the test group but for the one thing tested.

In Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two birth clinics: doctors and students ran the First, midwives the Second. Childbed fever killed mothers in the First more than twice as often. The clinics took patients by turns, a day each. Since nobody chose, neither clinic could have been sent the sicker women: by accident, a controlled trial.

In March 1847 Semmelweis's friend Jakob Kolletschka died after a student's scalpel pricked him during an autopsy, his body damaged like the dead mothers'. Semmelweis reasoned that matter from the corpse had entered through the cut, only its way in, and could cause the fever. Doctors came to the mothers straight from autopsies; midwives did none.

From May, Semmelweis had the doctors scrub their hands in chlorinated lime, and his clinic's deaths fell from over eighteen in a hundred to about one by July. His chief, Johann Klein, wanted more than counts. Semmelweis could not say what his matter was or how it did harm, because no one could yet see it. Shunned by many doctors, he died in an asylum in 1865, before germ theory explained his washing.

In London, John Snow held that cholera, which starts in the gut, is swallowed in water. In 1854 he mapped Soho's deaths around the Broad Street pump, then sought a test that could sink his idea. Had bad air been the cause, the seventy-odd brewery men by the pump, who drank only beer, would have died as often as their neighbours. None fell seriously ill; they never drank its water.

The parish took the pump's handle off on 8 September; many tellings call that the proof, but Snow did not. Fatal cases had already been falling for days before the handle came off, from 143 on the first of the month to 12 that day, partly because people had fled. A step taken while deaths are already dropping cannot show it stopped them.

In Paris, the chemist Louis Pasteur faced Félix Pouchet, spontaneous generation's defender, who held that life needs air's oxygen to arise, so sealed broth proved nothing. Pasteur stretched a flask's neck into a long, open S, like a swan's, and boiled broth in it. Air passed freely through the open tip, so the broth had the oxygen Pouchet demanded, but dust and its microbes settled on the moist glass of the bend. It stayed clear for months.

Pouchet also said the long boil had ruined the broth as food for life. Pasteur snapped one neck off short, letting dust fall straight in, and the broth soon teemed. The boil, then, had not spoiled the broth as food for microbes.

In Glasgow, the surgeon Joseph Lister watched operation wounds rot, a rot blamed on air's oxygen, and lost close to half his amputees. If the rot came instead from Pasteur's living specks in the air, Lister could leave the air alone and kill the specks where they reached each wound. Using carbolic acid from 1865, he cut amputation deaths by two thirds, though critics wanted wards with and without it compared.

The country doctor Robert Koch set out to prove that rod-shaped microbes caused anthrax. He put matter from the spleens of anthrax-killed animals into tiny cuts in mice, and all died; mice given healthy spleen blood alongside them lived. Both groups got the same cut, so the killer was not the cut but something in the sick animals' matter. The comparison could not single out the rods, so Koch grew them alone for generations in fluid from an ox's eye, and they still caused anthrax.

The first of four steps named after him demands a germ in every sick body and no healthy one. Koch found cholera's comma-shaped germ in every victim he examined, then in healthy carriers too. Koch kept the germ as the cause and judged the first step too strict: a germ can live in people without making them ill.

fair-trials-controls-and-placebos.title: Fair Trials: Controls, Blinding and Placebos
fair-trials-controls-and-placebos.context_blurb:
A sick person takes a remedy and gets better. Was it the remedy, or rest, hope, luck or his own body? A fair trial tells them apart with a comparison group, chance to decide who gets what, and blinding, which hides who got what.

In 1747, aboard the Salisbury, James Lind gave twelve scurvy-stricken sailors the same berth and food but each pair its own remedy, from cider to oranges and a lemon. Within a week one fruit-eater was back on duty; the rest lagged. Since all twelve had the same rest and food, the other pairs ruled out that rest and the ship's food alone had healed the two.

Lind also picked who got what, giving the seawater to the two sickest men. Matching groups by hand evens out only the differences a doctor thinks to check. Chance also evens out, on average, the differences no one checked. In the 1948 streptomycin trial, which Austin Bradford Hill helped design, sealed envelopes of random numbers placed each patient, so no doctor could steer the sickest.

Like the doctors of his day, Lind held that scurvy has several causes, damp air among them, seeing it as a fault of digestion rather than a shortage in the diet. Even while praising lemon juice at Haslar, the navy's hospital, he urged other remedies too, and boiled the juice into a "rob", not knowing boiling destroys its vitamin C.

A placebo is a fake treatment: a dummy pill, or a sham operation. Surgeons used to treat angina, chest pain from a heart muscle short of blood, by tying off a pair of arteries inside the chest wall. In 1959 Leonard Cobb's team gave eight patients the real operation and nine only its skin cuts, telling none which. About as many got better in each group. So the tying of the arteries added nothing to the relief, which came from hope, care or pain easing by itself.

In 1955 Henry Beecher pooled fifteen trials and claimed a dummy pill alone relieved about a third of patients. In 1997 Gunver Kienle and Helmut Kiene reread them and found no placebo effect in any. Sick people often recover anyway, so a dummy-pill group holds that too. Only patients given no pill at all, followed the same way, show what the dummy itself adds, and Beecher's trials had none.

In 2001 Peter Gøtzsche and Asbjørn Hróbjartsson pooled 114 trials that set a placebo group beside an untreated one. Against no treatment, placebos did nothing measurable to the illnesses themselves, but had small effects on what patients felt, such as pain. Their true size is still argued.

Osteoporosis is thinning of the bones, tracked by yearly hip scans. On a working medicine most women gain a little bone a year, but any one scan can read high or low by chance. Steven Cummings's team singled out women whose first-year scans showed a loss of over four percent, often only because a scan had read low. On the same medicine, 83 percent of them showed a gain in hip bone the next year. That swing back is regression to the mean.

In a Canadian trial for multiple sclerosis, a nerve disease, some patients had plasma exchange, the blood's liquid part drawn off and replaced, and others a fake. Two neurologists examined every patient at each visit, one knowing his treatment, one not; only those who knew rated plasma exchange ahead. Both judged the same patients at the same visits, so knowing the treatment had tilted the doctors' scores. Judged blind, it did no better than the fake, as John Noseworthy's team showed in 1994.

Thomas Francis's 1954 trial of Jonas Salk's polio vaccine enrolled about 1.8 million children, because paralytic polio was rare: it struck about fifty-seven in every hundred thousand given a dummy shot. A school of a thousand, half given the dummy, could expect less than a third of a case. A season with no cases there would show nothing either way, as so few cases were to be expected. The number of cases, not of children, decides what a trial can show.

Where dummy shots were used, children whose parents said no got nothing, yet caught paralytic polio at only thirty-six per hundred thousand, against fifty-seven. Where none were used, refused second-graders also fell ill more rarely than the watched grades. Families who sign up differ from those who do not: volunteers were mostly better off, and polio seemed to strike hardest where homes were cleanest.

when-results-do-not-replicate.title: When Results Do Not Replicate
when-results-do-not-replicate.context_blurb:
One exciting result is not yet knowledge: science trusts a finding once others repeat it. Early this century researchers began checking how often that happens, and found trouble that came mostly from chance and honest habits; their cure was more testing.

A result counts as significant when luck alone would rarely produce it: by custom, a false idea crosses that line about one time in twenty. In 2005 the physician John Ioannidis argued that many published findings may still be false. Picture a lab trying a hundred hunches when only one is right. About five wrong hunches slip through beside the right one, so about five in every six passes are false. Leah Jager and Jeffrey Leek later put the false share in top medical journals nearer 14 percent.

A study's power is its chance of catching a true effect as big as the one it hunts. In 2013 Katherine Button and Marcus Munafò's team put the power of a typical small neuroscience study at just 21 percent. A weak study misses most real effects while false ideas slip through at the usual rate, so flukes make up a bigger share of what passes.

In 2015 some 270 researchers led by Brian Nosek reported repeats of 100 studies from top psychology journals of 2008. Of the 97 originals with a significant result, only 35 came out significant again: about a third. Nosek's team warned that a failed repeat may miss a real effect.

In 2011 Uri Simonsohn, Leif Nelson and Joseph Simmons played twenty students a Beatles song or a control tune, and going by birth dates, the Beatles group came out younger by almost a year and a half. No song changes a birthday: the three ran the study to show that ordinary ways of handling data can make a false result look real. They added students until the result crossed the line, chose afterwards what to adjust for, and dropped a group from the write-up. The habit is now called p-hacking.

Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken showed in 2013 that even one honest test can mislead. Say a researcher looks at his scores, sees the effect is strongest among older volunteers, and tests only them. Had the scores fallen out differently, he would have tested another group, so his one test stands in for many, and its chance of passing by luck rises above one in twenty.

In 1979 the psychologist Robert Rosenthal named the file drawer problem: work that finds nothing stays in the drawer, so journals fill with successes. Neil Malhotra, Gabor Simonovits and Annie Franco later traced 221 experiments from one funded program. Of those that found nothing, nearly two thirds were never even written up by their own authors, who expected rejection or simply lost interest.

When Cornell's Daryl Bem reported in 2011 that students could sense events before they happened, Chris French, Stuart Ritchie and Richard Wiseman repeated one of his tests in three labs, with a registered plan and ample students, and found nothing. The journal that had printed Bem turned their paper away unreviewed, French said, because its editors held to a rule against printing repeats.

Peer review means experts read a paper before it is printed; they check its reasoning but see the write-up, not the raw data. The Dutch psychologist Diederik Stapel invented the data behind dozens of papers that passed review. He was first reported in late August 2011 by three young researchers he was supervising, who took their doubts to their department head. Asked to name the schools his data came from, Stapel admitted none existed.

Every real reading carries noise, a tiny random flicker that never repeats. In 2002 Princeton's Lydia Sohn saw matching noise, wiggle for wiggle, in two graphs by the Bell Labs physicist Jan Hendrik Schön, taken at very different temperatures. The match meant that both graphs came from a single set of data, used twice. A committee later found that Schön had reused whole data sets.

In a registered report, launched in 2013 by Chris Chambers at the journal Cortex, reviewers accept a study's design on paper, and the journal then prints it whatever it finds, provided the plan is kept. In 2021 Anne Scheel's team found that nearly all ordinary psychology papers in their sample, 96 percent, backed the first idea they tested, against under half of registered reports, 44 percent. The authors wrote that the gap suggests psychologists underreport negative results.

vaccines-the-science-and-the-scrutiny.title: Vaccines: The Science and the Scrutiny
vaccines-the-science-and-the-scrutiny.context_blurb:
A vaccine trains the body to know a germ before the real one arrives. That immunology is settled, and it helped end smallpox. Vaccines are also made by companies and overseen by governments, and that record has been examined in hearings, courts and studies.

A vaccine may hold a killed germ, a weakened living one or a single protein from its surface. Each carries antigens, molecular shapes that the immune system's own cells can learn to recognise. B cells that fit an antigen multiply, and many become plasma cells making antibodies against that one germ. A first dose is slow, and its antibody fades over months. Some cells from the first dose stay on as memory B cells; at a booster they quickly turn into plasma cells, so the response comes within days and is far larger.

In 1774 the Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty scratched cowpox into his wife's and sons' arms, but he never made his case public. In 1796 the country doctor Edward Jenner gave cowpox to James Phipps, then tested the boy with smallpox matter, and no disease followed. He tested others the same way and published 23 cases in 1798.

In eastern Nigeria late in 1966, the American doctor William Foege had too little vaccine for the mass campaign officials thought necessary. Guided by missionaries' radio reports, his teams vaccinated the people around each case, then the places it was likely to reach next along family and market routes. The outbreak ended within four weeks, and this ring vaccination became the worldwide campaign's method. Smallpox could be ended for good because no animal carried the virus, only people, so once no one was infected it had nowhere left to live. In 1980 it became the only human disease ever declared eradicated.

In 1955 some Cutter Laboratories lots of Salk's killed-virus polio vaccine held live virus, though they had passed their safety tests; by Paul Offit's count, about 200 children were left partly paralysed and 10 died. A congressional hearing that June laid most of the blame on too little checking by the federal Laboratory of Biologics Control, part of the National Institutes of Health. The institutes' director had set aside Bernice Eddy's 1954 report of paralysed test monkeys.

Lawsuits over the DTP shot rose from nine around 1980 to over 200 by the mid-decade, and by late 1985 only one American firm still made pertussis vaccine. The law Congress passed in 1986 made a trade: makers faced far fewer lawsuits, and families could be paid without proving that anyone was at fault. Makers stay liable for faulty manufacture or poor warnings, and a tax on each dose has funded about 5.4 billion dollars in awards.

Since 1990 the CDC and the FDA have run VAERS, which takes reports from anyone, a parent or a vaccine's maker, without first judging them. One report shows only that a problem came after the shot, and after is not because: a rash after a shot might come from a virus, a food or anything else. In 1999 fifteen reports flagged a real risk from a new vaccine, RotaShield. Yet a 2010 report from Ross Lazarus's Harvard Pilgrim Health Care project said vaccine side effects are common but underreported, with fewer than 1 in 100 reported. That figure was the project's reason for its work, not a count it made.

By 2013 the US schedule had grown from seven diseases in the early 1980s to fourteen germs. That year an Institute of Medicine committee saw no significant evidence that following it is unsafe, and credited vaccines for the decline of the diseases they prevent. But it reported that the schedule as a whole, the number, timing and order of its shots, had not been systematically studied, though each vaccine was tested before licensing and watched afterward.

In May 2025 the health department under Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who wants "gold standard science", said new vaccines would need safety trials against a placebo, a dummy shot, before approval. Steven Black, who helped lead Prevnar's baby-vaccine trial in the 1990s, said ethics ruled out a dummy shot there. Its comparison babies got a vaccine against a different disease, an experimental meningococcal shot that Black said gave them a possible benefit. Christine Stabell Benn and Martin Kulldorff argued in 2025 that few vaccines have had a double-blind placebo trial, medicine's gold standard, and proposed such trials for vaccines in use; Paul Offit called them unethical. Any trial needs the parents' informed consent.

when-the-state-decides-the-science.title: When the State Decides the Science
when-the-state-decides-the-science.context_blurb:
A scientific claim stands on evidence, not on who backs it. Last century, Stalin's government banned genetics, and American states sterilised thousands of people on the word of eugenics experts; today's rules for experiments on people grew from such harm.

Winter wheat bears grain only after a winter's cold. In the late 1920s the Soviet agronomist Trofim Lysenko wetted and chilled the seed, so wheat sown in spring headed that summer, and he claimed the change would pass to the next generation. Only one result could have shown that: seed from chilled plants, sown in spring without any chill of its own, still bearing grain. Plant biologists have since found that the chilled state is wiped clean in each new embryo, so every generation needs its own winter.

Lysenko also dismissed genes and Mendel's laws, which predict a three-to-one split of forms among a hybrid's offspring. In 1939 Ermolaeva, backed by Lysenko, published counts that she said proved the ratio false. Real counts scatter around any ratio, as a hundred coin tosses rarely land exactly fifty-fifty. In 1940 Andrey Kolmogorov, a mathematician, showed that her counts strayed from Mendel's ratio no more than chance allows, and no less: a new confirmation of Mendel's laws.

Soviet leaders wanted Lysenko's quick promises after the famine of the early 1930s, when breeding by genetics looked slow. With Stalin's approval, Lysenko's side won outright at a farm-science meeting in August 1948. Genetics was barred from teaching and research, and more than 3,000 biologists were dismissed or jailed. A directive soon ordered every stock of Drosophila fruit flies destroyed, among the creatures genetics labs most often bred to study heredity.

Lysenko denied that plants of one kind compete, so crews planting forest belts under a 1948 plan packed acorns into dense clumps, his "nests". By 1951, the ecologist Vladimir Sukachev recorded, not one nest-sown tree in the Ural lands was alive. Critics blamed the crowding, since seedlings of one kind compete hardest for the same light, water and nutrients. A fair test would have set the nests beside oaks sown singly on the same ground in the same years, so that crowding was the only difference.

His rival Nikolai Vavilov built in Leningrad the greatest crop-seed store of its day, full of landraces, the old local kinds, and the wild cousins of crops. He judged modern crops, bred alike, too uniform to resist new diseases, while old and wild kinds hold traits, such as drought resistance, that breeders can cross into new crops. In 1940 the secret police arrested him for opposing Lysenko, and in 1943 he died of starvation in prison.

In America, eugenics, the plan to breed better people by keeping the "unfit" from becoming parents, was taught in the early 1900s as science. Charles Davenport's Eugenics Record Office, founded in 1910, drew up family trees and counted poverty and "feeblemindedness" as inherited because they ran in families. But a family shares its home, food, schooling and poverty as well as its genes, so a family tree can never tell whether genes or a shared upbringing caused a trait. Davenport even sought genes for pellagra, which proved to come from a missing vitamin.

Under Virginia's 1924 sterilisation law, drafted on Harry Laughlin's model, the state colony's head, Albert Priddy, chose a young inmate, Carrie Buck, as the test case. Laughlin swore that her condition was inherited without ever meeting her: the historian Paul Lombardo found that his statement repeated what the colony's doctors had told him.

In 1927 the Supreme Court let Virginia sterilise Carrie, counting her baby Vivian as a third generation on a social worker's remark and one failed infant test. Vivian was placed on the honour roll in first grade, in April 1931; Stephen Jay Gould, who studied her school records, called her a perfectly normal, quite average student.

In 1947 three American judges at Nuremberg, trying Nazi doctors whose experiments had killed many prisoners, wrote ten rules for human experiments into their verdict. The first rule calls the voluntary consent of the person tested absolutely essential: he must choose freely, without force or fraud, and understand what he agrees to. The ninth lets the volunteer end the experiment himself if going on seems impossible to him: his own judgement is enough, with no one's leave, no reasons owed and no proof of harm. The tenth separately bids the scientist in charge halt the work if it is likely to injure, disable or kill.

the-covid-record-weighed.title: The COVID Record, Weighed
the-covid-record-weighed.context_blurb:
When COVID-19 swept the world in 2020, officials had to act fast on thin evidence, and scientists split over what to do. Studies and released records now let anyone weigh some of those choices and see where experts still disagree.

In October 2020 Harvard's Martin Kulldorff, Oxford's Sunetra Gupta and Stanford's Jay Bhattacharya put their names to the Great Barrington Declaration. They called their plan Focused Protection: shield the old and frail, who faced the greatest danger, and let the young and healthy return to normal life, schools included. It never proposed letting the virus sweep through every age alike. Critics answered in The Lancet that keeping so many people apart for long was impractical, and that spread among the young would reach everyone.

Francis Collins, who ran the National Institutes of Health, judged the plan dangerous. Four days after the signing, Collins emailed Anthony Fauci that the declaration's premises needed a quick and devastating published takedown, calling its authors "three fringe epidemiologists". A records request made the email public in 2021. In 2023 Collins called the three "very distinguished" and regretted some of his words, while holding that the plan would have cost lives.

Sweden never shut its preschools or its schools for children under sixteen that spring. Jonas Ludvigsson's team checked the records of all of Sweden's nearly two million children aged one to sixteen over those months. Not one had died of COVID-19, and 15 had needed intensive care, about one child in 130,000. The study did not measure whether children carried the virus home.

Anna Eva Hallin's team studied the reading tests of some 97,000 Swedish pupils in the first three grades and found that during the pandemic their reading was no worse than before, even among pupils from poorer homes. Even so, sickness and short closures upset teaching in about a third of Swedish schools.

Officials closed schools in 2020 as a precaution, following influenza models in which the young drive spread, while the new disease's risk to children was still unknown. When Stanford's Sean Reardon and Harvard's Thomas Kane matched local scores to time spent in remote school, they found bigger losses where districts stayed online longer, but many districts back in person lost ground too. They cautioned that remote districts may have differed in other ways too.

In January 2023 Tom Jefferson's Cochrane review of randomised trials found community mask-wearing probably made little or no difference to illnesses like flu or COVID. Its editor-in-chief, Karla Soares-Weiser, said in March that "masks don't work" was a misleading reading. The trials, she explained, tested whether urging people to wear masks slowed the spread, comparing groups urged to wear them with groups that were not. In the largest, only 42.3 percent of the mask group wore one, against 13.3 percent of the others.

The Lancet critics of October 2020 had also found no evidence yet of lasting protection after infection, when the disease was under a year old. By 2023 the COVID-19 Forecasting Team could pool sixty-five studies. Forty weeks after an infection, protection against severe illness was still high, near 90 percent, while protection against catching it again was falling, to about 36 percent for one newer form of the virus.

Three economists, Steve Hanke, Lars Jonung and Jonas Herby, pooled studies of deaths under the spring 2020 lockdowns in Europe and America. Their first estimate, in January 2022, was a fall in deaths of 0.2 percent; a revised version, later a book, raised it to 3.2 percent. Both figures set deaths under strict, legally required rules against deaths under lighter, more voluntary ones such as Sweden's, not against doing nothing. Seth Flaxman of Oxford objected that the review left out every study built on the science of how disease spreads.

Where the disease came from is still unsettled. In February 2020, 27 public-health scientists in The Lancet rejected any suggestion of an unnatural origin; about three in four new human diseases were then known to come from animals. In 2023 the FBI leaned toward a lab accident with moderate confidence, and the Energy Department agreed with low confidence, while four other agencies leaned toward animals, also with low confidence. In January 2025 the CIA, undecided in 2021 and 2023, judged a lab accident likelier but held this view with low confidence, saying both origins remain plausible.

In April 2025 Jay Bhattacharya, a declaration author, became the eighteenth director to lead the National Institutes of Health, the main US agency for medical research.
